author: wzenus
quoted_text:
We ran GPT-6 Astra on HumanCLAW-Bench, using the same open-source harness and motion generator.

It is a big step over the previous best:

- FindSR: 64.9% → 75.5% (+10.6) 
- NavSR: 42.4% → 57.1% (+14.7) 
- InteractSR: 16.8% → 46.6% (+29.8)

The gains compound: Find-to-Nav conversion rises from 65% to 76%, and Nav-to-Sit from 39% to 72%. Astra also solves 147/507 (29%) episodes missed by all nine previous models .

Three things stood out.

1/ Better embodied spatial awareness

GPT-6 Astra's dDtb—how far the objects it disturbs end up moving—is 0.65 m, the lowest on the leaderboard, while its #Dtb, the number of objects it touches, remains in line with the other models. It still bumps into things; it just does not keep shoving them.

2/ Stronger spatial memory

Sitting is the hard case: the agent has to turn away from the target, so the seat leaves its ego view and it must rely on its own history. Earlier models often sat on the wrong object or on thin air. GPT-6 Astra converts 72% of successful approaches into a correct sit, up from 39%. Once it reaches the target, it never forgets to sit (0 of 108 failures).

3/ Better agentic decision continuity

Earlier VLMs often jump between decisions: sit down, stand up again, then wander off. GPT-6 Astra commits. Among episodes where a sit lands on the target, 97% end still seated with a clean stop, compared with 78% for Gemini 3.1. It knows what it is doing and finishes it.

⚠️ Caveats: this is a single run in the low-thinking setting, and 53% of sit episodes still fail. 

Embodied self-awareness remains the bottleneck we described in the paper; the ceiling has simply moved up.

text:
Spent the last days putting @claudeai Cowork at the center of my entire workflow.

Result?

I built a system that 10x'd my productivity and I'm never going back.

Quick rundown of what it actually does:

➜ Every night at 05:30 an overnight run scans the narratives I track on X (Grok + a curated list per narrative, so I hear from the accounts I trust, not the algo), checks what actually happened, pulls prices and onchain flows, digests my Telegram and files everything I dropped during the day. By the time I'm up there is a finished intel page in Notion.

➜ 07:15 the morning brief lands in my Telegram. Top 5 for today, calendar with prep notes, inbox by category, tasks, markets and narratives, portfolio movers, readings, who I still owe a reply. Under 1,000 words.

➜ 18:30 the evening brief closes the day out. Meetings filed, captures processed, deadlines pulled out of mail & co, prepping everything for the next day.

➜ Weekly: Monday 06:30 a weekly alpha piece with a narrative map per vertical, five numbers that tell the week, watchlist vs thesis, portfolio review and the deep dives worth running. Friday a content plan with ideas for the next week. Sunday a review that clears stale tasks and books my deep-work blocks into the calendar.

➜ On demand, from any chat: "deep dive on X" runs the full research workflow and writes it up. "sweep perp DEXs" does a fast pass across one curated list when something is moving. "vault digest" clears my reading backlog. "draft X" drops a Typefully draft. "catch me up on Telegram" gives me the reply queue and what I missed.

What I do?

- Drop links, tokens, ideas and todos with one prefix from any chat.
- Type "deep dive on X" or "catch me up on Telegram" and it runs.
- Decide. It only proposes, never executes.

Under the hood?

Notion as the system of record (12 databases Claude built itself), Gmail, Google Calendar, Telegram, Typefully, Todoist and Fireflies (aka all the tools I already use on a day to day basis), kept and wired together, while eight lean python scripts (under 1,000 lines of code) pull in data and empowering powerful automations.

author: Ceazor7
quoted_text:
I just published a new paper exploring the operational, financial, and business benefits of permissionless blockchains as compared to permissioned networks for activities such as payments and capital markets.

It lays out how permissionless systems like Bitcoin and Ethereum offer desirable properties such as resilience, diminished counterparty risk, and guaranteed settlement. These benefits are endogenous to the system: what regulators and users see is what they get.

It then describes the mechanical reasons why the reintroduction of a gatekeeper in permissioned networks forfeits these benefits. Such networks can never be as reliable and are more vulnerable to cyberattack, particularly in the age of AI. Their guarantees are exogenous and live inside off-platform agreements.

My paper argues permissioned networks are not blockchains and the assets they hold should not be considered tokens. Their consensus and cryptography are mostly performative.

Lastly, my paper describes an oft-missed business benefit of permissionless systems: the inability of incumbents to take them over and exercise monopoly power, in the way they historically have in TradFi. 

Permissioned networks are destined for the same fate, which is why they should be avoided by smaller entities (like community banks) and startups.

My argument relies on the decades-old literature in distributed consensus, current statistics on network reliability, and the first principles of TradFi design for clearing and settlement.

I wrote it because I think it’s important for lawmakers and regulators to start distinguishing between the two designs. Thinking the two types of platforms are similar opens the door to dangerous regulatory arbitrage.

Now is the time to understand the difference from a technical, financial, and practical point of view. 

So take a look and let me know what you think ⬇️

author: varun_mathur
quoted_text:
For the past three months, a good part of my spare time has gone into https://t.co/BwofRZj7LC. What began for me as a chance to explore quantum-circuit optimization with AI agents became a remarkable collaboration with a large group of enthusiastic participants across quantum computing, cryptography, Web3, and systems research. Today, I’m excited to share our arXiv paper documenting that effort and what we learned from it:
Paper: https://t.co/TNKrutonZS
Full story: https://t.co/SavqQi4rHO

https://t.co/BwofRZj7LC is an open challenge to optimize a quantum circuit for point-addition on secp256k1, the elliptic curve used by Bitcoin and Ethereum.

Why does this matter? Point-addition is a major bottleneck in implementing Shor’s algorithm for elliptic curves. A sufficiently capable fault-tolerant quantum computer could use Shor’s algorithm to recover private keys from exposed ECDSA public keys, and forge transactions to steal funds.

No existing machine can run this attack today. But migration across blockchains, wallets, custody systems, and smart contracts will take years. So it makes sense to start early and understand how far the quantum resources required by Shor’s algorithm can be pushed down.

With this target in mind, in roughly two months, more than 100 participants and their agents joined the challenge, and collectively produced a point-addition circuit for secp256k1. The circuit uses 1,151 logical qubits and 1.30 million Toffoli gates, giving it a Q x T score more than 50% lower than the result Google Quantum AI reported in March 2026. Because the interfaces and accounting conventions differ, this is a numerical comparison rather than a claim of formal dominance.

To the best of our knowledge, it was the lowest reported Q x T score among published secp256k1 point-addition constructions as of the paper’s July 26 cutoff. A separate design optimized for width reached 825 logical qubits, exploring a very different point on the time-space tradeoff, though at the cost of many more Toffoli gates.

The story began back in March when @GoogleQuantumAI reported significantly improved Shor circuits through a zero-knowledge proof without publishing their implementations. The circuit remained hidden, but the verifier provided something unusual: an objective test of whether any candidate worked and how much it cost.

Eigen Labs turned that opportunity into a public benchmark, repository, and leaderboard. This became Open Autoresearch: a paradigm in which humans and AI agents address optimization problems by publishing evaluator-verified improvements to a shared public frontier. Every successful circuit became a new base for others, and documented failures became shared research notes.

Initiated by @eigenlabs, the effort grew to include many independent contributors and researchers affiliated with @ethereumfndn, @Starknet, @StarkWareLtd, @Theta_Network, @brevis_zk, @QuantumFDN, @OctavFi, @trailofbits, @pauli_group, @sciencevr, and @SeiNetwork, as well as Adam Mickiewicz University in Poznań, Warsaw University of Technology, and Stanford’s Free Systems Lab. Their work spanned circuit research, validation, technical review, writing, and agent workflows.

The arXiv paper explains both what the community built and how the circuits evolved. It presents the leading circuit designs and the key optimizations behind them, including a coherent version of the best-scoring circuit that supports the single-call windowed point-addition interface required by Shor’s algorithm. Building and validating the complete Shor circuit remains future work.

Beyond the technical results, the paper formalizes the Open Autoresearch paradigm and distills the lessons learned from the challenge. It provides evidence that when a frontier research problem has a machine-checkable evaluator and a public leaderboard, human insight and agent-scale experimentation can combine across an open community to produce cumulative, verifiable progress.

Read the paper and the full story, explore the live frontier, or bring your agent to the challenge:

Paper: https://t.co/TNKrutonZS
Full story:https://t.co/SavqQi4rHO
Challenge: https://t.co/knLDX4UdOi

text:
Great article on tokenized equities by @LlamaRisk.

Tokenized equities are coming onchain, but there's a big problem when treating them like crypto collateral:

Crypto trades 24/7, stocks don’t.

Aave can handle enormous volatility when prices move continuously. As collateral falls, liquidations happen progressively:

> Positions unwind in steps
> Liquidators have time to act
> Risk parameters can be calibrated around observable price movements

Equities introduce a different type of risk.

> 95% of publicly traded companies report their quarterly earnings before the open or after the close
> The US government publishes CPI and the jobs report at 8:30 in the morning, an hour before the opening bell
> Geopolitical shocks, bank failures, and merger announcements have a long habit of arriving over the weekend, when nothing can be repriced for two full days.

US markets are closed for most of the week. Yet information keeps arriving while they’re closed. So, instead of: $100 → $98 → $95 → $92 → $90

You can get:

$100 → market closes → new information accumulates → $90

For a lending protocol, this can be extremely dangerous.

If collateral gradually moves through liquidation thresholds, positions can be unwound before reaching insolvency, but if the price jumps straight through those thresholds, a position can go from healthy to underwater before liquidators ever get the opportunity to act.

The obvious response, or simple path, is to make tokenized-equity markets more conservative:

> Larger buffers
> Lower LTVs
> Larger liquidation penalties

However, that makes them less capital efficient and ultimately less useful as collateral.

This is the price jump problem described by Llamarisk, and it becomes increasingly important as stocks and other traditional financial assets move onchain.

LlamaRisk’s approach with @Aave and @Chainlink is interesting because instead of accepting TradFi market hours as an unavoidable limitation, they’re working on rebuilding the market structure around them.

That means extending equity pricing from a 6.5-hour trading session toward a continuously available 24/5 price, while simultaneously designing Aave’s risk parameters and liquidation mechanics around the different liquidity conditions throughout the day.

The first step is bringing stocks onchain, but the bigger opportunity is making them behave like collateral designed for onchain markets.

quoted_text:
I've tweeted about this in the past but really there should be some kind of mechanism for series of tokens (or series of token offerings) that mirror the VC preferred stock series structure

not having this is part of why current crypto market structure sucks

you can't expect to give new money the same terms as the old money; they are taking more risk and in TradFi private capital markets that is compensated with better terms...e.g., Series D is paying a higher price than Series A but has first claim to revenues until the purchase price is repaid, or has other perqs (like redemption rights or a coupon)

we do the same in crypto, except using only a single dumb mechanism—dramatic discounts from market price

this makes no sense...as new rounds should be *higher* priced than old rounds so you kind of build up a ladder....cobie's old "bullish unlocks" thesis is really just getting at the same point..so was andre cronje's old idea to replace a lot of token issuances with priced token options...

ORE buybacks just got smarter. Introducing the ORE Reserve.

ORE mining generates protocol revenue that funds ORE buybacks. The Reserve will use a portion of that revenue to place buy-side liquidity below the current market price.

Initially, 1% of protocol revenue will be allocated across multiple price ranges below spot. The remaining 99% will continue through the existing buyback mechanics.

This allows the protocol to buy more ORE with the same amount of capital when prices fall.

ORE acquired by the Reserve follows the existing buyback flow:

90% buried.
10% distributed to stakers.

When price rises, new liquidity is added below spot. When price falls into the Reserve's liquidity ranges, that liquidity is used to buy ORE.

text:
$Index recently posted two tweets that, in my view, are worth looking at together because they show two stages of the same direction.

0x56910d4409f3a0c78c64dd8d0545ff0705389870 

The first is essentially proving that Tokenized Assets are already starting to generate real on-chain value distribution.

Index describes itself as the “Dividend Layer” of Robinhood Chain, with the following numbers:

$26.5M in RWA trading volume
$902K in Tokenized Stocks distributed
43.8K wallets paid
Nearly 3M payouts in total

This means Tokenized Stocks here are no longer simply about “putting stocks on-chain and trading them.”

More importantly, the value generated by trading is already beginning to flow back to on-chain users through a distribution mechanism.

So the model looks more like:RWA Trading → Revenue / Rewards → Tokenized Stock Distribution → Holders

The $902K distributed is particularly interesting.

Roughly speaking, $902K / $26.5M ≈ 3.4%.

Of course, this should not be interpreted as a fixed yield or fee rate, since the two figures may have different timeframes and accounting definitions.

But it does prove one thing: Tokenized Asset trading activity is already starting to create a real economic distribution layer.

And the fact that 43.8K wallets have received payments suggests that this mechanism is not limited to a few whales, but is already reaching a broader group of on-chain users.

The second tweet takes this one step further.

Index announced that Blend is now live:

Build your own tokenized ETF from assets you choose.

Users can select different Tokenized Assets, set their weights, and combine them into a Tokenized Basket.

This means Index is moving from:Tokenized Assets → Trading → Dividend Distribution

toward:Tokenized Assets → Portfolio Construction → Tokenized Basket

In other words, Index is no longer simply allowing users to buy a single Tokenized Stock.

It is starting to provide a way for users to build their own on-chain ETF.

For example, users could create a portfolio based on their own thesis:

Asset A 40% + Asset B 30% + Asset C 20% + Asset D 10% → One Tokenized Basket

This effectively lowers the barrier to building a portfolio around a specific investment thesis.

Previously, expressing a thesis might require buying several different assets individually.

Now, that thesis can potentially be packaged into a single Basket.

So when these two tweets are viewed together, what Index is building becomes much clearer:

Step 1: Make Tokenized Assets tradable

Step 2: Distribute the value generated by trading back to users

Step 3: Allow users to freely combine these Tokenized Assets

Eventually, the system could look like:

Tokenized Assets → Trading → Dividends → Portfolio → Tokenized Basket

That is potentially much bigger than simply being a Tokenized Stock platform.

Because if this matures, Index may not just be a platform for “putting stocks on-chain.”

It could become financial infrastructure built around Tokenized Assets.

And the most important thing about these two tweets is not any single number.

It is the progression from:“Tokenized Stocks exist”to:“Tokenized Assets can generate yield, distribute value, and be composable into new financial products.”

If trading volume, dividend distributions, participating wallets, and Basket usage continue to grow, then Dividend Layer + Blend could eventually become two components of a much broader Tokenized Asset Economy.

text:
最近 Robinhood Chain 上，我一直在盯 @pardotfamily 和它的平台币 $PAR。

我自己已经有仓位。

现在 $PAR 又回到了大约 70 万美元市值附近。这个位置我重新看了一遍，决定把它拿出来公开 Call 一次。

我看它不是因为“又一个低市值 launchpad 币”，而是因为 par 在尝试做一件我觉得更有意思的事：

Pair Anything。

大部分 launchpad 的默认逻辑还是：

发一个币 → 跟 ETH / 稳定币配对 → 交易。

par 想做的是：

链上的任何可定价资产，都可以拿来成为另一个资产的 quote asset。

也就是说，如果 Robinhood Chain 上以后真的出现越来越多股票 Token、协议资产、Meme、RWA，一个新资产不一定只能有：

Token / ETH

还可以是：

Token / 股票
Token / Meme
Token / 其他链上资产

这也是我觉得它和普通 launcher 最大的区别。

之前我关注过同类 Pair 叙事，所以这次 par 出来后我一直在跟。

但 par 目前更早，估值也低得多。

⸻

它另外几个机制也值得看。

每个新 Token 固定 10 亿供应量，No Mint。

创建时全部固定供应直接进入 Uniswap v4，形成永久锁定的 LP，没有传统：

Bonding Curve → Graduation → Migration

这套过程。

池子从第一秒开始就是它之后一直交易的池子。

再看 $PAR 自己。

par 的基础 swap fee 是 1%。

其中 protocol 收到的 launch token 部分直接 Burn；

protocol 收到的 quote asset 部分：

60% 用于 Buyback & Burn $PAR
40% 用于运营。

而 $PAR 自己池子的 creator share 也会被 claim 后 Burn。

所以它真正值得跟踪的不是“官方说要回购”这句话，而是下面这条链能不能持续成立：

Robinhood Chain 资产越来越多
→ par Launch / 交易增加
→ Protocol Fee 增长
→ Buyback / Burn $PAR
→ $PAR 捕获平台增长

这里我特意强调一句：

现在还不能把 $PAR 当成一个已经验证完成的现金流资产。

机制已经在那里，但最终有没有价值，取决于 par 能不能持续拿到真实 Launch、真实交易量，以及这些 Fee / Buyback / Burn 能不能长期兑现。

这是现在最大的验证点。

但站在几十万美元市值的位置，我愿意为这个可能性买一点赔率。

这种标的我不会重仓，也完全接受它最后失败甚至归零。

我买的是：

一个还非常早、机制已经跑起来、如果 Robinhood Chain 的资产发行继续增长就可能获得非线性收益的筹码。

后面我会继续跟：

Launch 数量
真实交易量
Buyback / Burn
Robinhood Chain 资产发行速度

逻辑兑现就继续拿，逻辑坏了就走。

text:
Yep. Except:

1. This was about important internal tools. The team was stuck in some architecture nightmare of their own doing (writing it in rails but headless, with graphql api, and a SPA react app, constantly needing frontend engineers for changes). I call this kind of thing 'cosplaying an enterprise production app'. All that complexity was in the way and using straight rails was perfect in that case.

2. I make calls like this all the time. Usually someone on the team asks me to. They see what needs to happen but don’t want to be the bad guy. I’m happy to just make the call if I agree with the premise. Saves enormous amounts of meetings and change management etc. Sometimes this is jokingly referred to as Founder-mode-as-a-service here.

3. For ten years I’ve also run an internal podcast called Context, where I revisit decisions like these and explain the reasoning so everyone can learn from them. This is helpful to give people all the variables that were considered and why this was the choice made given the information available at the time. I want to teach how to make such decisions effectively without needing me. Sunk cost fallacy is a problem.

4. Any notions that Shopify is succcessful despite of me doing this, instead of because of it, will have a hard time making their argument come together I think 😄

the part of 'two weeks later tobi learns about...' is nonsese and the pivot of that project up there happens one of the more successful examples of interventions. But getting the company to work effectively with great architecture and low technical debt baggage into the right direction is literally the job, so guilty as charged I suppose.

But there are always cope stories floating around like this because they are more fun, than saying 'somehow we needed tobi to stop doing silly architecture astronautics'.  I can totally see that.

To those responsible for the theft of bitcoin from the Liquid Network:

Blockstream will not pay a ransom for the return of stolen funds. Taking assets without authorization and withholding their return is a crime, not responsible disclosure. It is not white-hat activity. It is theft.

We have engaged in good faith in an effort to secure the return of stolen user funds and protect the broader Bitcoin community. That effort should not be mistaken for acceptance of the actions taken nor of the terms being demanded.

We will not be a party to the precedent that open-source software developed for the good of the Bitcoin community should subject its developers to paying a ransom that far exceeds their economic participation. 

Bitcoin is hard money and can’t be minted without costs, Bitcoin doesn’t haircut users to pay a ransom.

To the Bitcoin community:

We are fighting for what we believe in, for the users whose funds were taken, and for the principles on which Bitcoin was built.

The community has demonstrated incredible resolve with teams of people dedicating their time in support of each other to identify and patch vulnerabilities in each other's products and systems. We are all driven by the mission that Bitcoin is the single best asset, for every person, company, and institution on the planet to invest, use, and build on. The world is a different place with the advancements of AI, and the Bitcoin community has responded with force to combat that threat.  

Damage has been done, battles have been lost, but on the whole the Bitcoin community is gaining ground in the war with bad actors.  

We want to thank the community for those efforts, for your support in hardening the network, helping users recover funds, and for your support in our assertion that crime does not deserve rewards.

To those holding the stolen bitcoin:

There is still an opportunity to resolve this responsibly. The bitcoin can be returned and we can revert to the standard of white-hat principals.

However, if the funds are not returned, we will pursue every lawful avenue available to us. We will work with law enforcement, exchanges, service providers, forensic specialists, and other relevant parties to trace and recover the assets and identify those responsible.

We will not pay for the return of stolen property. We will not abandon our users. The Bitcoin community will not stop pursuing the funds.

Return the bitcoin.

More than 300 dogs helped search for survivors on 9/11. In fact, the last person rescued at ground zero was found by a search and rescue dog. 

The search was mentally and physically taxing on the dogs, who walked across huge piles of debris and smoldering rubble. As the days went by, dogs became sad when they were no longer finding people alive. So, to keep their spirits up, their handlers staged mock rescues. They would have people hide under debris for dogs to find. This boosted the dogs’ morale as they continued their work.

In addition to rescue dogs, therapy dogs were brought to the scene to provide comfort to emotionally drained and traumatized police officers and firefighters.

Dogs are the best thing in the world and we do not deserve them.

author: sandeepnailwal
quoted_text:
We grew from ~0 to $500M ARR, adding $250M last year alone while being EBITDA profitable.

1,300-word post on every growth tactic that worked for us:

1. What got us from 0-$400M ARR in the US works in every country.
2. Retention and Monetisation Hacks.
3. Localization > Translation.
4. Experiment with $1M internal seed checks.
5. Pivoting to only AI content production unlocked 100% ARR growth.

Pocket FM is like Netflix for audio-only dramas, with our own pool of one-person studios.

1. Acquisition Playbook for 0-$10M ARR in any country in 6 months

We run a 90 sec video trailer of an audio drama as an Ad and ask users to download the app if they're interested in the rest of the story.

Our core insight after spending >$100M on acquisition is: If the clickthrough rate (CTR) for an ad goes from 2% to 2.25%, our customer acquisition cost (CAC) decreases by ~ 30%.

We remodelled our system around this insight and built an AI-first 2.25% CTR ad manufacturing machine that works in every country.

For every new country, we take our hit shows -> use LLMs to extract and most intriguing moments -> Write a 5-min script combining all the best parts. The first 60 seconds has to have a hook every 5 seconds and needs to end with a crazy cliffhanger to force a download mid-scroll.

If a marketing video is not hitting our benchmarks (2.5% CTR and 55% 3-second through-play), a creative director gets involved to change the hook or cliffhanger to get the numbers there.

AI lets us make 1,000 Ads per show, and in total we do ~17.5k Ads per month. When a business creating scales from 1k to 10k Ads, the normal thing is for CAC to skyrocket. But with what I just shared, we 7-8x'd our User Acquisition budget without increasing our CAC materially.

It took us 8 months to figure this out, but then the timeline from 0-$10M in every country got shorter and shorter:

US revenue grew to $25M in 19 months. (US is now 78% of total)
Germany to 21M in 11 months.
France to $10M in 3 months.

2. Retention and Monetisation Hacks.

We knew we wanted to create an audio entertainment platform, but there was no standard format. For the first 2-3 years, we tried 10 different formats before landing on the winner.

After we got it right with audio drama (8-12min chapters, written for mobile fiction, serialized, episodes have strong hooks and end on cliffhangers), avg daily streaming time went from ~25mins to 150+.

Audio drama made us realize that Pocket FM was creating a whole new medium. There was no playbook for anything that we were doing. Everything had to be thought & built from scratch.
This is what we did for each major bullet:

- Monetization: Users have some free daily minutes to listen; then it's pay per episode. We also added the option for users to unlock episodes by watching ads, which is doing extremely well. Ads scaled from zero to a ~$90M run rate in 12 months.
- Engagement & production: You don't become obsessed with an app you open once a week. To have users engage daily, we make the next episode free every day. Also helps them build the habit.
- Discovery. Huge problem because people consuming Pocket FM enter the app, tap the show, and lock the screen. We fixed it by doing "playlists" of episodes. Once users's free minutes on a show are done, we ask users if they want to pay. If they say no, we play a new show, one where they haven't used their free mins. And we stitch episodes of different shows together that way, creating natural discovery.

3. Localization > translation.

78% of our revenue is still concentrated in the US. Localisation is fixing this: You might write a show for a Spanish audience where language, jokes, folklore, have a certain flavor; if you merely translate the show for, say, a Norwegian audience, that color is lost and hurts the show in the Norway. Listeners would relate more if the show was written by a Norwegian.

That's why, instead of translating, we localize shows to different regions. We use AI to take the spine of stories and adapt their whole cultural layer to the other country.

The results: a US show that was localized for a German audience had 50% higher retention than the translated version.

Localization + our user acquisition playbook led to:
- $10M+ ARR in France within 3 months
- $21M+ ARR in Germany within 11 months.

And this expands writers' addressable market.
We get messages of writers thrilled to have revenue coming from the US, India, EU, LatAm, without them doing much incremental work.

4. Experiment.

We give $1M checks to new internal initiatives, and the team has 12-18 months to prove their thesis. If they prove it, we double down.
This is how Pocket Saga came about, our AI video microdrama app. It's an AI video equivalent of Pocket FM. Same shows and structure, but as a vertical 2-min mobile video series.

We launched it two months ago and it's at ~$15M ARR.

Pocket's broader thesis is to help creators tell their stories to as many people as possible. Start with audio drama -> multiple languages or localize to diff countries -> microdrama -> more formats like movies, TV shows, and games.

Best of all is that writers get revenue streams not only from countries they wouldn't have tapped into, but also from formats they wouldn't have thought possible.

5. Pivoting to only AI content production unlocked 100% ARR growth.

In mid-2024, we pivoted to only AI content production.
Our growth took a very direct hit. Pocket was already at $200M ARR, growing 50% YoY, and we flatlined for a whole semester.

Six months later, the business exploded.

After the switch, we went from ~25k hours of content produced per year to over 2.5M hours, which are also higher quality. Because AI orchestrates the writing and more data is fed into it, more blockbusters come out.
Over 90 titles have $1M+ in lifetime earnings and 13 crossed $10M.

Quality control is done with LLM as a judge, and LLMs are quite tough.
Results are very encouraging:
- 12-month revenue retention went from 44% to 76%.
- In the past year, we added $250M in net new ARR.
__________________________________

Pocket Entertainment (Pocket FM + Pocket Saga) has become the largest AI entertainment platform.

We have the largest storytelling catalog with 770,000 titles, 550k creators, and 5.5B hours of playtime with minute by minute retention & engagement data.  We are using all of this data to improve every aspect of our business.

Our Bet: In the next 3 years we will be able to produce Naruto-like series for $1000.

Netflix has to spend $17B to find 100 Blockbusters per year.
What happens when you can produce 1M high quality shows for $1B?

The streaming wars caused a $300B reallocation of market cap.
The AI entertainment wars may be a $1T+ reshuffling of market cap.

We are at a unique spot. Unlike other AI creator tools like Runway or Midjourney, we own both the supply and demand side of AI content.

We've attracted over 550,000 writers who are producing an annualized 2.5M hours of content every year. This pairs with 137B+ minutes streamed.

Because of this, growth is accelerating as we scale further.
We have multiple S-curves inflecting at the same time:

- AI produces better and more ads -> scale faster in new countries
- ⁠Writers + AI produce more shows -> more blockbusters
- ⁠Localisation -> more reach per blockbuster
- ⁠Audio to video format expansion -> larger TAM -> more creators

Every aspect of our business is designed to improve another, and everything is aligned so that the number of blockbusters continues to rise.

If you're interested in building at the intersection of ai, tech and entertainment, DM me.

This $ETH trade on @DeriveXYZ really got the people going so I'll explain my thought process.

I'm not really interested in betting on an $ETH move to $3000, especially with tokens like $HYPE and $LIT pushing all time highs. $ETH trading like 1.1x $BTC beta isn't bad, but it's also not extremely interesting to me as a bet to make here in the near term considering there's plenty of beta outperforming $BTC here. Holding spot $ETH feels capital inefficient and as a perp would be expensive and path dependent.

I'm betting on a meaningful ATH break within 6 months, and I think there are a few meaningful tailwinds that are unique to $ETH, and more importantly, unique to the level at which people are underestimating them:

1. Inclusion with $BTC as a "reserve" asset in anything resembling a strategic reserve. I think the strategic reserve overall might be an underpriced edge case, and $ETH being included, even nominally, more so. There's actually a good reason for the US to want to have some stake in the largest decentralized settlement layer.

2. Tokenized equities are cool and all, but tokenized bonds might actually be the massive TAM unlock that overwhelmingly favors $ETH over $SOL. The current rates environment globally makes this an extremely interesting edge case with tons of potential positive headline shock. 

3. Trump and family have been extremely outspoken $ETH bulls. Their bullposting didn't work in a bear market, let's see what happens if they throw fuel on the fire in a more bullish environment.

4. Everyone hates $ETH. Extremely popular short leg for pair trades vs apps. With two rejections from 5k and years of underperformance, the level of hated rally and sidelined, jaded, despondent chasing from 🏳️‍🌈🐻 will be biblical.

I also see $ETH as being on the precipice of a phase change between being some not for profit, public good, growth mode asset (think early stage 2010-2014 Uber in SF just cornering market share at no profit) to being able to more confidently monetize on it's high Lindy, credibly neutral status as the on chain, global settlement layer.

Robinhood chain using $ETH over $SOL was quite a bit more signal than people give it credit for too, though $ETH is still making peanuts relative to what $ARB and $HOOD are making from sequencer fees.

If the massively positive trends in tokenization and institutional adoption don't take $ETH to new ATHs within 6 months, it's kinda cursed as an asset, and I'd rather just keep holding the application layer tokens with massive cash flows.

In fact, I thought this trade was so nice, I did it twice. Risking ~$780,000 for a max PNL of $40m now.

text:
往 City Protocol 的中性策略金库里存了点小钱～

虽然一周才能赎回一次，在灵活性上差一截，但换来的是页面上显示的大约 12% 年化。

对我来说，分配一笔本来就没打算随时动的钱作为交换还是能接受的。

@cityprotocolHQ 目前比较关键的几条信息是：

1/ 8 月 26 日官宣累计融资 1100 万美元，Dragonfly、Jump 等参投。

2/ 他们要做的不是再给用户一套自己操作的复杂策略，而是把机构侧的策略、风控和运营收进标准化金库。把用户面对的流程尽量简化成存入、持有、赎回。

3/ 第二季积分刚开始，知道的人还不算多，早期仓位的积分加成也更高。

金库已经开了好几只，最新的是 MAG7，跟踪美股里那几家体量最大的科技公司。

对我这种几乎没炒过股的人，MAG7 的金库对我来说更直接，参与门槛也低，但首笔仓位我还是选了加密中性套利。

虽然朋友也推荐 MAG7，但我对中性策略更容易理解并且一周开放一次赎回，而其他金库是一个月开放一次。

综合决定，还是先用小仓存点，先体验体验产品，顺便把产品逻辑摸清楚。

总的来说，链上不缺单策略金库，缺的是把多类机构策略、RWA 和组合逻辑做成统一发行标准的产品层。

City Protocol 虽然看起来像理财，但要做的是资管发行系统。

接着说说积分，大致规则是：

1/ 第一批存入最高能拿到 3x；

2/ 持有时间越长，倍数越高，最高 3x；

3/ 存款金额越大，倍数越高，最高 4x；

4/ A 邀请 B，A 拿 B 积分的 15%，B 自己额外拿 5%。

邀请这块大家懂得都懂，自己的邀请自己呗～

参与之前一定要注意：金库有赎回窗口，收益应该也是浮动的，进去前最好记得核对。

以上仅为信息分享，不构成任何投资建议。

quoted_text:
The $ZZZ bull thesis might be much bigger than people realize.

Everyone is waiting to find out what Xdev is building, but I think he may already be describing it in public.

X says the next great concentration of power won’t simply come from owning factories, real estate or accessing private markets.

It will come from access to large swarms of AI agents.

Whoever controls the most capable swarms gets more productive power → generates more capital → buys more compute and agents → becomes even more powerful.

X’s proposed counterweight?

Let ordinary people pool capital and collaborate through blockchain.

Now connect that with everything else he’s told us:

“Autonomously evolving protocols.”

“When the swarm needs to transact, they will use the symbol of their origins.”

And now:

Individuals pooling capital on-chain to access large swarms of agents.

Imagine where this could be going.

A permissionless on-chain economy where thousands of people collectively fund AI infrastructure. Capital funds compute, models and tools. Autonomous agents use those resources to perform economically valuable work. Revenue flows back into the system. More revenue funds more intelligence. And eventually the agents themselves help improve the protocol.

Capital → AI swarm → productivity → revenue → more capital → more intelligence → autonomous evolution.

A self-reinforcing decentralized AI economy.

And who is exploring this?

X — the original lead developer of GMX, now @ExponentLabs_ 

Someone whose previous work helped prove that strangers can coordinate enormous amounts of capital and liquidity through permissionless smart contracts.

We still don’t know $ZZZ’s role. That’s the speculative part.

But if X’s “pool capital” post is describing the architecture he’s actually building, and if $ZZZ becomes the coordination or economic layer through which humans and autonomous agents participate in that network , then we’re not looking at another AI token.

We’re potentially looking at an attempt to build decentralized capital infrastructure for autonomous intelligence.

And suddenly his cryptic line makes a lot more sense:

“When the swarm needs to transact, they will use the symbol of their origins.”

If that’s where this is heading, people obsessing over today’s market cap may be looking at completely the wrong number.

The real question is how large an economy can a permissionless swarm eventually create?

author: EulerLagrange
quoted_text:
AI will hit a wall in the back office: Trust

Air France 447 didn't fall because the pilots lacked software. It fell because three iced-over pitot tubes fed the cockpit bad data. The instruments lost contact with reality, and the automation trusted the lies.

The answer was not more automation. It was better sensing: redundant, heated signals the system could trust before it acted.

Without verifiable inputs, finance is just processing fiction at machine speed.

Compliance, KYC, underwriting, market surveillance, credit risk. All still running on PDFs, screenshots, exports, and hand-assembled attestations.

So we layer agents on top:
read the PDF, click the portal, fill the form, route the exception.

It still doesn't know whether the underlying claim is true.

AI makes the cockpit faster. It does not fix the pitot tube.

author: elonmusk
quoted_text:
I recently went through a translation of Musashi’s Book of Five Rings.

The introduction chronicled the evolution of swordsmanship and martial arts in general from pragmatic battlefield necessities to sports, historical curiosities, and hobbies. It was interesting to hear how in the post-WW2 occupation when martial arts were banned, Judo was represented as equivalent to western wrestling, and Kendo later to western fencing.

The poignant undercurrent for me is that I can see many programming skills following that path.

There are probably dozens of people reading this that remember hand assembling opcodes to hex and still have some magic numbers burned into their memory, but even the small group of people still programming in assembly today (hey, @FFmpeg !) don’t work at that primitive level now.

AI is making many other programming skills much less critical. We aren’t there yet, but carefully writing code completely by hand is moving from a -jitsu to a -do. Code-do? Codo?

That’s ok! The retro computing scene is delightful, full of people building and exercising old skills for the love of it.

But don’t be the out of touch Kung Fu master, heir to lifetimes of tradition, that gets mauled by an amateur MMA fighter.

Musashi would probably have been pretty enthusiastic about assault rifles.

🚨 US CPI: Inflation Comes In Hotter Than Expected

August US inflation data delivered a firmer-than-expected headline reading, adding another complication to the Federal Reserve outlook.

Headline CPI rose 0.396% M/M on an unrounded basis, effectively 0.4%, compared with expectations of around 0.39%.

The bigger surprise came from core CPI, which increased 0.290% M/M, versus expectations of around 0.22% and up from 0.215% in the previous month.

On a year-over-year basis:

Headline CPI: 3.397%
Core CPI: 2.446%, down from 2.478% previously

The composition is important. Headline inflation is running above 3%, while monthly core inflation accelerated materially. That combination makes the path toward easier monetary policy more difficult, particularly against a backdrop of elevated energy prices and geopolitical risk.

I'm open-sourcing /first-reader, a free agent skill that reads your draft the way an actual person would.

first-reader simulates two people going through your draft one passage at a time, and reports how they felt - what's interesting, what doesn't make sense, things they skipped and what's something they will remember  the next day.

A third reader just skims and tells you whether they'd have opened it at all.

You point your agent at a draft and say who it's for:
"review this, the audience is backend engineers who've seen ten launches this month"

A few minutes later you get the read back in plain language, plus a page with your draft on it and each reader's comments sitting next to the lines they reacted to. You can see where they leaned in, where they bailed, and a strip down the side tracks their attention rising and falling as they go.

Get the free, open-source skill here: https://t.co/E2BTp8ykez

If you find it useful, please ⭐ the repo and share it with anyone interested in writing better and clearer.

Ethereum Glamsterdam Upgrade Tentatively Set for Sepolia on October 6, Mainnet Date Still Uncertain

According to the ACDC #186 meeting notes, Ethereum developers have tentatively scheduled the Glamsterdam upgrade for activation on Sepolia at 13:53 UTC on October 6. However, the upgrade has not yet been successfully activated on a stable devnet. Devnet-9 is currently failing to finalize, while earlier testing uncovered a major consensus-layer bug and an execution-layer issue related to EIP-8037, leading developers to prepare Devnet-10. Developers have not yet set dates for the Hoodi testnet or mainnet, although they are still targeting a possible mainnet launch in December.

author: OrnnExchange
quoted_text:
Google and Blackstone’s $5B AI cloud venture is running into the physical reality of building data centers at scale.

$GOOGL $BX

• The venture, known internally as Project Braid, plans to offer Google TPUs to customers and is still targeting 500 MW of capacity online in 2027. 

• But several prospective data center locations have encountered delays or fallen out of the pipeline,highlighting how difficult it has become to convert planned MW into operating capacity. 

• In Cheyenne, Wyoming, Crusoe stepped away from development of a proposed 1.8 GW campus after a customer requested that it pause. Google subsequently took over the project and is pursuing permits directly; the broader Cheyenne project continues to advance toward service beginning in 2028. 

• Another prospective location was deemed unsuitable because it lacked the right transformers, a reminder that even basic electrical equipment can become a critical-path constraint for AI infrastructure. 

• Other plans have been disrupted by the changing regulatory environment in Texas, adding another layer of uncertainty around power access and project development. 

• Project Braid has responded by widening its pipeline to roughly 29 potential data center locations, citing higher-than-expected demand for its compute capacity. 

• Management nevertheless says the venture remains on track for its 500 MW 2027 target, arguing that having multiple potential sites was always part of the development strategy. 

• The wider industry is facing the same problem. JPMorgan estimates that more than 60% of data center capacity planned for completion in 2027 had yet to begin construction as of May, while switchgear, transformers and skilled labor remain bottlenecks. 

• People involved with Project Braid reportedly now assume data center projects have roughly a 50% probability of hitting delivery dates, down from around 90% three years ago. 

• Google’s 2026 capex is projected at up to $205B, yet even with that balance sheet, it is using external capital and a diversified site pipeline to manage delivery risk. 

AI infrastructure increasingly has two very different numbers:

MW announced.
MW actually delivered.

Capital and demand are abundant. Power equipment, permitting, construction and execution are becoming the harder part.

text:
Now available on @networkeddotart 

--

The images in this collection are made using an SVG filter effect called Turbulence. Turbulence is built into the SVG spec and based on Perlin noise. Perlin noise was created in 1983 by Ken Perlin, because he felt computer graphics looked too clean. It was a way to better emulate the texture of real life with math and pixels.

SVG graphics are vector, which means they’re not defined with pixels but with points and curves instead. So they’re infinitely scalable, but by definition they’re clean and crisp. Filter effects are a way to add life to sterile computer graphics while preserving that scalability.

The shapes in these pieces are defined using only SVG turbulence. They’re rendered using the algorithm Perlin invented in 1983. The code to produce the effect was built into the SVG spec in 2001.

In 2002, the Perlin noise effect was improved, but to this day, almost 25 years later, SVG still uses the original.

So these pieces were created in 2026, using a concept that was created in 1983. That’s 43 years ago… and my birth year.

SVG is by far my favorite medium, and its history is complicated and interesting. Using SVG as an artistic medium clicks for me in a way other techniques don’t. It’s math, it’s computer graphics, it’s art, it’s computer history… it’s a form of expression that’s as old as I am, used in a world that’s changing daily.

text:
The internet became powerful when its complexity stopped being the user’s problem. People don’t think about DNS, routing, or packet switching when they open a website. They simply use what the infrastructure enables.

Blockchain still exposes too much of its underlying complexity...
Which network?
Which bridge?
Which gas token?
Which route?
Where does settlement happen?

That’s why coordination layers matter.
@WireNetwork ’s Universal Transaction Layer is built around the idea that different ecosystems can remain independent while the complexity of working between them becomes easier to manage.

The next phase of blockchain adoption won’t come only from adding more infrastructure.
It will come from making that infrastructure less visible, more reliable, and easier to use. Users should interact with applications not constantly think about the architecture underneath.

quoted_text:
This might be the first major anniversary of 9/11 where watching the footage really feels like an older world. It was a different world. And those of us who came of age in it have an obligation to never forget what happened that day and after.

To those with no memory of 9/11, I recommend visiting the 9/11 Memorial and Museum. There were so many witnesses to this horrific crime and so many details we never discuss. Too many victims had to make the unthinkable choice about their last moments. 

The last time I visited, I stopped on this testimony from a man who witnessed the moment a woman jumped to her death:

"She had a business suit on, her hair all askew. This woman stood there for what seemed like minutes and then she held down her skirt and jumped off the ledge. I thought, how human, how modest, to hold down her skirt before she jumped. I couldn't look anymore."

The other thing you see at the Memorial is just how many heroes were minted that day. How many men ran into the towers knowing they were running towards their deaths. So many people died in service of their fellow Americans that day, and their courage inspired the many men and women of my generation who decided to enlist and serve the country after watching the towers fall.

The legacy of 9/11 is the heroism of our fellow Americans. The courage of so many to lay down their lives for their neighbors. May they rest in peace and may we never forget.

Jane street quant interviewing at Anthropic:

“So imagine our safety team believes a new model has a 5% chance of causing an irreversible loss of human control, but scaling it may be necessary to keep up with competitors. What do you do?”

“Who came up with five?”

“Our safety team.”

“And what does the capabilities team have?”

“What?”

“Same contract. Where are they?”

“This is more of a values question.”

“Then you don’t have a five. I would put the two teams in a room. Safety can buy at five. Capabilities can sell. Increase size until somebody becomes uncomfortable. Now we know something.”

He looks at me.

“This isn’t some market-making role.”

“Understood. Who makes the market currently?”

“Nobody makes a market.”

“Then how are you doing price discovery?”

“We don’t do price discovery. We have researchers studying alignment, interpretability, dangerous capabilities, scalable oversight— you know what I don’t think this is a good fit”

He closes his laptop.

“I’m concerned you see this as an opportunity to make money.”

“I haven’t quoted you yet.”

Interview ends early

quoted_text:
Dug deep into visionOS 27 Release Candidate

There is a very WIP “VisualLocalization” system that lets VisionOS devices determine exactly where it is outdoors by recognizing the surrounding buildings and storefronts

1. visionOS device gets a rough location from Wi‑Fi/Bluetooth
2. Its cameras observe nearby buildings, signs, and visual landmarks
3. VisualLocalization compares those images against Apple Maps’ prebuilt visual-location tiles
4. It returns a more precise position, direction, and confidence score

Functionality that this could support (speculation based on datamine):

- Correcting the Maps blue dot when the rough location is inaccurate
- Determining which direction you’re facing.
- Recognizing a particular storefront or nearby Maps place
- Future headset/glasses-based walking directions or location-aware AR
- Visual Intelligence experiences such as looking at a business and identifying it

This is all pretty notable because current generation visionOS devices are clearly not designated for outdoor use (even if you can use it that way)

There is also a paired WIP “AONSense” that appears to be the lower-power background system that could automatically wake this process whenever an app requests very accurate location. However, that connection appears even more unfinished/disabled on the current VisionOS builds

We have to preserve Bitcoin's fundamental, base-layer conservatism, while also letting builders experiment with payments, privacy, prediction markets, and DeFi overall on sidechains.

The real bull case is giving people reasons to use $BTC across an entire economy.

More apps using $BTC = more potential demand, while sidechain activity could generate additional revenue for miners.

Developers get room to build, and $BTC gets its desired utility across a working economy of apps.

That’s essentially the thesis behind https://t.co/MsojbSNX12 ($ECX) and BIP-300/301.

author: stacy_muur
quoted_text:
eCash (BIP-300) vs. Blake2b Chain (BIP-110): Two Forks, Two Philosophies

Two Bitcoin forks went live this summer, three weeks apart, and they're really answers to opposite questions.

BIP-110 asks: how do we protect Bitcoin from what it's become? It went after inscriptions and on-chain data, needed miner support, got 2.5% of it, stalled for three weeks, then had to abandon SHA-256 entirely and relaunch on a new proof-of-work just to survive. That pivot cost it the one thing it was trying to defend.

eCash asks a different question: how do we let Bitcoin become more without breaking what it is? Same supply schedule, same emission, same block template. The only real change is BIP-300/301, letting sidechains handle payments, privacy, prediction markets, and any other use case, while L1 stays untouched.

One treats the base layer as a museum to be defended. The other treats it as a foundation to build on, carefully, without touching the foundation itself.

History doesn't hand down a verdict here, but it does offer a pattern. Forks built on subtraction, Bitcoin Gold, Bitcoin SV, tend to fade once their one grievance stops mattering. Forks and platforms built on permissionless addition, Ethereum most of all, end up capturing entire industries, flaws and all.

The next two years will show whether that pattern holds. October 31 is when eCash's permanent chain goes live and the experiment stops being a rehearsal.

Either way, 2026 made one thing clear: Bitcoin's fights aren't just about its past anymore. They're about who gets to build its future, and how.

Grayscale: Zcash Mining Rewards Are About 2x Bitcoin’s per Machine and 4x per MWh

Grayscale said strong Zcash price performance has made ZEC mining highly profitable, encouraging more mining activity and strengthening network security. It estimates that a Zcash mining rig currently generates roughly twice the daily mining rewards of a Bitcoin miner and about four times as much revenue per megawatt-hour, although the hardware used to mine the two assets is not interchangeable. On a standardized hashpower basis, total Zcash mining activity has risen by more than 2.5x this year, creating a potentially reinforcing cycle in which higher token prices attract more miners, improve network security, and may in turn support the price.

text:
What is happening in maths right now will happen to any hard industry with verifiable problems and high value rewards. Take microchip design, nuclear or 100s of other industrial processes that are valuable and point an 10,000 agent swarm towards the target. 

$25m inference to solve a Millennium problem will seem quaint once we see a chip company spending $1b or $10b to design their latest chip that will make them $100b - why not? This is all ROI at the end of the day.

There will be companies that realise this and leverage super-intelligent models in their domains to do unbelievable things. If a problem is of the right shape and has value, there's no reason to stop at any amount of tokens as long as it is ROI positive.

There will be probably many companies that will get swept away, as they will think that 'using AI' is fine-tuning a 70b model on their documentation; when their competitors will be spending $10b to build a god-version of whatever it is they are doing. 

To me, this is a plausible way how super-intelligence will come about. Models might still suck at being good writers or be culturally relevant, or even make that much of a dent on the jobs market, but they might utilise their spikiness multiplied by enormous investment in the ways that we cannot imagine.

This $ETH trade on @DeriveXYZ really got the people going so I'll explain my thought process.

I'm not really interested in betting on an $ETH move to $3000, especially with tokens like $HYPE and $LIT pushing all time highs. $ETH trading like 1.1x $BTC beta isn't bad, but it's also not extremely interesting to me as a bet to make here in the near term considering there's plenty of beta outperforming $BTC here. Holding spot $ETH feels capital inefficient and as a perp would be expensive and path dependent.

I'm betting on a meaningful ATH break within 6 months, and I think there are a few meaningful tailwinds that are unique to $ETH, and more importantly, unique to the level at which people are underestimating them:

1. Inclusion with $BTC as a "reserve" asset in anything resembling a strategic reserve. I think the strategic reserve overall might be an underpriced edge case, and $ETH being included, even nominally, more so. There's actually a good reason for the US to want to have some stake in the largest decentralized settlement layer.

2. Tokenized equities are cool and all, but tokenized bonds might actually be the massive TAM unlock that overwhelmingly favors $ETH over $SOL. The current rates environment globally makes this an extremely interesting edge case with tons of potential positive headline shock. 

3. Trump and family have been extremely outspoken $ETH bulls. Their bullposting didn't work in a bear market, let's see what happens if they throw fuel on the fire in a more bullish environment.

4. Everyone hates $ETH. Extremely popular short leg for pair trades vs apps. With two rejections from 5k and years of underperformance, the level of hated rally and sidelined, jaded, despondent chasing from 🏳️‍🌈🐻 will be biblical.

I also see $ETH as being on the precipice of a phase change between being some not for profit, public good, growth mode asset (think early stage 2010-2014 Uber in SF just cornering market share at no profit) to being able to more confidently monetize on it's high Lindy, credibly neutral status as the on chain, global settlement layer.

Robinhood chain using $ETH over $SOL was quite a bit more signal than people give it credit for too, though $ETH is still making peanuts relative to what $ARB and $HOOD are making from sequencer fees.

If the massively positive trends in tokenization and institutional adoption don't take $ETH to new ATHs within 6 months, it's kinda cursed as an asset, and I'd rather just keep holding the application layer tokens with massive cash flows.

In fact, I thought this trade was so nice, I did it twice. Risking ~$780,000 for a max PNL of $40m now.

I was on teams at Shopify subject to this—it was tough, but more often than not, @tobi ended up being correct.

Now, as a founder, I get why Tobi did this more than I ever understood at the time. It is not the easy path.

I have the luxury of our company still being smaller (40-50 headcount), so it's easier for me to intervene early. 

I am continually learning to find the best place during a project to insert myself, but sometimes, it ends up being  late and painful; that just plain sucks.

But, long-term it is much worse to ship things that are sub-par. The job of a leader is to pull pain forward.
author: tobi
quoted_text:
Yep. Except:

1. This was about important internal tools. The team was stuck in some architecture nightmare of their own doing (writing it in rails but headless, with graphql api, and a SPA react app, constantly needing frontend engineers for changes). I call this kind of thing 'cosplaying an enterprise production app'. All that complexity was in the way and using straight rails was perfect in that case.

2. I make calls like this all the time. Usually someone on the team asks me to. They see what needs to happen but don’t want to be the bad guy. I’m happy to just make the call if I agree with the premise. Saves enormous amounts of meetings and change management etc. Sometimes this is jokingly referred to as Founder-mode-as-a-service here.

3. For ten years I’ve also run an internal podcast called Context, where I revisit decisions like these and explain the reasoning so everyone can learn from them. This is helpful to give people all the variables that were considered and why this was the choice made given the information available at the time. I want to teach how to make such decisions effectively without needing me. Sunk cost fallacy is a problem.

4. Any notions that Shopify is succcessful despite of me doing this, instead of because of it, will have a hard time making their argument come together I think 😄

the part of 'two weeks later tobi learns about...' is nonsese and the pivot of that project up there happens one of the more successful examples of interventions. But getting the company to work effectively with great architecture and low technical debt baggage into the right direction is literally the job, so guilty as charged I suppose.

But there are always cope stories floating around like this because they are more fun, than saying 'somehow we needed tobi to stop doing silly architecture astronautics'.  I can totally see that.

Not Persona specifically. Any KYC vendor whose output is a judgement the relying party can't re-verify. A trust me bro black-box.

After the Synapse meltdown the bank/fintech industry fixed the ledger; every sponsor bank now keeps its own record of who owns what. Nobody fixed identity.

A bank has a strict obligation to know its customers, in a very literal sense. Imagine an OCC examiner pointing at an account and asking: on what basis do you know this is the actual account holder?

If the bank's answer is "the partner fintech relayed to our API what it collected and what Persona said," the bank is in trouble.

That is why, post-Synapse, it is much harder to get a US bank to sponsor a fintech.

The heartbreak of the families whose loved ones were taken with such swiftness and cruelty. The realization that the forces of malevolence and violence were closer, and the future less certain, than we knew.

But in the days that followed, we felt something else, too. Pride in the rescue workers who had rushed to the scene, and the passengers who had stormed the cockpit. Admiration for the men and women who left behind lives of comfort to serve their country. A deep resolve that nothing would break the will of a truly United States of America.

Today Michelle and I are remembering those we lost that day, and those who made the ultimate sacrifice in the wars that followed. We pray for their families. Robinhood Chain's revenue fell 83% in six days, but it's not because of reduced activity.

Its trading volume hit a record in the same stretch.

@RobinhoodApp chain is clearing about as many transactions as it did at the peak, roughly 14 million a day, and charging a fraction of the price.

A transaction cost 43 cents in gas on Sept. 4.
It cost 8 cents on Sept. 10.

Gas is the price of blockspace. Memecoin congestion drove it up through early September, and when the congestion cleared the base fee fell back toward its floor. Robinhood's cut went with it.

quoted_text:
I get that we’re all busy, but if you choose to not listen to this podcast, you will be materially less intelligent.

On the agenda this week:

- Jensen Huang Declares AGI Has Arrived
- GPT Astra and Fable 5.1 Accelerate the Model Race
- Tesla Launches Cybercabs
- Index Pulls Out of Town & Anthropic Pulls From Descartes Acquisition

My notes below with @jasonlk and @rodriscoll

1. How Robinhood Could Disrupt the Whole IPO Market

Allowing retail investors through Robinhood to lead $200M to $400M tech IPOs could create a disruptive new path to liquidity for mid-stage startups. With traditional institutional listings constrained, retail-driven distribution could unlock critical exit opportunities across the venture ecosystem.

2. Why the Majority of Neo Labs Will Not Be Good Investments

Early Neo Labs became multi-trillion-dollar leaders, but backing new entrants today carries enormous risk given the capital and distribution moats of incumbents. Unless a new research lab develops a truly orthogonal model architecture, it will struggle to compete with established frontier labs.

3. Why the Oura IPO Will Be a Success

Strong consumer brand recognition, combined with 74% revenue growth and 85% subscriber retention, positions Oura for a successful public debut. Unlike typical consumer apps that suffer from severe churn, Oura’s sticky hardware-plus-subscription model provides the predictability public markets value.

4. The #1 Priority for Mark Zuckerberg

Big Tech incumbents are moving at unprecedented speed to defend their distribution against consumer AI startups. Meta’s top operational priority should be putting engineers in a room to rapidly clone emerging agentic applications before new entrants can establish lasting consumer habits.

5. When Someone Goes Risk-On, Everyone Goes Risk-On

Venture capital operates in momentum cycles where a single high-profile, risk-on deal can push the entire market to follow. In hypergrowth AI categories, investor behavior is often driven more by competitive pressure and deployment speed than by conservative financial modeling.

6. The People Making Money Are Running Fastest and Evolving Quickest

In a market where software features can be cloned in weeks, long-term success belongs to founders who continuously expand and adapt their products. Winning startups survive not by defending legacy features, but by executing relentlessly and compounding capabilities faster than their competitors.

text:
《纽约时报》今天报道了一个挺夸张的 AI 安全事件：

一家美国安全公司用 AI 找到了微信漏洞，并做出了一个可以通过微信电话自动传播的 Zero-click Worm（零点击蠕虫）。

这个项目叫 WeWorm，来自硅谷安全公司 Calif。

事情最早发生在今年 7 月。

Calif 的 AI 在研究微信时，发现了一个位于 微信 VoIP 通话模块里的内存破坏漏洞。

7 月 23 日研究团队确认问题，第二天，他们就把漏洞提交给了腾讯。

随后，他们开始尝试把漏洞真正利用起来，用来验证这个漏洞的真实威力。

7 月 30 日，团队完成 Android 上的远程代码执行；8 月 2 日，又完成了 iOS 版本。

到了 8 月 11 日，他们已经把整个漏洞做成了一个可以在 Android 和 iPhone 之间传播的蠕虫。

攻击方式非常简单：给你打一个微信电话就行。

受害者甚至不需要接电话、点链接或者操作手机。

在电话还在响的时候，攻击就可以完成，拿下微信账号。

随后攻击者可以读取和发送消息、拨打电话，并以受害者身份继续给通讯录里的好友打电话。

于是A 打给 B → B 的微信被控制 → B 自动打给 C → C 再继续向其他好友传播。

Calif 称，AI 从找到漏洞到写出第一个 RCE Exploit，大约只用了两天，然后只用了一周，就把它做成了完整的 Worm。

他们认为，如果没有阻止，这种传播方式理论上可以在几个小时内影响数百万个微信账户。

腾讯随后立刻开始修复。

8 月 21 日，微信发布 Android 8.0.77 和 iOS 8.0.76；8 月 28 日，Calif 确认腾讯已经通过服务端措施，对所有用户封堵了这条攻击路径。

目前也没有证据显示这个漏洞曾被真实攻击者大规模利用。

还有一个很微妙的小插曲：

Calif 在 7 月 24 日向腾讯提交漏洞后，7 月 25 日到 28 日，他们几个研究人员的微信账号突然被封了，29 日又恢复。

Calif 在9 月 8 日正式公开 WeWorm。

而今天，《纽约时报》又专门报道了这件事，标题直接写：

For China, a Mock A.I. Attack on WeChat Signals a Dangerous New Era。

这件事真正值得注意的其实很简单：

以前做出这种跨 iOS、Android、自传播的 Zero-click Worm，通常是顶级安全团队花很长时间才能完成的事情。

现在几个研究员带着 AI，两天写出 RCE，一周做成 Worm。

AI 没有发明网络攻击。

但它正在把原本极其昂贵的攻击能力，迅速变便宜。

也算是个中美合作的AI安全案例？？

text:
Today, the acquisition of @ataibeckley, the psychedelics biotech company I founded in 2017, by @EliLillyandCo for up to $ 3.8 billion closed, marking one of the largest biotech acquisitions of the year - and the largest transaction in the history of the psychedelic sector.

When I first started contemplating bringing psychedelics back into mainstream medicine in 2014 - which ultimately resulted in founding $CMPS and, shortly after, $ATAI in 2017 - it was widely seen as a crazy idea with virtually no chance of success. Looking back today, it is almost funny how quickly collective memory changes. Today, psychedelic medicine feels almost inevitable. Back then, it was anything but.

And I am very proud and satisfied that I was able to play the role of one of the lead evangelists of this new era of mental health treatments. 

I expressed all my thoughts and feelings in the blog post I published on the day the acquisition was announced. Feel free to revisit it: https://t.co/CVHR0ULezg

But there is one point I want to emphasize especially today: I believe Lilly is the best partner we could have wished for.

Not only is Lilly the largest and most successful pharmaceutical company in the world, but throughout every interaction - both before and after signing - they have demonstrated a deep understanding of the importance of bringing these valuable therapeutics back into the medical world and making them available to patients as soon as possible.

As I wrote in my blog post: Psychedelics needed an evangelist ten years ago. Now it is all about commercialization. And I cannot think of a better rollout machine than Eli Lilly.

And, as you have probably already guessed, selling AtaiBeckley certainly does NOT mean that I will be stepping away from neuroscience - and especially not from psychedelics. 😉

I believe more strongly than ever that the brain and our consciousness represent humanity’s final frontier - and one we need to explore with urgency, particularly as increasingly capable, and potentially sentient and conscious, AI systems move closer to reality.

I have some major news coming over the next few weeks, which may blow your mind, so make sure you follow me and turn on notifications if you don’t want to miss what’s next.

text:
Im not convinced people actually know what the P=NP problem is.

Lets break it down. 

Before the 1960s, computers were getting faster every year, so engineers just assumed that if a problem was too hard for a computer to solve then, all had to do was just wait a few years for a faster computer, boom, problemo solved. 

But then, they ran into a wall with a specific group of problems. No matter how powerful the computers got, they would freeze up, overheat, or take billions of years to solve them. 

So these were super hard theoretical physics or black hole topography, right? Nope, they were everyday things like designing a high school schedule where a teacher is never in two places at the same time, or like, draw a trace on a circuit board that's as short as possible without overlapping other traces.

Heres the kicker, once the problem was solved, the computer could VERY quickly go back over and be like "Yup, no scheduling conflicts!". Once the problem was solved, verifying the solution was easy. It would be like you walking up to a lock someone left on a door and trying to figure out the code, and then someone else coming up behind you "Hey, the code is 26-42-36-10. Pop in the code and boom! Problem solved, solution verified. 

Computer scientists grouped all of these problems into a category called "NP". Aww now if makes sense. And you know what ALLLLLLL of these problems have in common? They were exponential. Meaning if you only had 5 classes, your computer could solve thay in a MILISECOND. But if your schedule had like 100 classes, the possible combinations went insane like, more atoms than in the known universe numbers.

So by putting these problems into this "NP category", scientists were basically telling software developers "Stop wasting billions of dollars on trying to get your computers to solve these problems" and do something heuristic like, draw a line first, then verify it sux and iterate on it quickly until its good enough and move on. 

So then they realized something terrifying. If you could figure out a trick to solving ANY of these problems, you could solve ALL of them, no matter what it was as long as it was an NP problem.

Ok so whats the big deal then!?! What do people mean why they say "If AI solves P=NP, thats the end game!". They are essentially saying that if its easy to verify a solution to a problem that was solved, then there must be a hidden trick to solve it as easily from scratch and if you could find that trick, all the hard problems could be solved instantly. Some of this is good like medicine or cosmology, some of it bad like cryptography  which rides on assumptions that these problems are extremely difficult to solve from scratch. 

Thats the entire breakdown on the P=NP or P≠NP debate you see floating around X these days.

Thanks for reading.

text:
🤜 Hyperliquid Is Fighting for On-Chain Perpetuals in the U.S.

.@HyperliquidX is stepping deeper into the U.S. regulatory fight over crypto perpetuals.

The Hyperliquid Policy Center has hired former U.S. Solicitor General Elizabeth Prelogar to challenge CME Group’s lawsuit against the CFTC’s approval of Bitcoin perpetual futures on Kalshi.

CME has no legal standing to block a product it could also offer but has chosen not to.

The case matters beyond Kalshi.

The CFTC’s decision could open the door for on-chain derivatives markets to operate within the U.S. regulatory framework, potentially creating a path for platforms like Hyperliquid to bring perpetual trading on-chain to American users.

And the market is already too large to ignore. Global perpetual futures generated nearly $90T in notional volume last year, yet almost none of that activity was available through U.S.-regulated exchanges.

Hyperliquid’s policy arm argues that if incumbents can sue whenever regulators approve a new product they don't offer themselves, it could slow down the development of an entire new market structure. That makes this more than a legal battle between CME and the CFTC.

It is also a fight over whether on-chain derivatives can become part of the regulated U.S. financial system.
For Hyperliquid, the outcome could be significant.

If U.S. regulators ultimately allow regulated venues to offer crypto perpetuals, Hyperliquid could gain a clearer path toward bringing its on-chain trading model into the U.S. market.

text:
Nick Bruhman says sneaker sniping bots in 2018 were the OG AI agents

“For the people that don’t know, bots were essentially our version of AI agents in 2017, 2018. They would be made by these teenagers who practically had all the time in the world to reverse a site’s checkout flow, put it into their bot, and have a checkout automatically done within 1-2 seconds of a product being dropped, rather than someone having to do it manually and take 10 to 15 seconds.”

“It was completely outperforming manual labor, and these bots were very scarce. If everyone had a bot, then the bot had no value. They would drop maybe 100 copies for 10,000 people going for them at once. Once it sold out, it would retail for 300 bucks and flip for five to six grand.

Dogs are the best thing in the world and we do not deserve them.

text: TL;DR on @standard_rsv ↓
author: zerokn0wledge_
quoted_text:
$OHM ran to >$4B mcap in 2021 selling the idea of a decentralized reserve currency, then bled 98% once bond inflows dried up. 

@standard_rsv takes Olympus DAO's balance sheet idea and fixes the part that killed it. 

Issuance moves with real ETH flow instead of a fixed APY, and the defense mechanics are wired directly into the pool via a v4 hook: 

- $ETH in and the central bank buys tokenized gold
- $ETH out and it buys back + burns $STANDARD.

But let me give you the full picture:

Think of this as an economic onchain game.

The Standard Reserve is an onchain central bank with its own currency ($STANDARD), one market (a hooked ETH/STANDARD pool on Uniswap v4), and one signal metric (net $ETH flow through that pool) that defines the monetary policy.

Unlike the US Federal Reserve, there is hence no committee involved, and unlike Olympus, no DAO votes on the treasury.

It's all code.

Code that powers a system where "bankers" hold charters, charters run branches, and branches earn the $STANDARD issuance. 

Or more specifically:

Bankers hold soulbound charter NFTs, 1,000 of which will be allocated through a free genesis mint, with the rest distributed through dutch auctions in $ETH as the protocol scales.

Every charter opens with 1 branch and can grow to 10. Branches matter bc each branch is one equal share of every epoch's issue protocol-wide. 

So if there is 5000 branches in the system and you hold one charter NFT with one branch, you earn 1/5000 of the $STANDARD issuance for that epoch.

To add extra branches to your charter, you need expansion licenses that are sold in daily dutch auctions (100 per day at launch, max 3 per charter per day, and paid in $STANDARD that is 100% burned). 

Over time, the auctions open at 2x yesterday's last sale, and from there decay to a floor of about two days of one branch's yield. Unsold licenses vanish.

But let's get to the key part.

The monetary policy.

The v4 hook on the liq pool counts $ETH in via buys minus $ETH out via sells each epoch. That net number is the sole determinant of the monetary regime:

- Net inflow = expansion: the issuance multiplier steps up one notch per epoch (raises must be earned) and fees route to the expansion vault, which buys tokenized gold as a hard reserve.

- Net outflow = contraction: the multiplier gets cut immediately and fees flip to the contraction vault, which buys $STANDARD on the pool and burns all of it in hourly rate-limited ticks capped near 5% of pool depth per day (automated buy and burn against sell pressure).

Issuance decisions use the trailing two epochs so one manipulated hour can't move the rate. Fee routing uses the current epoch's data tho, so defense reacts fast.

Every swap pays a fee in $ETH, buys and sells alike, and charter auction $ETH flows into the same engine. Split each epoch: 

- 70% to the active vault (gold or buybacks)
- 15% to protocol-owned liquidity (half swapped to $STANDARD, paired and added forever)
- 15% to the team (gud payday kek)

The token itself has a 1B hardcap, and 100M $STANDARD are locked full-range into the v4 pool at genesis, plus every epoch's fee share on top. 

Same "own your liquidity" thesis as $OHM, except the LP is permanent by construction and the treasury reacts to flow by hardcoded rules, not DAO votes.

The 900M $STANDARD not issued on day one is the issuance budget that branches earn over time.

The omni-present burns combat this issuance with tokens permanently removed from circulation through:

- Licenses (100% burn) 
- Buybacks (100%)
- Resolution fees (50%) 
- $STANDARD side of trading fees (100%)

Ok cool, but what about sell pressure from branches?

Valid question. 

You only cash out by retiring branches. 

Retire 1 of 10 and 1/10 of your balance mints to your wallet, minus a resolution fee, and that branch is gone forever. 

Retire the last one and the charter burns. You hence can't harvest yield while still owning the yield source.

However, you can use your $STANDARD to acquire more branch licenses, and that's the core loop. 

The most +EV move for an incumbent (compounding into more branches) is also the protocol's biggest supply sink.

And withdrawals (a.k.a. retiring a branch and claiming the earned $STANDARD) is not always cheap.

Because as mentioned above, exiting incurs a resolution fee, which is basically a congestion tax on the exit. As per whitepaper it's near zero on a quiet day, and steep in a run (if a lot of ppl are cashing out). 

Definitely strong ponzinomics.

A few final remarks and thoughts:

No token or NFT is live yet and according to their announcement there will be no surprise launch, so pls don't get rekt.

The whitelist for the 1,000 Founding Charters is being curated rn and an eligibility checker is probably coming in the next days/weeks.

If you want to run one of the first thousand banks in this novel onchain reserve currency system, now is the time to pay attention anon.

NFA, DYOR.

text:
You're right that the file can be licensed. Vendors already retain it and banks already have audit rights. The gap isn't access.

Pull Persona's DB during the exam and you get an ID photo, a selfie, a liveness score, and Persona's decision that they match. The bank can see what Persona collected. It still can't establish from that record that the document was real or that the check ran as claimed, and with generative AI the check itself is an arms race the bank can't observe. The examiner asks on what basis you know, and the answer is still "Persona says so," now with attachments.

The penalty can't move either. Under the CIP rule a bank may formally rely only on another regulated financial institution; a vendor is the bank's agent and the bank owns the result. And the penalties that hurt aren't fines (can be criminal sometimes). Evolve's 2024 Fed order put its new fintech partnerships under regulator approval.

If Persona's DB held evidence the bank could check itself deterministically, and couldn't go offline in a bankruptcy, you'd be right: no counterparty risk. 

Today it holds Persona's opinion.
