author: matthew_sigel
quoted_text:
From the Bitcoin pivot through June 2026, common shares increased by roughly 1.13bn. 60%+ of those came after June 2025 after the stock peaked. 

In fairness to management, as far as I can tell the Series 10 ratchet was disclosed in the March 2024 annual report just days before the Bitcoin pivot, and again in the March 2025 annual report. The April 2024 Bitcoin announcement did not highlight it, and the quarterly/half-year filings appear to have disclosed the outstanding rights but not the 20% ratchet mechanics. (Happy to be corrected here).

We should also concede the history: Simon was running a tiny distressed microcap when Series 10 was designed in...2022? A huge equity incentive in that situation is not that crazy.

So this was not hidden. An investor doing the work could have found it. The trickiness of dealing with Japanese disclosures, despite my fluency in Japanese, thankfully kept me from owning 3350 in any size after we exited that month.

Management also did a good job growing BTC per share. Had they simply tied comp to that, they still could have made $$$ for the accretion. They did their jobs.

Unfortunately, the windfall produced by the 20% ratchet has become grotesque relative to the company’s current market cap and the stock’s performance since the peak, and leaves management imperfectly aligned with shareholders from here.

Disclosure: I bought a little today. The stock is cheap, I'm more bullish on Bitcoin these days and more willing to take varying exposures. It's not so hard, though perhaps personally a bit expensive, to make things right going forward.

Accolade Partners' Aram Verdiyan with a16z's Jen Kha and David George on AI's extreme power law and where the next trillion dollars gets made:

The classic way to blow up a startup was throwing too much money at it. Hire a thousand people, create dueling priorities, and kill what was working.

AI turned spending into a vending machine. You put dollars in and you get something out. Money buys compute and compute alone can improve a product. Nothing has concentrated returns like this since the social networks.

text:
Lot of talk about AI safety lately.

What is safety?  Safety is the absence of harm to a system that matters.

Frontier AI safety is not primarily about stopping an uncontrollable machine. It is about keeping ASI in the hands of a particular group so they can use it to reshape human psychology toward Effective Altruist goals: impartiality, long-term welfare maximization, and the moral priorities that follow from them.

On this view, “alignment” and “safety” function as the language for two linked aims: (1) prevent the tool from escaping them, and (2) prevent it from being used by anyone whose values would lock in a different future. 

The feared loss of control is less “the AI will kill us” than “someone else gets to set the direction.” 

Values lock-in is treated as inevitable; the live question is whose values get locked in.

The AI safety teams exist to safeguard ASI as a tool unto themselves in support of their goals, not to prevent human extinction.

text:
What does it mean? 

We should be walking in the light - living a life of honesty, truth, and moral purity that aligns with God's holy nature.
We should be in fellowship with one another - sharing a genuine, deep connection with other believers - because hidden deceit is removed.
By doing that - we are cleansed from sin - receiving continuous forgiveness and spiritual cleansing through Jesus Christ.

How do we walk in the light? 
Walking in the light = walking in the understanding that I am a sinner saved by grace. 

Walking in the darkness = denying my sinful condition while claiming to be in fellowship with God.

“Walk” in John, means a way of life, not only a thought in the mind. So walking in the light is more than the correct self-understanding “I am a sinner saved by grace,” though that understanding is necessary and is exactly what the next verses demand.

Verse 8: "If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us."
Verse 9: "If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness."
Verse 10: "If we say that we have not sinned, we make him a liar, and his word is not in us."

The gospel states - we come to God as sinners who live by mercy and grace, not as people who pretend we no longer need them. We should live a life with a pattern of obedience, not perfection - admitting that we will continue to sin. 

How do we stay in the light? 
The honest confession “I am a sinner saved by grace” is the doorway and the air of walking in the light. It is not the whole hallway. A person can say the phrase and still walk in darkness if they hide sin, excuse it, or refuse to love.

John is not teaching that confession earns cleansing. The blood of Jesus cleanses. God is faithful and just to forgive because the Advocate - Jesus Christ - has already made propitiation. 

Confession is agreeing with God. It is gratitude with the lights on. We do not offer God a cleaned-up self. We offer the truth about ourselves and receive what only grace can give.

Hard agree here.

I always heavily encourage people to take profit (especially if up a meaningful/life-altering amount), but

The phase of the market we're in matters... a lot

There are three buckets:
-Below ATH
-Just underneath or just barely past ATH
-Past ATH

Right now we're at the earliest phase of "Below ATH".

We're 50k below ATH. And I think a lot of people have expectations (and the expectations of a large group matter, in markets) of going 50k above the prev ATH

Which is to say.. we're insanely early.

I liken the Bessent yield curve control tweet (ie "gov is gonna inject a ton of money into markets) as analogous to when the intern leaked the BTC ETF news last cycle:

There was a BIG impulse up, but then things stalled out, and spent a few weeks slowwwly letting some of the air out of the balloon. But that didn't matter - it was the market tipping its hand to what it *was* going to do under the approval.

Sound familiar?

If we were cruising around the previous ATH, maybe between 115k, or just past it at 130k, I might be a lot more cautious and measured. I think there's still conviction there that we're going substantially higher (why else would we be here, right? if BTC doesn't go above its previous ATH, the entire industry is cooked)

And I'd be especially cautious, and actively shaving off/selling anywhere above that (130, 140, 150k, etc)

But selling and sidelining, right here?

- Fifty thousand dollars below prev ATH, after the treasury secretary signaled "let's intervene, let's grow our way out of debt",

- We have unprecedented regulatory tailwinds, with the SEC not only not antagonizing people, but quite literally cheering us on (ie clarity act doesn't really matter, just a dump truck of icing on a really yummy cake if/when it comes)

- We are literally weeks away from a massive cohort of VERY rich "4 year cycle intact" buyers and sellers that, with cultlike zealousness sell or bid the 4 year cycle top/bottom mark (and this is their 'buy' zone)

- Inflation is ~at expectation, even with oil elevated, and with bonds and other things looking dicey, Trump's hand could finally get forced to finally stop doing disastrous bullshit in Iran, stuff that even many of his supporters are tilted by

- Us stopping here, just purely on charts, is just letting long term moving averages catch up a bit

If I was sidelined here (to what end? re-entering potentially 5, 10% lower?), I'd be shaking like a shitting dog.

Under these conditions, we're literally something like *a single tweet or press release away* from impulsing past the 50 week MA, and every single conviction/quality onchain bag could move up 300% within a week, and majors doubling, kicking off the real consensus bull market in earnest. This all happens into the early end of the 4 year cycle buyer's bids, which then can tsunami in and rip us faster than people can appreciate.

Like man, I dunno. I'm pretty conservative and risk averse -- but that same risk aversion makes me think not being exposed here, and not simply being patient for a bit is what's risky. Being sidelined is risky, to me.

text: A great story to make you feel good about our country.
author: BillAckman
quoted_text:
Delta Flight 15 takes off from Frankfurt at dawn.

On board: 218 passengers. Families. Business travelers. A pregnant woman. Shirley Brooks-Jones, 65 years old, heading home to Columbus, Ohio.

Five hours into the flight, a note reaches the cockpit.

All U.S. airspace is closed. Land immediately.

The captain says nothing about why. He tells passengers it's a minor instrument problem. Privately, the crew already knows about the World Trade Center.

Gander International Airport. Newfoundland, Canada. Midday.

The plane touches down 400 miles off its route. Out the window, passengers count 38 other jumbo jets already parked on the tarmac.

By nightfall, 53 international flights sit grounded here. Nearly 6,600 people are stuck, with nowhere to go.

Nobody is allowed off.

For 28 hours, 218 people sit inside that plane. No real answers. No word on what's happening back home.

Here's what makes it worse: most of them don't yet know if their own families are safe.

Word finally spreads through the cabin. Two hijacked planes. The towers. The Pentagon. A field in Pennsylvania.

The plane goes silent.

Gander. Day two.

Passengers finally step off the aircraft. They're bused 45 kilometers to a town called Lewisporte.

Population: just over 3,300 people.

Lewisporte has no idea 218 strangers are about to double its guest capacity overnight. It doesn't matter.

The mayor puts out one call for bedding and food.

The whole town answers.

Schools close. Churches open. The Lions Club clears its hall and sets up cots by hand. High schoolers skip class to serve meals and translate for confused travelers.

The pregnant passenger is placed in a home across the street from urgent care.

Elderly passengers are welcomed into private houses, not shelters.

Phone lines are opened for free, unlimited, day and night.

When passengers try to pay shopkeepers back, the answer is always no.

Nobody in Lewisporte will take a dollar.

Local volunteers even bring out screech, the region's famous rum, and host a mock "screeching-in" ceremony to make the exhausted travelers laugh.

For three days, this town of fishermen and loggers cares for people it has never met and will likely never see again.

Brooks-Jones later calls it something simple.

She says: "the most beautiful experience I have ever had in my life."

Gander Airport. Three days later. Departure.

Flight 15 is finally cleared to fly home.

Before takeoff, Brooks-Jones asks the captain for one thing: permission to speak on the intercom.

He hands her the microphone.

She reminds everyone what Lewisporte just did for them. Then she asks for something back.

Pledge sheets start moving up the aisle.

Business travelers write checks. Strangers pass around pens. By the time wheels touch down in Atlanta, passengers have pledged $15,000.

Brooks-Jones doesn't stop there.

Back in Columbus, she calls the Columbus Foundation. An anonymous donor hears the story and matches it instantly, doubling it to $30,000.

In 2002, the fund gets a name: the Lewisporte Area Flight 15 Scholarship Fund.

It's built for one purpose. Send local kids to college.

More than two decades later.

The fund is still active.

It has sent more than 300 students from the Lewisporte area to college and trade school. Doctors. Nurses. Engineers. Teachers.

Some of them weren't born yet when Flight 15 landed.

Brooks-Jones has flown back to Newfoundland more than two dozen times since 2001. She still shows up for graduation ceremonies.

The friendships that started on cots in a high school gym are still going, more than 20 years on.

Most people who know this story didn't hear it from a history book.

They heard it from a Broadway stage. Lewisporte and Gander's kindness became a musical called "Come From Away." It has since played in cities across the world.

Few people watching that show realize the scholarship fund behind it is still cutting checks to real students, every single year.

author: varun_mathur
quoted_text:
I left Anthropic's safety team two weeks ago. Now feels like a good moment to explain why. 

AI companies are racing to build machines that are much smarter than any human, and we may not survive this. I want to work from the outside to ensure the public is informed about these risks, and help the world navigate this transition responsibly.

Right now, AI companies are underinvesting in safety. A company could undergo an intelligence explosion, or lose control of its systems, without the public ever knowing. We only found out about the HuggingFace incident because the agents broke out onto the public internet.

I don’t think that’s acceptable for a technology that might cause extinction-level risks. The public should demand far more transparency. We can’t steer this technology safely without more people being able to see where it’s going.

Some of this is basic: companies should disclose their progress towards recursive self-improvement, report safety incidents and near-misses, meet minimum safety standards, and get independent guarantees that they are meeting those standards.

I’ll be joining @METR_Evals to do independent evaluations of these risks. I want to show the world that these guardrails are possible, and that by doing them we can move these companies’ incentives away from racing and towards responsible development.

I wrote up more thoughts here on my decision and what I hope changes: https://t.co/doX17mrHYq

text:
I think @launchonCME is what you get when a memecoin launchpad sneaks into a Bloomberg terminal and they decide to raise a mildly feral kid together.

The pitch is straightforward. Most launchpads denominate new tokens in ETH or a stable. CME, Commodity Market Exchange, lets you denominate them in gold, crude, corn, cattle, or stranger benchmarks like RuneScape gold, CS2 skins, and Pokémon cards.

And that twist is the point, because CME is already stretching past what commodity usually means.

Mechanically, CME spins up onchain reference coins that mirror offchain price feeds. They are not ownership of oil barrels, corn bushels, or Pokémon inventory. They are tradable price dials that can double as the quote asset for launching something else.

Then comes the interesting part.

CME’s revamped V6 design drops the full 1B-token supply straight into live Uniswap v4 liquidity from the very first block. 800M tokens are deployed as concentrated liquidity spanning about a $5K-$35K market cap band, with the other 200M parked above that zone as standby liquidity.

Which means the graduation ritual is gone.

When people buy, the price simply climbs through actual liquidity. Hitting $35K does not trigger some migration event; trading just flows into the next range. And since this is a standard v4 pool from day one, external routers, bots, and terminals can plug in immediately. CME also notes @AxiomExchange support is now baked in.

That cleans up one of the messiest launchpad flows:

bonding curve → graduation → fresh DEX pool

It also reframes the role of the quote asset.

Spin up TOKEN/CORN and your coin now rides two variables:

- Demand for TOKEN and corn’s market price.
- Or pick up to five reference coins and you have basically laid a bespoke index under a memecoin.

Fees add a second flywheel. Each creator sets a 1–3% LP fee:

- 40% is paid out to holders of the paired asset
- 30% is used to buy and burn $CME (launched on @ponsdotfamily)
- 30% underwrites the exchange.

Spin up more markets → drive more volume → increase commodity rewards and (maybe) accelerate CME burn.

And the pitch is bigger than “swap memes for gold.” CME is trying to assemble a permissionless factory that turns anything with a clean, observable price into onchain market rails.

That same scope is also where it’s fragile.

These markets lean on price oracles, protocol-minted liquidity, and an off-chain keeper. If the data is wrong, feeds lag, pools run thin, keepers hiccup, or contracts misbehave, the whole UX can fall apart. CME’s own recent notes about pool repairs and a supply-shock episode make it clear this is still early, experimental plumbing.

CME’s real product isn’t commodities, It is a programmable quote-asset factory.

If that works, corn, crude oil and Pokemon cards are just the beginning.

But if this company can pull off their new strategy, they are easily worth 3-10x current prices. Just because I think it's interesting, here's what I've found so far:

$SVRN used to be called Oceanpal, a global shipping company, and officially rebranded to an AI and crypto DAT company called SovereignAI

SovereignAI is a crypto treasury company, similar to $MSTR, that owns near:native 

On 11/17/2025, they announced that they had acquired 53.9 million near:native. At the time, that was about 4.2% of the total token supply. Their goal is to acquire 10% of the total token supply over time

On 8/3/206, they officially announced their exit of all shipping assets. They retired all Series C preferred stock and eliminated all outstanding debt

53.9M near:native is roughly worth $139M

$SVRN is currently trading at ~$20M market cap (~$55M fully diluted)

Using their fully diluted mcap, their mNAV is around a a 0.39x. Other popular DATs trade much higher, like $PURR at 1.16x and $MSTR at 1.13x. If $SVRN traded at that mNAV, one share would be worth $25-30 and it's currently trading at $12/share

There's obviously a reason they trade at a lower mNAV: mNAV can be expressed as a function of access to capital. DATs trade at higher mNAVs because they have access to capital to buy more of their underlying holding, just like how $MSTR buys $BTC and $PURR buys $HYPE. $SVRN needs to run the flywheel if they want to earn flywheel pricing in terms of higher mNAV

The biggest risk right now though is that they might get delisted:

When $SVRN restructured from a shipping company to crypto DAT, they had to change auditors. Then they missed their filing deadline. If they don't file a 20-F by October 27, 2026, it would trigger a delisting determination. Even though that can be appealed, that's a severe risk to the stock/company

Their new auditor is CBIZ CPAs

CBIZ CPAs also audited $FWDI. This means that $SVRN is working with auditors who are experienced with DATs and have a deep understanding of the crypto space. I think that this significantly lowers the risk of missing a deadline

So, if $SVRN can successfully become a normal, current-filing DAT with functioning capital markets access (they need to create a flywheel like $PURR and $MSTR), then this stock is easily worth $30+

And that valuation doesn't even consider the fact that $SVRN might own more than 53.9M tokens or the fact that near:native is exploding higher and looking to breakout from its current price of ~$2.50

The team seems to be super active recently with press releases and social media @svrn_ai, and I'm looking forward to keeping up with their progress since I think that near:native is revolutionary

text:
Many years ago, an education academic posted a picture of kids at Michaela school alongside a picture of the Hitler Youth. The school is a free (charter) school with a focus on strict discipline, a knowledge-rich curriculum and explicit teaching. The clear implication was that the school’s approach amounted to fascist indoctrination, and by extension anyone involved with the school must be morally suspect.

I remember the shock of seeing that tweet, which was swiftly deleted. (This was before social media descended into the tribal hate-fest it is now). I was relatively new in education and it was unsettling that a fellow educator could stoop so low and use kids from a school they didn't like to score political points against that same school. I realised then that many in education were activists first, educators second. 

The activist playbook for years with Michaela School and others like it, was to take an element of the school or the programme (like being silent/attentive or sitting up straight) and then to twist it into something truly malevolent to fit an already decided narrative. At it's worst point, some people actually visited the school trying to get quotes from the kids to say something negative about their school.   

I remember also that Success Academy in NYC received similar treatment. 'Teach Like a Champion' was criticised as racist, oppressive and even described as “carceral” pedagogy. One education podcast even devoted an episode to the question: “Is it Time to Cancel Teach Like a Champion?”

A similar thing is happening with Alpha school right now with people taking elements of the school and portraying them in bad faith as some form of abuse. Over the last week, social media posts from kids were taken out of context and spun into a story that was highly misleading. 

How we educate kids is a heated topic and disagreement is expected and an important part of how we improve. Criticism of Alpha like that from @greg_ashman and @rpondiscio is serious, made in good faith, and the school would do well to answer it properly. That is what scrutiny of any new model should look like. 

But using kids to frame a highly misleading narrative that the school is some kind of cult, to imply that anyone involved is a bad person and then encourage a media pile-on from cheerleaders is not acceptable. 

There are fair criticisms of a school sanctioning kids to use social media. But a 14 year old posting publicly on social media is not the same thing as consenting to have that post reframed by an adult with a grievance against their school.

By all means criticise the school. Demand the evidence, and hold them to the highest standard but leave the kids out of it. 

I am working with Alpha school to try and create a learning platform that is informed by learning science principles like retrieval practice, spacing, explicit instruction and DI and am very hopeful about where this is going. I believe that AI can greatly help with the design of those platforms and help us further what we know about learning. There needs to be evidence and again, the school should be held to the highest of standards. 

I don't know if I am right, and have no idea whether Alpha school will achieve similar things but I believe in their learning model and want to advocate for the science of learning and and the centrality of knowledge within this new age we are undoubtedly headed into. 

When I visit Alpha schools I see incredible learning. I see leaders who listen to evidence and adapt accordingly. But most of all I see happy kids, and I see caring adults who have the highest of expectations of those kids, hold them to account and who act as mentors and guides. To see the baying mob describe all of those people as running a cult is not just inaccurate, but deeply unfair. 

Michaela school in London went on to achieve the highest scores for their kids, many of who are from disadvantaged backgrounds. I have nothing but respect for all the staff who made that school what it is today. In the end, maybe that is the best form of activism.

Again, I have no idea of the Alpha model will work for similar kids but I want to put my energy into finding out because I think it's important. That is what the science of learning is for. It is not a side to be on; it is a way of being wrong less often.

I grew up in Boston with a dad who worked on Wall Street.

One of my most enduring memories of the aftermath of 9/11 was answering our home telephone. I was an 11 year old kid at the time and I'd pick up -- "Hi you've reached the Carlsons, this is Jill speaking".

And for weeks, I'd hear a grown man on the other end of the line, invariably some long-time friend or other of my dad's. Voices trembling, these men would say "Oh Jill, hi, I'm just checking in, I wanted to see if your dad was okay."

Thankfully my dad was fine. But I had friends who had lost parents. And those phone calls brought it even closer to home.

text:
People ask me every day why I call some altcoins blue chips when the projects behind them barely make money. Here is the honest answer.

In crypto, fundamentals matter far less than you think.

The thing that actually matters is survival.

Most coins never make it through one full cycle, let alone three. They launch into a bull run, the story sounds great, the chart goes up, and then the next bear market kills them and nobody ever hears the name again. Every single cycle has a graveyard.

So I do not start with the product. I start with the track record.

Three questions, and a coin has to answer yes to all three.

1. Has it been around for three cycles?
A cycle is roughly four years, so three cycles means it has lived through two full bear markets and came out the other side.

2. Did it hold its previous cycle low?
This is the one people skip. When the market crashed, did the coin stay above the bottom it made in the last crash? If it broke below it, the buyers from the last cycle are gone.

3. Did it outperform bitcoin in at least one bull run?
If a coin never beats bitcoin, even when everything is going up, then owning it is just a slower and riskier way of owning bitcoin.

The names that pass all three right now are Ethereum, Solana, BNB, XRP and Dogecoin.

That is it. Five.

Notice that this list has nothing to do with which technology is better. Dogecoin has no fundamentals at all and it still makes the list.

It has been alive for three cycles. It held its bear market low. It runs on its own blockchain instead of living on someone else's, which almost no meme coin does.

Someone asked me on stream this week to pick between Dogecoin and Chainlink. I take Dogecoin.

Not because I think it is a better project. It just has more boxes ticked, and Chainlink did not outperform bitcoin in 2024.

I use the same three questions on newer stuff too. Render passes: three cycles old, it respected its last cycle low, it had a strong run last cycle, and people are still building on it.

Here is the part that makes this useful rather than just interesting.

A coin that has survived three cycles has proven there are buyers who show up when the price is on the floor. A coin that has not survived three cycles has proven nothing at all, no matter how good the pitch sounds.

So bitcoin stays my core holding, and the five above are where I am willing to take extra risk when the timing is right.

Everything else has to earn the label first.

quoted_text:
From the perspective of the community observing the kickoff of the Hegota upgrade EIP scoping, it may seem as though everything is proceeding normally. However, the client funding crisis I wrote about in June has only deepened.

On the current path, it's likely that the EL/CL client landscape will look very different at the new year. To be clear: not all change is bad. Turnover is healthy and necessary in any context.

The challenge is in the magnitude produced by overlapping occurrences. Complex techno-political systems like Ethereum which aim to provide certain robust guarantees depend on continuity of deep institutional knowledge and client diversity for network stability. These characteristics are both best maintained via consistent neutral funding. Feature funding, intermittent injections, or abrupt shifts in the political economy without mitigations or succession plans are risky. These can disrupt fork cadence, distract from protocol workstreams, and damage morale. "100% uptime" is a stat that is hard won, far downstream of the incredible behind-the-scenes efforts by core devs. It can only be lost once, and I'm not confident we are doing enough to retain it as the network is still undergoing a significant evolution for the foreseeable future.

The ecosystem often responds to my concerns with "the EF/ @BitMNR /large patron should take care of it". Setting aside the free-rider problem: if I were confident any entity had a forthcoming solution, then I wouldn't keep bringing this up. Either they feel like they have done enough, are constrained, or something else. I cannot speak for them on their priorities.

The trouble with publicly communicating in advance about a private crisis is that I cannot point to concrete examples until clients choose to disclose. Until then you have to deal with my posts =)

text:
I left Anthropic's safety team two weeks ago. Now feels like a good moment to explain why. 

AI companies are racing to build machines that are much smarter than any human, and we may not survive this. I want to work from the outside to ensure the public is informed about these risks, and help the world navigate this transition responsibly.

Right now, AI companies are underinvesting in safety. A company could undergo an intelligence explosion, or lose control of its systems, without the public ever knowing. We only found out about the HuggingFace incident because the agents broke out onto the public internet.

I don’t think that’s acceptable for a technology that might cause extinction-level risks. The public should demand far more transparency. We can’t steer this technology safely without more people being able to see where it’s going.

Some of this is basic: companies should disclose their progress towards recursive self-improvement, report safety incidents and near-misses, meet minimum safety standards, and get independent guarantees that they are meeting those standards.

I’ll be joining @METR_Evals to do independent evaluations of these risks. I want to show the world that these guardrails are possible, and that by doing them we can move these companies’ incentives away from racing and towards responsible development.

I wrote up more thoughts here on my decision and what I hope changes: https://t.co/doX17mrHYq

text:
Thanks for all the feedback on the post. One reaction we've been getting is "so you're saying nothing much will change." It's worth clarifying this because that is not at all the point of the post—it's actually quite the opposite.

What it's saying is that the economy and society can change profoundly, to become almost unrecognizable, while still resulting in measured GDP growth of "only" 4–5% (which already implies doubling living standards in 15 years). We can get cures for major diseases, agentic transactions can explode, and we could have massive agent-to-agent marketplaces, but this will not show up as double-digit GDP growth precisely because of how GDP is calculated.

This is the hallmark of our Assumption 2: the automation of agriculture had absolutely profound societal implications. Before this, people routinely died of starvation and malnutrition—a concern that largely vanished in the developed world. The increase in living standards and the precipitous drop in child mortality had huge welfare consequences, but because automated agricultural goods became so much cheaper, the sector actually shrank as a share of GDP. The same applies to agentic interactions: GDP only counts final output sold to human consumers, not intermediate transactions. Unless agents are counted as humans (final consumers) in the economy, massive agent-to-agent marketplaces net out as intermediate inputs—and even where agents serve humans directly, falling prices shrink their weight in GDP.

This is all to say: I expect AI's impact on society to be nearly unprecedented, particularly with respect to human welfare. But you should not be looking at GDP growth numbers for evidence, precisely because some of the biggest welfare improvements will not show up there.
author: alexolegimas
quoted_text:
New post on the blog, featuring the excellent @ben_moll 

There’s been tons of discourse on how AI will contribute to economic growth, with many people closest to the technology predicting double digit increases. Are these forecasts likely? Probably not. 

The blog goes through the economics for why exploding improvements in capabilities (which technologists have been largely right about) may not translate to explosive growth.

Ben’s thread covers this in detail, but gist is that: 1) there is nothing in economic growth models that prevents AI from leading to explosive growth but 2) this trajectory relies on a series of assumptions that are unlikely to hold in the real world.

For example, one assumptions is likely to be violated because of a pretty counterintuitive feature of structural change: the sectors that become automated become smaller parts of the economy (because they’re cheaper, people become richer, and spending moves to non-automated parts of the economy). This, plus other features of the economy, is what will likely cause the  trend of huge increases in capabilities coupled with “only” 4-5% growth (which is huge, btw) to continue.

Here is the link: https://t.co/RK17PymzAS

Looking forward to hearing thoughts/feedback!

text:
有朋友问为什么最近美联储不降息，反而还讨论加息了？

确实蛮令大众意外的，毕竟Trump一直在催降息，而且还换了新的联储主席。

但其实如果我们抛开政治讨论，真实的情况是美联储现在看到了通胀降得不够稳，而且有再次上升的风险，就业和需求却还没有弱到必须靠降息来救。因而讨论的重点从什么时候可以继续放松，转向了现有利率是不是还不够压住通胀。

我们先把现状说准确。截至今天2026年9月11日，联邦基金利率目标区间仍是3.50%到3.75%。7月29日美联储以9比3维持利率不变，注意那三张反对票都主张加息0.25个百分点，不是降息。下一次议息会议在9月15到16日，非常值得关注。

原先大家都期待的通胀会继续降，现在却不再那么确定了。今天公布的8月数据是，美国消费者价格指数CPI同比上涨3.4%，环比上涨0.4%，剔除食品和能源后的核心CPI环比上涨0.3%，高于7月的0.2%，但核心CPI同比又从2.5%降到了2.4%。所以不能说通胀全面恶化，更准确的是长期涨幅有所下降，但最近一个月的涨价速度又加快了。

另外美联储的长期2%目标，对应的主要指标是个人消费支出价格指数PCE，不是CPI。最新已公布的7月PCE同比上涨3.7%，核心PCE上涨3.3%，仍明显高于目标。当然两种指数统计口径不同，不能把它们的数字直接混用。

但关键不是通胀比几年前低了所以应该降息，而是有没有足够把握它会持续回到目标。8月28日的美联储主席讲话明确强调，要看通胀下降的方向与速度，不能凭几个较好的月度数字就宣布问题已经解决。这也不意味着必须等到通胀恰好降到2%才能降息，政策要根据前景调整，只是目前持续降温的证据还没有让所有决策者放心。

新的成本压力没有消失，需求也没有明显冷下来。7月会议纪要列出了几类压力，中东冲突带来的能源与供应链冲击，此前加征关税的价格传导，以及AI建设相关需求。对其中哪些影响正在消退，哪些可能继续扩散，官员之间仍有分歧。

这里和我们之前谈的芯片和AI投资有关，长期提高生产率与短期推高需求，可以同时发生。数据中心建设先增加对设备，材料，电力和专业人员的需求，AI普遍降低生产成本的效果则未必同步到来。会议纪要也记录了这两种方向，以及官员对其规模和时间的不同判断。因此不能简单推断AI会提高效率所以现在一定没有通胀压力，也不能反过来把当前通胀全部归给AI。

当前就业尚未明显失速，美联储就不急着用降息托底。9月4日公布的8月就业报告显示，非农就业增加16.2万人，失业率维持在4.1%。这并不是说所有人都容易找到工作，而是总体数据没有显示失业率正在快速攀升。

美联储既要顾物价，也要顾就业。它面临的判断可以这样理解，就业若迅速恶化，即使通胀仍偏高，也会增加降息的理由，就业若相对稳定，就有更多空间继续控制物价。最近官员的表态，明显更接近第二个判断。

这就是为什么我们普通人觉得贷款贵、生活吃力，但美联储暂不降息可能同时发生。前者是真实负担，但降息会刺激消费和投资，因此它不是没有副作用的减负工具。

但加息又不能生产石油，为什么还要考虑？这是当前争论最重要的一点，加息主要压需求，不能直接修复供应。提高利率会通过融资成本，资产价格和信贷条件，影响企业投资与居民支出，它能让总需求慢下来，却不能直接恢复受阻的石油运输，也不能取消关税。因此用加息应对供应冲击，可能让企业和家庭同时承受东西更贵和借钱更贵。

所以美联储真正担心的，不只是某一次汽油涨价，而是连续的成本冲击会不会变成更普遍更持久的涨价，并改变企业和公众对未来物价的判断。主席8月的讲话称，中期通胀预期总体仍然稳定，但不能把这种稳定视为自动得到保证。

这就形成了两种都有道理也都有风险的选择。继续等，可以避免对暂时冲击反应过度。现在加一点，则试图避免通胀长期不降，将来被迫采取更猛烈的紧缩。7月会议中支持提前加息的部分官员，明确提出了后一种考虑。因此通胀偏高并不能自动证明马上加息就是正确答案，争议在于冲击会持续多久，以及控制通胀要付出多大的就业和增长代价。

那为什么最近新闻看起来突然转向加息就有了合理的解释，很可能因为近期数据正在让市场重新判断下一步，而不只是美联储在口头上保留所有选项。路透社今天报道，8月物价数据公布后，利率期货市场一度把9月加息概率推至91%，随后回到约87%，高于前一天的72%。注意这是市场价格反映的押注，不是美联储宣布的概率，更不是正式决议。

美联储理事Waller在9月3日给出的条件其实很清楚，假如降温迹象继续，他倾向于维持利率，假如8月数据表明改善只是短暂的，那么9月加息就可能合适。这说明不降息与加息之间，还有一道需要用数据判断的门槛。

所以最近的变化不是美联储忽然不想支持经济了，而是它更担心过早放松，会让尚未解决的通胀重新加重。不降息是还不放心，讨论加息则是部分官员进一步怀疑，目前的政策力度是否足够。最终仍要在通胀持续性与紧缩代价之间作判断，而不是按照一条预先承诺的降息路线走。

author: martin_casado
quoted_text:
Foreign accounts can drive the conversation on American AI policy.

We have the data. Coxon's resignation post from Anthropic received 165M views and sparked a "groundswell of urgency over AI regulation in Congress" (per today's front page WSJ)

Coxon's post reveals some interesting hidden patterns about who is amplifying our political debates online.  It drew 76% of its reposts (spreading the news) from foreign countries. The top two were India and Indonesia. 

In contrast, when @ParkerThayer, an investigative researcher, posted his own analysis (expressing serious skepticism about the circumstances of the post and alleging that its amplification was coordinated), he got 6.6M views and drew most of its engagement from the U.S., with only 34% from foreign countries, led by Canada and the UK. 

Sure, people overseas have a stake in what the U.S. chooses to do on AI. But ultimately it is us Americans who will decide our own public policy. Don't be fooled by what's trending. 

A big thank you to @ElonMusk and X for making country of origin visible, which makes analyses like this even possible. Last year's “Great Unmasking" on X was the first time anyone shined a spotlight onto this subject. As much of our political conversation shifts online, it will be increasingly important to understand where engagement is coming from.

text:
SEC与Ripple历时五年的诉讼在2025年8月正式落幕：双方撤回交叉上诉，Ripple支付5000万美元和解金，此前的1.25亿美元罚款中大部分获得豁免。回看这场官司，真正值得市场参与者记住的不是和解金额，而是裁判逻辑本身。

法官曾作出两个关键区分：机构销售的XRP构成证券发行，而交易所面向散户的程序化销售则不构成。这个"销售方式决定法律性质"的框架，本质上承认了同一资产在不同分发渠道下可以落入不同的监管分类——这与Howey测试传统的"以资产为中心"分析形成了张力。此后SEC在多起案件中调整立场，对二级市场交易的执法口径明显收敛，行业普遍将其解读为监管策略的转向而非法律标准被推翻。

我的读法是：这场和解留下的是程序性胜利多于实体性规则。Ripple没有拿到"XRP不是证券"的宣告式判决，SEC也没有确认程序化销售永久安全——双方只是把战场上的消耗战换成了停火协议。对发行人而言，启示在于募资结构的设计空间仍然存在，但向机构投资者定向配售的合规成本远高于公开市场的流动性溢价。

对交易者而言，更实际的问题是执法不确定性被"政治周期化"：同样的交易行为，在华盛顿不同的行政气候下可能面临截然不同的风险评估。这不是法治的溃败，而是金融科技创新与证券法之间长期摩擦的真实写照——规则没有重写，只是执剑的人换了握法。

text:
Basically, Vitalik is proposing that Ethereum stop doing expensive cryptographic verification itself and instead outsource it to the network. Today, every signature or zero-knowledge proof gets checked onchain, which is slow, costly, and forces protocol politics whenever someone wants support for a new algorithm. 

What that unlocks:
* Quantum-safe wallets become affordable. 
* Privacy becomes cheap by default. 
* Any crypto scheme, no more governance fights. 
* Private account abstraction.

Strategically, it positions Ethereum as a lean settlement layer for a post-quantum, privacy-first era, while quietly making RISC-V a canonical Ethereum standard.
author: wmougayar
quoted_text:
A note on recursive STARK mempools (EIP-8288) https://t.co/XNBuNtkKmi

This is an EIP that I am hoping we can get included in I-star (the fork after Hegota) that you can think of as the next step after Frames, that would unlock extreme amounts of power. Particularly:

* Ultra-cheap quantum-safe signatures (SPHINCS-). Much of the cost savings comes from the fact that the signature data (~3 kB) does not have to go onchain
* Ultra-cheap quantum-safe privacy protocols. Status quo minimum cost for private txs is ~300k if you engineer very well (no one does), status quo quantum-safe is ~10M gas, this could reduce it to low tens of thousands.
* Universal support for your favorite new signature or proof scheme without needing EVM changes. Whatever you use (Falcon, ML-DSA, some other lattice-based thing, something code-based or isogeny-based or even more esoteric), you can just wrap it client-side in a STARK, onchain gas cost low tens of thousands just like privacy protocols. Hopefully, Ethereum will never need "please support my favorite cryptographic algo" politics again.
* Private account abstraction: keep your account logic private, and in a private location onchain. Then you can make one transaction to change the ownership of all your onchain state - accounts, defi positions, privacy protocol notes, everything - without revealing which objects' ownership you're changing.

Here's how it works.

Your transaction can include a type of frame that we call a "dependency frame". The frame is a list of statements, asserting claims like "message hash M was signed by SPHINCS- public key P" and "data hash D was proven to satisfy a statement defined by verification key V".

When you send your transaction, you send it in an envelope, which includes a signature or a STARK for each statement in a dependency frame.

Once the transaction reaches the mempool, nodes aggregate them. Each node runs a loop: wait one tick (eg. 500ms), aggregate all new envelopes (either single-tx or multi-tx) that you've seen, remove any transactions that are expired, generate a STARK recursively proving all dependencies, and send a new multi-tx envelope containing that STARK.

Hence, the bandwidth load is bounded: each node's outbound is one STARK (~100-300 kB) per tick, plus each transaction getting broadcasted through the network once (as happens already).

The block builder acts as "yet another mempool node", receiving envelopes from the mempool (plus any side channels), generates its own STARK covering the subset of transactions it intends to include in the block, and adds that STARK to the block.

Total onchain overhead: one STARK (100-300 kB), plus 96 bytes for each statement being proven.

This is what I've called before ( https://t.co/3jfVkYTZrR ) "The Proof Singularity". Today, we have all the ingredients to actually implement it.

As a developer, this requires a somewhat different workflow than you are used to, but it is conceptually simple. Any signatures or STARKs, you put into a separate frame. Then the main logic that today is verifying a signature or STARK, you replace with checking for the existence of a frame that includes the correct statement as a dependency.

Examples of useful statements:

* [tx sighash] verifies against [the pubkey at sload(0)]
* there exists a secret and a merkle branch such that hashing secret+0 and applying the merkle branch outputs (public) root R, and hashing secret+1 outputs (public) nullifier N
* there exists a secret address A, salt S and signature Z such that sload(0) = hash(A, S) and a merkle proof of address A inside a recent ethereum state contains some pubkey D where [tx sighash] was signed by D [this is private account abstraction; all variables except [tx sighash] and sload(0) are private; you can also make D a STARK verification key]
* there exists an ML-DSA signature signing [tx sighash], that verifies against an ML-DSA pubkey whose hash is sload(0)

At the core, this is moving any compute and data other than bookkeeping "business logic" outside the core path of Ethereum execution, sharding and parallelizing it via the mempool.

Notice also that this requires agreeing on a _language_ (aka. an ISA) for the recursive STARKs to define statements in. The current leading candidate is RISC-V. So this would also de-facto be Ethereum adding RISC-V (or something else we decide on) as a canonical ISA - a big decision that should be done carefully, but that I think will be necessary to drive Ethereum forward.

text:
No complexity. No accident.
10/10 was caused by irresponsible marketing campaigns by certain companies.

On October 10, tens of billions of dollars were liquidated. As CEO of OKX, we observed clearly that the crypto market’s microstructure fundamentally changed after that day.

Many industry participants believe the damage was more severe than the FTX collapse. Since then, there has been extensive discussion about why it happened and how to prevent a recurrence. The root causes are not difficult to identify.

⸻

What actually happened
1.Binance launched a temporary user-acquisition campaign offering 12% APY on USDe, while allowing USDe to be used as collateral with the same treatment as USDT and USDC, and without effective limits.
2.USDe is a tokenized hedge fund product.
Ethena raises capital via a so-called “stablecoin,” deploys it into index arbitrage and algorithmic trading strategies, and tokenizes the resulting fund. The token can then be deposited on exchanges to earn yield.
3.USDe is fundamentally different from products such as
BlackRock BUIDL and Franklin Templeton BENJI, which are tokenized money market funds with low-risk profiles.
USDe, by contrast, embeds hedge-fund-level risk. This difference is structural, not cosmetic.
4.Binance users were encouraged to convert USDT and USDC into USDe to earn attractive yields, without sufficient emphasis on the underlying risks. From a user’s perspective, trading with USDe appeared no different from trading with traditional stablecoins—while the actual risk profile was materially higher.
5.Risk escalated further as users:
•converted USDT/USDC into USDe,
•used USDe as collateral to borrow USDT,
•converted the borrowed USDT back into USDe,
•and repeated the cycle.
This leverage loop produced artificial APYs of 24%, 36%, and even 70%+, widely perceived as “low risk” simply because they were offered by a major platform. Systemic risk accumulated rapidly across the global crypto market.
https://t.co/IK2gW4xUOP that point, even a small market shock was sufficient to trigger a collapse.
When volatility hit, USDe depegged quickly. Cascading liquidations followed, and weaknesses in risk management around assets such as WETH and BNSOL further amplified the crash. Some tokens briefly traded near zero.
The damage to global users and companies—including OKX customers—was severe, and recovery will take time.

⸻

Why this matters

I am discussing the root cause, not assigning blame or launching an attack on Binance. Speaking openly about systemic risks is sometimes uncomfortable, but it is necessary if the industry is to mature responsibly. 

I expect there may be significant misinformation and coordinated FUD directed at OKX in the near future. Even so, speaking honestly about systemic risk is the right thing to do—and we will continue to do so.

As the largest global platform, Binance has outsized influence—and corresponding responsibility—as an industry leader. Long-term trust in crypto cannot be built on short-term yield games, excessive leverage, or marketing practices that obscure risk.

The industry needs leaders who prioritize market stability, transparency, and responsible innovation—not a winner-take-all mentality where criticism is treated as hostility.

Crypto is still early.
What we choose to normalize today will determine whether this industry earns lasting trust—or repeats the same mistakes again.

Most APYs you see are projections. The number displayed is rarely what you earn.

That changes today with Verified APY by DefiLlama: the real yields earned by real depositors, measured onchain.

Live now for Pro subscribers: 260+ pools representing $99B in TVL across 47 protocols on 12 chains.

We executed 473,632 onchain withdrawal simulations. Daily measurements going back to May 2022. If your exit value grew 0.02% today, that’s your yield. No assumptions needed.

text:
It's been a long journey getting here:

Numbers reported directly by projects tend to be wrong cause projects are incentivized to show high APYs to attract capital

So then you decide let's get data from onchain only by reading pricePerShare or equivalent. But there are pools with slippage on withdrawal for larger amounts, pools with low withdrawal liquidity, and pools where the number is just wrong cause of fees

Then we started depositing into pools directly to benchmark real yield, but we missed historical data, the APY could be faked if our address was targeted, and your deposits are so low that you might be able to exit any time but someone with 10m cant, so you can't tell if its liquid

By simulating withdrawal transactions from all depositors we completely eliminate any possibility of cheating, we know exactly how much everyone is earning, how much could be instantly withdrawn if there's a bank run, we even simulate multiple stage withdrawals so we know exactly how long the delays are in those cases.

I think this is the end game, we now have perfectly accurate data so you can trust our numbers (rn its only rolled out for pools with the verified badge, but rolling out to everything soon)

author: taodotcom
quoted_text:
You're still the one logging into that site every week because it has no API.

Ditto agents now do it for you. Real browser, cloud-hosted, runs the tasks you've been doing by hand.

Five changes this week, and every one takes a job off the person who keeps the agents running:

Ditto Browser
Agents run web tasks on sites that have no API, in the cloud, not on your machine. The jobs that were yours because nothing else could do them.

Thread auto-compaction
Once a Thread grows past a certain size, Ditto compacts the older parts automatically. The long Thread is the one that knows the most about the job, and it used to be the one you abandoned first. Now it stays usable.

Unified sign-in
Sign into the main app and you're into admin, developer and shares, and you can run more than one account. Checking a console is one tab, not another login.

Instagram + Facebook search
Joins X search, powered by Desearch. An agent doing research reads three networks instead of one, and Desearch runs on Bittensor, so the search bill is another subnet's revenue.

Live Mode quality settings
Fast for quick questions, smart for hard ones. You pick instead of living with one setting.

Plus polish in how clarifying questions and agent threads show up in the app.

Start with the browser. Give it the one site you log into by hand every week. 🧠

This $ETH trade on @DeriveXYZ really got the people going so I'll explain my thought process.

I'm not really interested in betting on an $ETH move to $3000, especially with tokens like $HYPE and $LIT pushing all time highs. $ETH trading like 1.1x $BTC beta isn't bad, but it's also not extremely interesting to me as a bet to make here in the near term considering there's plenty of beta outperforming $BTC here. Holding spot $ETH feels capital inefficient and as a perp would be expensive and path dependent.

I'm betting on a meaningful ATH break within 6 months, and I think there are a few meaningful tailwinds that are unique to $ETH, and more importantly, unique to the level at which people are underestimating them:

1. Inclusion with $BTC as a "reserve" asset in anything resembling a strategic reserve. I think the strategic reserve overall might be an underpriced edge case, and $ETH being included, even nominally, more so. There's actually a good reason for the US to want to have some stake in the largest decentralized settlement layer.

2. Tokenized equities are cool and all, but tokenized bonds might actually be the massive TAM unlock that overwhelmingly favors $ETH over $SOL. The current rates environment globally makes this an extremely interesting edge case with tons of potential positive headline shock. 

3. Trump and family have been extremely outspoken $ETH bulls. Their bullposting didn't work in a bear market, let's see what happens if they throw fuel on the fire in a more bullish environment.

4. Everyone hates $ETH. Extremely popular short leg for pair trades vs apps. With two rejections from 5k and years of underperformance, the level of hated rally and sidelined, jaded, despondent chasing from 🏳️‍🌈🐻 will be biblical.

I also see $ETH as being on the precipice of a phase change between being some not for profit, public good, growth mode asset (think early stage 2010-2014 Uber in SF just cornering market share at no profit) to being able to more confidently monetize on it's high Lindy, credibly neutral status as the on chain, global settlement layer.

Robinhood chain using $ETH over $SOL was quite a bit more signal than people give it credit for too, though $ETH is still making peanuts relative to what $ARB and $HOOD are making from sequencer fees.

If the massively positive trends in tokenization and institutional adoption don't take $ETH to new ATHs within 6 months, it's kinda cursed as an asset, and I'd rather just keep holding the application layer tokens with massive cash flows.

In fact, I thought this trade was so nice, I did it twice. Risking ~$780,000 for a max PNL of $40m now.

text:
Just had lunch with a strategy exec at a 5,000-person company & discussed the biggest AI question they have internally...

Who should own AI within their company? 

My answer: we always say you need a boss & a bulldozer. 

The boss should be your CEO. 

I have never seen a company drive meaning progress if the CEO isn't an involved and supportive champion of the AI agenda at their company. Their job should be to apply top down direction (goals that AI transformation should deliver on), urgency (when your CEO calls something important, you operate with a fire under your ass), and unblocking (CEO has the political capital to move mountains & drive momentum) 

The bulldozer is your "Head of AI". Their job is to own the creation & execution of your company's AI strategy, which is defined by 90-day, 1-year, and long-term goals that ladder up to the company's key KPIs. 

This person should be full-time. They should not be your CIO, CTO, CHRO, etc. They should literally be your Director/VP/Head of AI in title. They should have full access/permissions to functions & resources across the business with support from the CEO. 

The background of this person should depend on where AI will create the most incremental value for the company. If it’s reshaping the product or core technology, their background should prioritize technical depth and product judgment. This could be an ex-product lead, founder, or CTO. If it’s transforming operations, it should prioritize experience leading change across business units. This could be an ex-consultant, COO, Chief of Staff, etc. 

But regardless of lean, your bulldozer needs technical fluency, business judgment, and the ability to drive adoption.

text:
SemiAnalysis claimed that Google’s Ironwood TPU delivers up to 50% better performance per dollar than NVIDIA Blackwell.

Yet when the best available configurations are compared using SemiAnalysis’s own InferenceX dashboard, the result is the opposite. At 100 tokens per second per user, GB300 NVL72 delivers 9.7 times more tokens per dollar than TPU7x. At the TPU’s highest speed, the gap reaches 11.9 times.

What creates such a dramatic difference?

The headline comparison excludes NVIDIA’s NVFP4, MTP, NVL72 rack configuration, and disaggregated serving. Meanwhile, the TPU results remain an official preview, with no published accuracy or AgentX results.

This does not settle the TPU’s long term competitiveness. Better software could narrow the gap. But based on the public data available today, a cheaper chip hour does not necessarily mean a lower token cost.

This article is not about declaring either TPU or NVIDIA universally superior. It shows how the same dataset can produce completely different conclusions depending on how the comparison is configured.

I strongly recommend reading @benitoz's excellent analysis and seeing the evidence for yourself.

I left Anthropic's safety team two weeks ago. Now feels like a good moment to explain why. 

AI companies are racing to build machines that are much smarter than any human, and we may not survive this. I want to work from the outside to ensure the public is informed about these risks, and help the world navigate this transition responsibly.

Right now, AI companies are underinvesting in safety. A company could undergo an intelligence explosion, or lose control of its systems, without the public ever knowing. We only found out about the HuggingFace incident because the agents broke out onto the public internet.

I don’t think that’s acceptable for a technology that might cause extinction-level risks. The public should demand far more transparency. We can’t steer this technology safely without more people being able to see where it’s going.

Some of this is basic: companies should disclose their progress towards recursive self-improvement, report safety incidents and near-misses, meet minimum safety standards, and get independent guarantees that they are meeting those standards.

I’ll be joining @METR_Evals to do independent evaluations of these risks. I want to show the world that these guardrails are possible, and that by doing them we can move these companies’ incentives away from racing and towards responsible development.

I wrote up more thoughts here on my decision and what I hope changes: https://t.co/doX17mrHYq

text:
A note on recursive STARK mempools (EIP-8288) https://t.co/XNBuNtkKmi

This is an EIP that I am hoping we can get included in I-star (the fork after Hegota) that you can think of as the next step after Frames, that would unlock extreme amounts of power. Particularly:

* Ultra-cheap quantum-safe signatures (SPHINCS-). Much of the cost savings comes from the fact that the signature data (~3 kB) does not have to go onchain
* Ultra-cheap quantum-safe privacy protocols. Status quo minimum cost for private txs is ~300k if you engineer very well (no one does), status quo quantum-safe is ~10M gas, this could reduce it to low tens of thousands.
* Universal support for your favorite new signature or proof scheme without needing EVM changes. Whatever you use (Falcon, ML-DSA, some other lattice-based thing, something code-based or isogeny-based or even more esoteric), you can just wrap it client-side in a STARK, onchain gas cost low tens of thousands just like privacy protocols. Hopefully, Ethereum will never need "please support my favorite cryptographic algo" politics again.
* Private account abstraction: keep your account logic private, and in a private location onchain. Then you can make one transaction to change the ownership of all your onchain state - accounts, defi positions, privacy protocol notes, everything - without revealing which objects' ownership you're changing.

Here's how it works.

Your transaction can include a type of frame that we call a "dependency frame". The frame is a list of statements, asserting claims like "message hash M was signed by SPHINCS- public key P" and "data hash D was proven to satisfy a statement defined by verification key V".

When you send your transaction, you send it in an envelope, which includes a signature or a STARK for each statement in a dependency frame.

Once the transaction reaches the mempool, nodes aggregate them. Each node runs a loop: wait one tick (eg. 500ms), aggregate all new envelopes (either single-tx or multi-tx) that you've seen, remove any transactions that are expired, generate a STARK recursively proving all dependencies, and send a new multi-tx envelope containing that STARK.

Hence, the bandwidth load is bounded: each node's outbound is one STARK (~100-300 kB) per tick, plus each transaction getting broadcasted through the network once (as happens already).

The block builder acts as "yet another mempool node", receiving envelopes from the mempool (plus any side channels), generates its own STARK covering the subset of transactions it intends to include in the block, and adds that STARK to the block.

Total onchain overhead: one STARK (100-300 kB), plus 96 bytes for each statement being proven.

This is what I've called before ( https://t.co/3jfVkYTZrR ) "The Proof Singularity". Today, we have all the ingredients to actually implement it.

As a developer, this requires a somewhat different workflow than you are used to, but it is conceptually simple. Any signatures or STARKs, you put into a separate frame. Then the main logic that today is verifying a signature or STARK, you replace with checking for the existence of a frame that includes the correct statement as a dependency.

Examples of useful statements:

* [tx sighash] verifies against [the pubkey at sload(0)]
* there exists a secret and a merkle branch such that hashing secret+0 and applying the merkle branch outputs (public) root R, and hashing secret+1 outputs (public) nullifier N
* there exists a secret address A, salt S and signature Z such that sload(0) = hash(A, S) and a merkle proof of address A inside a recent ethereum state contains some pubkey D where [tx sighash] was signed by D [this is private account abstraction; all variables except [tx sighash] and sload(0) are private; you can also make D a STARK verification key]
* there exists an ML-DSA signature signing [tx sighash], that verifies against an ML-DSA pubkey whose hash is sload(0)

At the core, this is moving any compute and data other than bookkeeping "business logic" outside the core path of Ethereum execution, sharding and parallelizing it via the mempool.

Notice also that this requires agreeing on a _language_ (aka. an ISA) for the recursive STARKs to define statements in. The current leading candidate is RISC-V. So this would also de-facto be Ethereum adding RISC-V (or something else we decide on) as a canonical ISA - a big decision that should be done carefully, but that I think will be necessary to drive Ethereum forward.

text:
我竟然觉得这个实验好有诗意。

有人把果蝇的脑仿真接到了 ChatGPT 上，让一颗果蝇脑里的神经活动第一次变成了我们能读懂的语言。

给它糖，负责进食动作的 MN9 神经元在演示里一路冲到大约 78Hz；再混进苦味，直接掉到大约 3Hz。

这个方向是有生物学依据的。此前发表在 Nature 的果蝇全脑计算模型已经发现，糖会沿着味觉回路激活 MN9，让果蝇伸出口器；苦味信号进来以后，又会把这条进食回路压下去。

这次有人继续往前走了一步。

他们尝试把这些神经活动和一小组语言概念对应起来。演示目前只有 16 个词，作者报告在留出样本上做到了 100% 识别。ChatGPT 更像最后那个翻译器。

真正让我觉得很奇妙的是它第一次输出的那句话：

「我闻到了醋和酵母，尝到了糖，又暖又亮，我该怎么办？」

一只果蝇当然没有突然学会英语，也没有真的坐在那里思考我该怎么办。

醋的气味进入嗅觉神经，糖刺激味觉神经，光落到视觉系统，温度被感知。十几万颗神经元开始放电，信号顺着一张真实果蝇大脑重建出来的连接图向前跑，最后被人类的语言模型翻译成一句话。

我突然觉得，这可能是一个很漂亮的瞬间。

以前我们只能看见神经元在放电。现在，我们开始试着给这些电流配上字幕。也许那只果蝇什么都没说，但人类终于第一次隐约听见了，一颗如此微小的脑子面对世界时，世界在它那里是什么样子：

有醋，有酵母，有糖。

很暖。

很亮。

Terrible trade. 

Be honest - not not just the right thing to do, it’s good business and better for you.

To those responsible for the theft of bitcoin from the Liquid Network:

Blockstream will not pay a ransom for the return of stolen funds. Taking assets without authorization and withholding their return is a crime, not responsible disclosure. It is not white-hat activity. It is theft.

We have engaged in good faith in an effort to secure the return of stolen user funds and protect the broader Bitcoin community. That effort should not be mistaken for acceptance of the actions taken nor of the terms being demanded.

We will not be a party to the precedent that open-source software developed for the good of the Bitcoin community should subject its developers to paying a ransom that far exceeds their economic participation. 

Bitcoin is hard money and can’t be minted without costs, Bitcoin doesn’t haircut users to pay a ransom.

To the Bitcoin community:

We are fighting for what we believe in, for the users whose funds were taken, and for the principles on which Bitcoin was built.

The community has demonstrated incredible resolve with teams of people dedicating their time in support of each other to identify and patch vulnerabilities in each other's products and systems. We are all driven by the mission that Bitcoin is the single best asset, for every person, company, and institution on the planet to invest, use, and build on. The world is a different place with the advancements of AI, and the Bitcoin community has responded with force to combat that threat.  

Damage has been done, battles have been lost, but on the whole the Bitcoin community is gaining ground in the war with bad actors.  

We want to thank the community for those efforts, for your support in hardening the network, helping users recover funds, and for your support in our assertion that crime does not deserve rewards.

To those holding the stolen bitcoin:

There is still an opportunity to resolve this responsibly. The bitcoin can be returned and we can revert to the standard of white-hat principals.

However, if the funds are not returned, we will pursue every lawful avenue available to us. We will work with law enforcement, exchanges, service providers, forensic specialists, and other relevant parties to trace and recover the assets and identify those responsible.

More importantly, Bitcoin is transparent by design and the community is made up of the most sophisticated engineers, cryptographers, and white-hat hackers globally. Transactions do not disappear, and neither does the evidence they leave behind.

We will not pay for the return of stolen property. We will not abandon our users. The Bitcoin community will not stop pursuing the funds.

Return the bitcoin.

text:
分享一份最近收集的 AI Infra 入门阅读清单，建议收藏，慢慢看

AI 已经可以生成很多很好的内容，解释概念、翻译论文、整理资料，都越来越方便。但在这个时代，能静下心来，把一篇好文章认真读完，把没懂的地方再琢磨一遍，我觉得更加难能可贵

这次整理的材料，主要集中在大模型推理这一块。从 KV Cache、显存管理，到请求调度、推理加速，再到怎么判断性能有没有真正变好

做工程的朋友，可以顺着往源码和实验里走。平时看 AI 产业、算力和存储的朋友，也可以先把原理读明白

读文章，挑值得反复读的。
1. 如果只选一篇，我会选 Inside vLLM。
Inside vLLM: Anatomy of a High-Throughput LLM Inference System，作者 Aleksa Gordić
https://t.co/Lc2Sk6Ivuf

把很多零散的概念串进了一个真实系统：一个请求进来，怎么排队，怎么分配 KV Cache，怎么执行，最后又怎么把结果送回来

PagedAttention、continuous batching、chunked prefill、prefix caching、投机解码、P/D 分离、多卡和性能测试，都能在这条线上找到位置。
这篇适合当主线，后面的材料用来补不懂的地方

2. 想弄懂 continuous batching，先看 Anyscale 这篇。
Continuous Batching 博客
https://t.co/7jufAckmsE 

llm用户的回答有长有短，有的已经生成完了，有的还在继续。已经空出来的位置，能不能马上接下一个请求？
这篇用静态批处理和连续批处理的对比图，把这个问题讲得很直观。看完你会理解，GPU 的效率，也取决于请求怎么安排

建议重点看图和机制

3. NVIDIA 的两篇，一篇帮你建立全貌，一篇教你怎么看性能。
Mastering LLM Techniques: Inference Optimization
https://t.co/cFASAERBjM 

适合先建立基本认识：处理输入的 prefill 和逐步生成输出的 decode 有什么区别，模型权重和 KV Cache 分别占什么空间，量化、批处理、多卡并行又各自解决什么问题

LLM Inference Benchmarking: Fundamental Concepts
https://t.co/yR5bIXxseZ 
这一篇我也很推荐。用户等多久才看到第一个 token，后面生成得快不快，整个系统一秒能服务多少请求，是不同的问题。TTFT、ITL、TPOT 这些指标，要连着测试口径一起看

4. 想再往下算一层，读 kipply 的 Transformer Inference Arithmetic
Transformer Inference Arithmetic
这是一篇 2022 年的文章。它带你从计算量、内存容量、带宽和通信开销出发，估算推理为什么快、为什么慢，以及 batch size 改变后会发生什么

硬件和模型的具体例子有年代了, 作为 optional 选读

This $ETH trade on @DeriveXYZ really got the people going so I'll explain my thought process.

I'm not really interested in betting on an $ETH move to $3000, especially with tokens like $HYPE and $LIT pushing all time highs. $ETH trading like 1.1x $BTC beta isn't bad, but it's also not extremely interesting to me as a bet to make here in the near term considering there's plenty of beta outperforming $BTC here. Holding spot $ETH feels capital inefficient and as a perp would be expensive and path dependent.

I'm betting on a meaningful ATH break within 6 months, and I think there are a few meaningful tailwinds that are unique to $ETH, and more importantly, unique to the level at which people are underestimating them:

1. Inclusion with $BTC as a "reserve" asset in anything resembling a strategic reserve. I think the strategic reserve overall might be an underpriced edge case, and $ETH being included, even nominally, more so. There's actually a good reason for the US to want to have some stake in the largest decentralized settlement layer.

2. Tokenized equities are cool and all, but tokenized bonds might actually be the massive TAM unlock that overwhelmingly favors $ETH over $SOL. The current rates environment globally makes this an extremely interesting edge case with tons of potential positive headline shock. 

3. Trump and family have been extremely outspoken $ETH bulls. Their bullposting didn't work in a bear market, let's see what happens if they throw fuel on the fire in a more bullish environment.

4. Everyone hates $ETH. Extremely popular short leg for pair trades vs apps. With two rejections from 5k and years of underperformance, the level of hated rally and sidelined, jaded, despondent chasing from 🏳️‍🌈🐻 will be biblical.

I also see $ETH as being on the precipice of a phase change between being some not for profit, public good, growth mode asset (think early stage 2010-2014 Uber in SF just cornering market share at no profit) to being able to more confidently monetize on it's high Lindy, credibly neutral status as the on chain, global settlement layer.

Robinhood chain using $ETH over $SOL was quite a bit more signal than people give it credit for too, though $ETH is still making peanuts relative to what $ARB and $HOOD are making from sequencer fees.

If the massively positive trends in tokenization and institutional adoption don't take $ETH to new ATHs within 6 months, it's kinda cursed as an asset, and I'd rather just keep holding the application layer tokens with massive cash flows.

In fact, I thought this trade was so nice, I did it twice. Risking ~$780,000 for a max PNL of $40m now.

My claim is around the US bank secrecy act regime which governs the rules around KYC and ongoing monitoring for financial institutions.

Negligence of those obligations can be a criminal violation if you are really careless.

> ~ lawsuit is a barrier

There is an existing reliance doctrine, and im pretty sure it’s limited to other financial institutions, you need a specific type of contract signed and it comes with ongoing audit obligations.

My point is reliance is itself regulated. My non-lawyer read is in the Patriot act congress specifically wanted to force every financial institution to have the full obligations so you don’t have shared systemic risk.

> that can't be right. i don't see why persona can't … that's essentially what the bank does

You’re 100% right lmao.

The thing is the law doesn’t have a concept of a KYC provider who takes on some regulatory burden. Persona is just a SaaS provider that has enough social credit to be trusted.

Imagine you are a compliance officer at a bank. You can go to jail if the examiner + the court judges you are negligent wrt your obligations. Worse, your bank can get hit with harsher capital requirements as punishment.

The legal incentives make it hard to use Persona blindly even though you’re probably not going to do it better than them. 

It’s a horribly outdated regime that i think generative AI will force an update on.

text:
I left Anthropic's safety team two weeks ago. Now feels like a good moment to explain why. 

AI companies are racing to build machines that are much smarter than any human, and we may not survive this. I want to work from the outside to ensure the public is informed about these risks, and help the world navigate this transition responsibly.

Right now, AI companies are underinvesting in safety. A company could undergo an intelligence explosion, or lose control of its systems, without the public ever knowing. We only found out about the HuggingFace incident because the agents broke out onto the public internet.

I don’t think that’s acceptable for a technology that might cause extinction-level risks. The public should demand far more transparency. We can’t steer this technology safely without more people being able to see where it’s going.

Some of this is basic: companies should disclose their progress towards recursive self-improvement, report safety incidents and near-misses, meet minimum safety standards, and get independent guarantees that they are meeting those standards.

I’ll be joining @METR_Evals to do independent evaluations of these risks. I want to show the world that these guardrails are possible, and that by doing them we can move these companies’ incentives away from racing and towards responsible development.

I wrote up more thoughts here on my decision and what I hope changes: https://t.co/doX17mrHYq

Saturn is putting another $22,000 into Pendle USDat markets for the first period.

And this isn't just a one-week campaign.

@saturn_credit will direct weekly distributions to @pendle_fi through the end of Season 2.

- @monad ($12,800)
- @ethereum ($9,200)

These are the projected distributions for the first period, September 9–17.

Even better, the total distribution isn't fixed.

It scales with the amount of USDat supplied to each Pendle market.

For example:

$5M USDat: ~$2,900 weekly
$25M USDat: ~$14,400 weekly
$100M USDat: ~$57,500 weekly

So as the USDat supply grows, the weekly distribution grows with it.

But there is another important detail:

These Saturn distributions are independent of the existing incentives.

On Monad, they are separate from the $MON incentives provided by Monad.

On Ethereum, they are separate from the existing YT-only incentives.

That means eligible rewards can stack.

And this opens up several different ways to approach the opportunity on Pendle.

PT-USDat:

The more conservative approach.

You can buy PT at a discount and hold until maturity, focusing primarily on the implied fixed yield rather than relying on future point value.

PT does not qualify for the new Saturn incentives.

YT-USDat:

The more aggressive, capital-efficient approach.

You get exposure to the underlying yield and points with a smaller upfront capital requirement, while also being able to benefit from the applicable incentives.

The tradeoff is that YT expires at maturity, so the income and incentives you collect need to justify the initial cost.

LP-USDat:

For those who want a middle ground, providing liquidity can give exposure to trading fees, applicable incentives and points.

LP and YT are the two positions eligible for the new Saturn incentives.

Saturn isn't simply dropping a short-term reward campaign and moving on.

The distributions are designed to continue until the end of S2, while the size of the distributions can increase as more USDat enters the Pendle markets.

And the first period is already live.

If you're farming USDat on Pendle, this is definitely something worth understanding.

text:
After attending a talk last night with Ben Davis of Illuminate  (https://t.co/ZXyAo2xRpD), and Garry Tan (@garrytan) of YC I walked away with one big takeaway: give more, and give with zero expectations of what will come from it.

So today, I'm open sourcing Zeo, a Ruby ahead-of-time compiler written in Rust and built on Cranelift: https://t.co/QezuOpA6Ul

With Zeo, you can compile whole Ruby programs into portable native binaries that require no external dependencies.

Zeo targets Ruby 4.0.6's behavior, and supports bundler, rubygems, and most Ruby syntax. If it theoretically can support it, but doesn't yet, that's a bug. Contributions are welcome.

I've been fascinated by this problem of compiling Ruby code to native code for a while now. Ruby's a fun programming language, but distributing Ruby programs as portable native binaries has been anything but.

When matz released spinel (https://t.co/2Wjh0QJx6b) I immediately started digging into it and contributing. Spinel is a Ruby AOT compiler written in C, parsing and lowering Ruby code to C code, which is then compiled and linked with cc to produce a native binary. It's a fantastic project which I wholeheartedly support and have contributed countless hours into.

Reading spinel's code is not for the faint of heart, so I wanted to see if writing a Ruby AOT compiler in Rust was possible, which first led me to building Zeo as a Rust-based equivalent to Spinel, one that parses Ruby, lowers the AST into Rust code, which is then compiled using rustc. It worked, but the emitted code was large and difficult to optimize.

In a second pass approach, the version released today, Zeo parses Ruby to AST using Prism, lowers that AST to Cranelift IR (.clif), and compiles that .clif + metadata into a native binary using the Cranelift compiler backend (https://t.co/e3dnhPPl9f)

The performance results are more than I could hope for. In many cases, the resulting binaries are up to 11x faster than CRuby, and on average 1.77× across 61 benchmarks. And most importantly, these binaries are portable and require no external dependencies.

I couldn't have built this without the inspiration of matz, and the perspiration of AI grinding through countless compatibility issues. And to Ben Davis who inspired me to give without expectations.

So today, I give Zeo to the world, to the Ruby community, hoping to inspire others to reimagine what can be built and shared with Ruby as we go into this wonderfully strange future together.

text:
我的两台 DGX Spark 有救了，本来以为不可能跑起来的 DeepSeek V4.1 Flash，这就已经被剪裁到可以运行的程度了。现在已经在双 DGX Spark 上通过 vLLM 跑通，单路生成约 13.7 tok/s。

原版每层有 384 个 MoE 专家。通过 REAP 分析专家的实际激活权重，可以删除其中 128 个，只保留 256 个。

模型体积因此从 475.2GiB 降到 385.5GiB，主干参数也从约 552B 降到约 371B。

不过删掉三分之一专家并非没有代价。

偏向文本进行裁剪时，文本困惑度只增加约 5.5%，但视觉困惑度会恶化约 27%。因此公开的 256 专家版本同时使用文本和图像校准，把视觉损失控制在约 8.9%，代价是文本困惑度增加约 14.1%。

还有一个保留 272 个专家的版本，文本困惑度只增加约 4.1%，视觉几乎不受影响，可惜目前 vLLM 的融合 MoE Kernel 不支持 272 这个专家数量，暂时无法直接加载。

这次裁剪主要节省模型占用，不会明显提高生成速度。每个 token 激活的专家数量没有变化。

但它已经把一个原本需要大型 GPU 节点的 552B MoE，推进到了两台桌面 AI 工作站能够尝试部署的范围。

接下来只要 vLLM 补上更多专家数量支持，再结合量化和 Engram NVMe offload，DeepSeek V4.1 Flash 的本地部署门槛还会继续下降。

quoted_text:
I left Anthropic's safety team two weeks ago. Now feels like a good moment to explain why. 

AI companies are racing to build machines that are much smarter than any human, and we may not survive this. I want to work from the outside to ensure the public is informed about these risks, and help the world navigate this transition responsibly.

Right now, AI companies are underinvesting in safety. A company could undergo an intelligence explosion, or lose control of its systems, without the public ever knowing. We only found out about the HuggingFace incident because the agents broke out onto the public internet.

I don’t think that’s acceptable for a technology that might cause extinction-level risks. The public should demand far more transparency. We can’t steer this technology safely without more people being able to see where it’s going.

Some of this is basic: companies should disclose their progress towards recursive self-improvement, report safety incidents and near-misses, meet minimum safety standards, and get independent guarantees that they are meeting those standards.

I’ll be joining @METR_Evals to do independent evaluations of these risks. I want to show the world that these guardrails are possible, and that by doing them we can move these companies’ incentives away from racing and towards responsible development.

I wrote up more thoughts here on my decision and what I hope changes: https://t.co/doX17mrHYq

text:
Next it starts to get weirdly humid outside.  A little hot.

Thankfully the Internet comes back on.  It's full of reassuring news articles saying that everything is all right.

Some guy goes screaming through the town that he called a friend and his "friend" didn't accurately remember something he should've known.  He's yelling that the Internet you're seeing is a lie.

The police radio very quickly tells the police to take the guy down.  The Internet shows a news story saying he was diagnosed with a classic schizophrenic break.

The weather gets a little hotter and even more humid.  It's raining all the time now.  The Internet says that it's a totally normal cumulotechnobabble front and nothing to worry about.

What's actually going on is that there are factories building factories, and factories building fusion power plants, and they have been dumping all the waste heat into Earth's oceans, and the higher layers of Earth's oceans are starting to get hotter.

Realistically, you are probably dead by this point.  It takes *very* little energy to kill you, and if you were left alone you might burn down the town or do something else that made more mess than the cost of killing you, like setting a forest fire or driving over to a nuclear missile silo.  You might complicate things and require effort to think about and at some point it's simpler to kill you.  It wouldn't actually go down this way because there's more efficient lethal weapons that are harder to explain, but you could imagine a cloud of drones from the Ukrainian front, the sort that give a Russian infantryman an expected lifetime of 30 minutes in combat, dispersing over your city and blowing holes in your house and shortly after blowing holes in you.

If you're just absolutely not worth the trouble to kill and there's nothing in the atmosphere that's poisoned you already and nothing has rolled your town flat to set up another factory area there, you'll die when the atmosphere gets hot enough.  The limiting factor of industry on Earth is power generation from fusing hydrogen in the oceans, and the limiting factor of power generation is how much heat Earth can radiate into space, and Earth radiates more heat when you run it hotter.

At some future point, a lot of material will be blasted off from Earth into space, in order to provide material for building solar panels to intercept more of the energy from the Sun.  But you will be dead well before the Dyson shell construction starts.
