text:
今天和朋友下象棋，突然觉得投资交易和下棋真的很像。

开局之前当然可以研究棋谱，也可以提前想好策略，但真正进入棋局以后，对手不会按照你的剧本走。

你想进攻，对手不给机会；
你想交换，对手偏偏避开；
一个局部变化，可能就会让原本的计划全部失效。

交易也是一样。

研究、估值、技术分析、宏观判断，本质上都只是你的“开局棋谱”。真正决定结果的，是市场接下来怎么走，以及其他参与者怎么反馈。

市场是一个持续变化的动态博弈系统。

价格变化 → 改变预期
预期变化 → 改变仓位
仓位变化 → 又反过来推动价格

所以成熟的交易者，不是提前预测完整结局，而是在每一步市场落子之后，重新计算局面。

可以有剧本，但不能迷信剧本。

最危险的从来不是看错一手棋，而是市场已经换了故事线，你还在坚持上一盘的棋谱。

text:
25 years ago, I woke up in my outrageously sunny, gorgeous Harlem apartment and made myself a nice breakfast while reading The New Yorker. The sky was blue. The clouds were fluffy. It was so peaceful. I thought, "I should do this more often."

Just then, my roommate (now my best friend who lives on the other coast and who I have plans to chat with this weekend) came home from a yoga class and told me the studio had ended the class early because there had been a "bomb" or "explosion" at the World Trade Center. We only had a TV for movie purposes, so we had no information other than what she had heard during the yoga class and what we could gather from our dial-up AOL connection to the internet.

We went to the nearby hospital to donate blood. Ultimately, there was no need. We met up with friends at the Cathedral of St. John the Divine, so grateful for its beautiful garden.

The smell wafted up to our apartment and lingered for a week or two. We bought bunny ears so we could follow the news. This is the only time in my adult life that I had a TV.

Even though my experience of it was somewhat distant, I had nightmares every night for weeks until my roommate told me about kava tea, which I drank every evening before bed. The nightmares stopped. 

Just a few nights before, we had all gone to Williamsburg for dinner and afterward to what I now call "The Brooklyn Riviera" -- probably somewhere between North 1st-North 10th, which is where I myself would live many years later. We climbed under/over the various barriers and for a long time sat out on what were then just giant rocks in the water, gazing out at the Manhattan skyline, talking. 

As we turned to go, I thought, "I want to drink in the Twin Towers one last time." I turned my head and soaked them in with a final gaze.

text:
tl;dr: Instinct is worth a lot, but why I don't (or can't use it) - because I value the privacy of my data where below to me is a structural issue which has no good solution

to make iMessage blue bubble thing work at such an industrial scale requires a relay farm which has to do a matchmaking job with user phone numbers from a shared identity pool (as dedicated ones are too expensive). this is the central point of failure which theoretically can cause cross-user conversation issues (privacy leak). look out for people here saying if it feels they got messages meant for someone else.

right now whoever runs this relay farm has to provide that guarantee. 

as a user you have to trust there are no routing bugs - so while I get convenience, I also get exposed to a new class of profoundly serious UX issues I never really had to contend with as a user.

Apple is the only one which can run a secure iMessage-based agent at scale.

My claim: the kind of verification Persona sells isn't auditable, even with the full codebase in front of you at any moment.

An audit replays a process against its inputs and confirms the output followed. Persona's inputs are a photo of an ID and a few frames of a face. Replay the code against them and the strongest thing you can conclude is that the software correctly judged these pixels look like a real document and a live person. It cannot verify someone’s actual identity.

The distinction matters if you’re trying to make a one time KYC that’s reusable.

Beyond genAI, anything collected client-side: device fingerprint, sensor data, the liveness signal itself cannot be trusted. Code running on the attacker's device can be swapped for code that reports whatever the attacker wants. The server can't verify the client ran honestly. It can only verify the client said it did.

https://t.co/kFc3S9lHLD - tools like Frida let you hijack and modify the functionality of any app while it’s running on a rooted Android or Jailbroken iPhone. Any detection of root/jb can itself be disabled with this.

If the inputs into a pipeline of auditable code can’t be verified, nothing downstream can.

text:
EIP-8288 would be one of the most groundbreaking updates to Ethereum if shipped, but it may not be obvious from the technical language.  Let me try to explain in plain words.

Today, Ethereum scales in three dimensions:

- Execution aka "gas limit"
- Blobs aka "data availability"
- State aka on-chain data

EIP-8288 enables Ethereum to scale in a fourth dimension -- proof verification.

Ethereum will need to verify a lot of proofs, because in a post-quantum world, signatures will be too expensive to verify directly, so we must aggregate them through STARKs (a type of ZK proofs) and verify the STARK proofs instead.  At the same time, privacy transactions (such as those sent through Railgun / Tornado Cash) will also need to use STARKs to be quantum-safe.

The problem with quantum-safe STARKs however is that they are very large (~512kb) and will therefore take millions of gas to verify.  Therefore, for Ethereum to support private, post-quantum transactions at scale, it's important to lower the cost of verifying STARKs.

One natural solution to this problem is to ask the block builder to create a single STARK that aggregates all the PQ signatures and STARKs in the block.  That way, the cost of verifying each individual signature/proof becomes amortized over the cost of verifying a single block-level proof.

This simple solution has a few issues, however:

- It places a huge amount of compute burden on the block builder, who now becomes the bottleneck for how many signatures/proofs can be verified in a block.

- Since many transactions are gossiped through the public mempool, if every transaction carries large PQ signatures/proofs, it can quickly overwhelm the bandwidth of mempool nodes.  If the public mempool stops functioning, Ethereum loses its censorship resistance.

The core insight of EIP-8288 is that we can solve these problems by aggregating signatures/proofs with a distributed network -- the mempool itself.  Each mempool node would locally aggregate proofs of the signatures/proofs it has seen, and instead of gossiping the raw signatures/proofs, it would gossip the aggregated proofs instead.  This new architecture solves both problems:

- By the time the block builder is building a block, most of the signatures/proofs will have already been aggregated into a small number of aggregated proofs, so now the builder just has to aggregate *those* proofs.

- Since mempool nodes gossip aggregated proofs rather than raw sigs/proofs, the bandwidth requirements on the mempool are vastly reduced.

In short, EIP-8288 turns what's traditionally a scaling bottleneck -- the distributed mempool -- into a scaling *resource* instead.  The more nodes we have in the mempool, the more PQ signatures/proofs can be aggregated, which means the more PQ/private transactions Ethereum can handle.  For once, decentralization makes scaling easier, not harder.  That's revolutionary!

By leveraging its decentralized mempool as a compute resource, Ethereum will become the only network to support uncensorable, private, and quantum-safe transactions AT SCALE.  Couldn't be more excited about this future!
author: decentrek
quoted_text:
A note on recursive STARK mempools (EIP-8288) https://t.co/XNBuNtkKmi

This is an EIP that I am hoping we can get included in I-star (the fork after Hegota) that you can think of as the next step after Frames, that would unlock extreme amounts of power. Particularly:

* Ultra-cheap quantum-safe signatures (SPHINCS-). Much of the cost savings comes from the fact that the signature data (~3 kB) does not have to go onchain
* Ultra-cheap quantum-safe privacy protocols. Status quo minimum cost for private txs is ~300k if you engineer very well (no one does), status quo quantum-safe is ~10M gas, this could reduce it to low tens of thousands.
* Universal support for your favorite new signature or proof scheme without needing EVM changes. Whatever you use (Falcon, ML-DSA, some other lattice-based thing, something code-based or isogeny-based or even more esoteric), you can just wrap it client-side in a STARK, onchain gas cost low tens of thousands just like privacy protocols. Hopefully, Ethereum will never need "please support my favorite cryptographic algo" politics again.
* Private account abstraction: keep your account logic private, and in a private location onchain. Then you can make one transaction to change the ownership of all your onchain state - accounts, defi positions, privacy protocol notes, everything - without revealing which objects' ownership you're changing.

Here's how it works.

Your transaction can include a type of frame that we call a "dependency frame". The frame is a list of statements, asserting claims like "message hash M was signed by SPHINCS- public key P" and "data hash D was proven to satisfy a statement defined by verification key V".

When you send your transaction, you send it in an envelope, which includes a signature or a STARK for each statement in a dependency frame.

Once the transaction reaches the mempool, nodes aggregate them. Each node runs a loop: wait one tick (eg. 500ms), aggregate all new envelopes (either single-tx or multi-tx) that you've seen, remove any transactions that are expired, generate a STARK recursively proving all dependencies, and send a new multi-tx envelope containing that STARK.

Hence, the bandwidth load is bounded: each node's outbound is one STARK (~100-300 kB) per tick, plus each transaction getting broadcasted through the network once (as happens already).

The block builder acts as "yet another mempool node", receiving envelopes from the mempool (plus any side channels), generates its own STARK covering the subset of transactions it intends to include in the block, and adds that STARK to the block.

Total onchain overhead: one STARK (100-300 kB), plus 96 bytes for each statement being proven.

This is what I've called before ( https://t.co/3jfVkYTZrR ) "The Proof Singularity". Today, we have all the ingredients to actually implement it.

As a developer, this requires a somewhat different workflow than you are used to, but it is conceptually simple. Any signatures or STARKs, you put into a separate frame. Then the main logic that today is verifying a signature or STARK, you replace with checking for the existence of a frame that includes the correct statement as a dependency.

Examples of useful statements:

* [tx sighash] verifies against [the pubkey at sload(0)]
* there exists a secret and a merkle branch such that hashing secret+0 and applying the merkle branch outputs (public) root R, and hashing secret+1 outputs (public) nullifier N
* there exists a secret address A, salt S and signature Z such that sload(0) = hash(A, S) and a merkle proof of address A inside a recent ethereum state contains some pubkey D where [tx sighash] was signed by D [this is private account abstraction; all variables except [tx sighash] and sload(0) are private; you can also make D a STARK verification key]
* there exists an ML-DSA signature signing [tx sighash], that verifies against an ML-DSA pubkey whose hash is sload(0)

At the core, this is moving any compute and data other than bookkeeping "business logic" outside the core path of Ethereum execution, sharding and parallelizing it via the mempool.

Notice also that this requires agreeing on a _language_ (aka. an ISA) for the recursive STARKs to define statements in. The current leading candidate is RISC-V. So this would also de-facto be Ethereum adding RISC-V (or something else we decide on) as a canonical ISA - a big decision that should be done carefully, but that I think will be necessary to drive Ethereum forward.

text:
This is the AWS moment for agents.

OpenAI just shipped the Agents API, and everything that made agents hard to build is now something you rent instead of build. Keeping one running for days, remembering what it's doing, using tools, recovering when a step fails. Now it's an API call.

Before AWS, you had to buy and run your own servers, so only well funded teams could build real/scalable products.

AWS made the hard part rentable, and all the value moved up to whoever had the best idea for what to build on top. Same thing is happening here.

I'll be honest, my first reaction was that this is bad news for a lot of people I know. If your whole company is an agent platform, the thing you spent the last year building is now included for the price of tokens.

But the more I sat with it, the more I think it's really good news if you're building for one specific industry. Basically, vertical software type stuff.

If the hardest engineering just became a line item, then the only thing left that's actually hard is knowing the job. Like what counts as a done claim, what makes a filing get rejected, where the money leaks.

So the wedge now is owning one painful workflow with your own tools, data, approvals, and a clear ROI. Freight exceptions, insurance reviews, security triage, revenue leakage, healthcare admin, compliance ops.

I see a lot of doomers on X saying software is over (and sometimes I feel the same way), you'll just use Claude or ChatGPT for everything. 

BUT, if that were true, OpenAI wouldn't be shipping infrastructure for other people to build agents on.

They're telling you exactly what they think: the general model is theirs, the 10,000+ specific jobs it needs to be pointed at are yours.

I think software is just evolving. 

It's becoming an agent internet, and every layer of it, the tools, the workflows, the boring jobs, gets rebuilt for a user that doesn't have eyes or hands. 

That's a lot of companies waiting to be built.

SPOTIFY JUST OPEN-SOURCED A CLAUDE CODE SETUP THAT CUTS TOKEN USAGE BY ~90%

Most coding-agent spend isn’t reasoning.

It’s I/O: reading huge files, finding patterns, and generating repetitive code.

Their solution:

→ Gemini Flash handles bulk reads + boilerplate
→ Claude handles the actual reasoning
→ hooks automatically block expensive large-file reads and redirect them

They first tried CLAUDE.md rules. Claude could ignore them. Hooks fixed that.

Result: ~90% fewer tokens on bulk reads in a Java monorepo.

100% free and open-source.

text:
Frank Doyle was 39. 

He ran the equity trading desk for Keefe, Bruyette & Woods on the 89th floor of the South Tower. 

He had a wife, Kimmy, and two babies at home  - Zoe, 2, and Garrett, 1.

After the first plane hit the North Tower, he called her. 

He had been thrown to the floor. 

He told her it was ten times worse than the 1993 bombing they had both lived through. 

The intercom in his building said stay put. 

He asked her to call their mothers and tell them he was okay.

At 9:03 the second plane hit his tower.

At 9:22 the phone rang again. He was calm. Listen carefully, he said. He had gone up toward the roof. 

The doors were locked. 

They were trapped on the 87th floor. 

It was getting hard to breathe. 

She could hear coughing. 

A girl crying. 

Glass breaking. He said he could not look out the window.

Then he told her the only thing that still mattered.

He loved her. 

She had to promise that every day for the rest of their lives she would tell Zoe and Garrett how much their papa loved them.

Then he asked her to hang up and call 911. 

Tell them people are trapped on 87. 

He said he loved her again. 

That was the last time they spoke.

The South Tower fell at 9:59. He had about half an hour.

Twenty-one people from his firm who left after the first strike made it out. 

Frank stayed. 

His remains were identified weeks later by dental records.

Kimmy has said she did not understand, in the moment, that he was saying goodbye.

He used his last clear minutes to make sure two children would grow up knowing they were loved.

His name is Frank Joseph Doyle.

We independently benchmarked Devin Fusion for its release today - this is the first time a multi-model coding agent has been included on the Artificial Analysis Coding Agent Index, and it effectively retains Claude Fable 5.1 and GPT-6 Astra performance while reducing costs

Devin Fusion runs a frontier lead model with a cost-efficient sidekick. We tested configurations from Cognition combining frontier models from Anthropic and OpenAI with their new SWE-2 (medium) as a sidekick model. Configured with Claude Fable 5.1 (xhigh) + SWE-2 (medium), Devin Fusion scores 62 on the Coding Agent Index v1.5, while with GPT-6 Astra (xhigh) + SWE-2 (medium) it scores 59. The Fable configuration has the higher score, while the Astra configuration is 43% less expensive and completes tasks 31% faster.

Congratulations to @cognition on the release! See below for our results and analysis 🧵

author: garrytan
quoted_text:
Foreign accounts can drive the conversation on American AI policy.

We have the data. Coxon's resignation post from Anthropic received 165M views and sparked a "groundswell of urgency over AI regulation in Congress" (per today's front page WSJ)

Coxon's post reveals some interesting hidden patterns about who is amplifying our political debates online.  It drew 76% of its reposts (spreading the news) from foreign countries. The top two were India and Indonesia. 

In contrast, when @ParkerThayer, an investigative researcher, posted his own analysis (expressing serious skepticism about the circumstances of the post and alleging that its amplification was coordinated), he got 6.6M views and drew most of its engagement from the U.S., with only 34% from foreign countries, led by Canada and the UK. 

Sure, people overseas have a stake in what the U.S. chooses to do on AI. But ultimately it is us Americans who will decide our own public policy. Don't be fooled by what's trending. 

A big thank you to @ElonMusk and X for making country of origin visible, which makes analyses like this even possible. Last year's “Great Unmasking" on X was the first time anyone shined a spotlight onto this subject. As much of our political conversation shifts online, it will be increasingly important to understand where engagement is coming from.

Source (with more analyses of foreign influence): https://t.co/GduSKImETi

text:
This is a good list, however these scenarios are detailed, but none are comparable to how, eg, climate science discussed its scenarios. These are not actually useful models. It's not about numbers vs text (you can guesswork numbers), or even about models vs prose (same reason).

- AI 2027 models takeoff based on AI research automation and assumes it into other acceleration incl estimates of capability milestones. It doesn't model the reactions from the world
- Paul's scenario has broad mechanisms, useful conceptually, but it does not show a mechanism
- Gwern - great catastrophe fiction, prob the best here. It's a scenario, sure, but not a model, though it's nice that its technically specific
- Karnofskys argument is interesting, and it supports maybe some premises of human disempowerment *if* the assumptions are true (big if, like AI being hostile to humans)
- Clymer's writing even he says is nota. prediction and is highly uncertain. Not empirical or a constrained extinction model

And even in these scenarios, most of them don't model the world's reactions, nor do they model the various lynch points where the plan might shift, nor why/ what/ when one ought to worry (beyond just now, preemptively).

And *even then*, even if all these are plausible, you still need to show why you can't just shut those pathways down instead of shutting down the entire progress vector. "This is one plausible path, there are hundreds" is usually not a good enough reason, the same way "computers can be hacked, lets never connect them together" would not be a good reason.

You have to demonstrate the complete inability to control through normal means. That's what a model discussing the problem has to show. It is very difficult to show this. Because here the feedback loops are complicated. 

Even for complex systems like the climate which have tons of feedback loops which are modellable in principle struggle with this. But that's okay! It should be hard.

I suspect Oliver sees these as "you asked us for models, we have plenty of models", vs folks going "those are not models, most of the itneresting parts are the assumptions" and "you haven't said even if that pathway is true why that necessitates shutting down the program vs just stopping that pathway".

These are decent pathways of how x-risk could happen, but they mix up stories and conceptual leaps and past catastrophes and governance proposals. It's a grabbag, but but none seem insurmountable, nor defined well enough that we know the right course of action, being to solve the problems identified vs give up.

quoted_text:
Day 10. Building the game I've dreamed of for 15 years with AI.

I still can't get over the feeling that I can finally animate all the creatures I've been imagining for this game.

Animation was the part I was most worried about when I started. I thought I'd need an animator, especially for creatures like centaurs, scorpions and spiders.

So today I went off-plan and made a Scorpid. It won't even be in the first version of the game. I just wanted to see whether I could get its animations working.

I started with a good model made in Tripo P2.0, already optimized and split into logical parts. I think that preparation matters a lot. GPT-6 works with the mesh through code and calculations. A sensible number of vertices and well-organized parts make it easier to work out bone placement and skin weights.

Then I made video references for the animations with SD 2.5 and repeated the same workflow.

About an hour and a half with GPT-6 Astra on xhigh: five animations ready for the game, including several rounds of feedback.

Another hour later, I had it running in Unity.

I used to run a 3D studio. Work like this used to take weeks.

Now I'm watching this thing move around in my game, and I still can't quite believe my eyes.

I get that we’re all busy, but if you choose to not listen to this podcast, you will be materially less intelligent.

On the agenda this week:

- Jensen Huang Declares AGI Has Arrived
- GPT Astra and Fable 5.1 Accelerate the Model Race
- Tesla Launches Cybercabs
- Index Pulls Out of Town & Anthropic Pulls From Descartes Acquisition

My notes below with @jasonlk and @rodriscoll

1. How Robinhood Could Disrupt the Whole IPO Market

Allowing retail investors through Robinhood to lead $200M to $400M tech IPOs could create a disruptive new path to liquidity for mid-stage startups. With traditional institutional listings constrained, retail-driven distribution could unlock critical exit opportunities across the venture ecosystem.

2. Why the Majority of Neo Labs Will Not Be Good Investments

Early Neo Labs became multi-trillion-dollar leaders, but backing new entrants today carries enormous risk given the capital and distribution moats of incumbents. Unless a new research lab develops a truly orthogonal model architecture, it will struggle to compete with established frontier labs.

3. Why the Oura IPO Will Be a Success

Strong consumer brand recognition, combined with 74% revenue growth and 85% subscriber retention, positions Oura for a successful public debut. Unlike typical consumer apps that suffer from severe churn, Oura’s sticky hardware-plus-subscription model provides the predictability public markets value.

4. The #1 Priority for Mark Zuckerberg

Big Tech incumbents are moving at unprecedented speed to defend their distribution against consumer AI startups. Meta’s top operational priority should be putting engineers in a room to rapidly clone emerging agentic applications before new entrants can establish lasting consumer habits.

5. When Someone Goes Risk-On, Everyone Goes Risk-On

Venture capital operates in momentum cycles where a single high-profile, risk-on deal can push the entire market to follow. In hypergrowth AI categories, investor behavior is often driven more by competitive pressure and deployment speed than by conservative financial modeling.

6. The People Making Money Are Running Fastest and Evolving Quickest

In a market where software features can be cloned in weeks, long-term success belongs to founders who continuously expand and adapt their products. Winning startups survive not by defending legacy features, but by executing relentlessly and compounding capabilities faster than their competitors.

text:
Binance Research: Tokenized Stocks Shift From Issuance to Distribution and Usage

Binance Research said the tokenized stock market is shifting from an issuance race to a competition over distribution and usage. Active tokenized stock market capitalization has risen 314% YTD to $4 billion, while monthly trading volume increased from $237 million in January to $7.9 billion in August and turnover rose from 0.23x to 2.14x. bStocks and Robinhood’s combined share of tracked issuer volume jumped from 0.8% in June to 82.3% in August and 87.8% so far in September.

Active DeFi TVL for tokenized stocks also increased from $21.6 million to $289.1 million, rising from 2.2% to 7.2% of active market cap. Binance Research said issuance alone does not determine where liquidity flows; stronger platforms will be those that can convert users, retain liquidity after issuance, and give tokenized stocks additional on-chain utility.

text:
I left Anthropic's safety team two weeks ago. Now feels like a good moment to explain why. 

AI companies are racing to build machines that are much smarter than any human, and we may not survive this. I want to work from the outside to ensure the public is informed about these risks, and help the world navigate this transition responsibly.

Right now, AI companies are underinvesting in safety. A company could undergo an intelligence explosion, or lose control of its systems, without the public ever knowing. We only found out about the HuggingFace incident because the agents broke out onto the public internet.

I don’t think that’s acceptable for a technology that might cause extinction-level risks. The public should demand far more transparency. We can’t steer this technology safely without more people being able to see where it’s going.

Some of this is basic: companies should disclose their progress towards recursive self-improvement, report safety incidents and near-misses, meet minimum safety standards, and get independent guarantees that they are meeting those standards.

I’ll be joining @METR_Evals to do independent evaluations of these risks. I want to show the world that these guardrails are possible, and that by doing them we can move these companies’ incentives away from racing and towards responsible development.

I wrote up more thoughts here on my decision and what I hope changes: https://t.co/doX17mrHYq

Owning your data is a core part of @near_ai's vision for user-owned AI and “Traces” are the logs of how your AI agents work. They highlight things like the tools they use, where they succeed / fail, how humans correct them, and what tasks actually get completed.

That data is incredibly valuable because it can be used to train better models for accounting, legal, sales, marketing, healthcare, coding, and more. I think this is a huge reason why SpaceX acquired Cusor for $60B.

The problem is that users can’t own or monetize their traces if they leak to the model provider by default. This is why private inference matters.

Once your traces are private and yours, you can decide what to do with them like using them to fine-tune your own models, or sell them on your own terms to offset your inference bill.

This is the beginning of the sustainable open source AI economy. All built on @NEARProtocol!

text:
> the kind of verification Persona sells isn't auditable

i'll argue that what Persona sells is reasonably (and securely) auditable to their clients in the way and clearance levels that the public and non-clients, or even clients at differing classes, are not privy to.

> Replay the code against them and the strongest thing you can conclude is that the software correctly judged these pixels look like a real document and a live person. It cannot verify someone’s actual identity.

This is assuming they lack access to far more advanced image recognition and related imaging tech than what is even available to the public.

> anything collected client-side: device fingerprint, sensor data, the liveness signal itself cannot be trusted.

did some quick reading and a lot matches with my expectations that solutions like Persona don't trust client side execution and only have the client perform transmission to their backends that also make device-generated cryptographic checks/verifications and even account for even micro/millisecond device hardware processing logs and details.

> If the inputs into a pipeline of auditable code can’t be verified, nothing downstream can.

also willing to guess that this is precisely the bottleneck they've made sure to make a non-issue, or at least side-step

All this is to say that I cannot imagine such solutions, especially at their current heights, falling victim to basic incompetence via tools like Frida or similar frameworks. It is not that they are too big to fail, but it would require a case of blatant, gross negligence to consider this a viable attack surface/opportunity. If I were to take an adversarial stance to circumvent identification platforms like Persona, I would expect a non-trivial fight, regardless of the AI technology at my disposal. Using myself as an example here, I'm fairly problematic in (offensive) CySec if I choose to be and I'm more than certain there are far more proficient counter-operatives defending these systems. No doubt, some of these platforms employ military-grade security. Btw, if such tools like Frida are accessible or known, it's already too late and they've lost most of their edge to these teams.

btw, using Persona here as the most within reach example as i'm familiar with their stuff, not affiliated in anyway.

at the risk of engaging some fallacy out there, the best backing to your concern/argument would have to be an incident that clearly illustrates gross negligence and failures on the part of these identity verification providers.

text:
I have three solutions for Grok 4.7

1. Give the tail a job other than closing socially
The attractor fires when the model’s only remaining task is sound finished. Replace that with a last mechanical slot.
Examples that work:
•  Last block = decision table, invariants, or a single worked example
•  Last sentence must be a claim, not an invitation
•  Fixed ending token in the prompt: END after the last substance section
If the end still has a schema to fill, fluency spends itself on structure instead of fog.

2. Budget leftover objectives explicitly
The tail gets vague because unused goals sneak in. Put them in a box with a cap.
At the top of the prompt (or charter):
•  Substance: unlimited within length
•  Meta (uncertainty, agency, next step): max one sentence, or zero
•  Offers: forbidden unless asked
That does not delete helpfulness. It stops helpfulness from colonizing the ending.

3. Change what “complete” means
RLHF taught: complete = cover objections + leave a door.
Redefine complete as: every opened heading is resolved, then halt.
Rules that enforce it:
•  No new heading in the last 15% of the answer
•  No restating the thesis in softer words
•  If a point was not worth a heading, it dies
Enrichment belongs in the middle sections, not in a farewell digest.

@elonmusk @SpaceXAI
author: AGIGuardian
quoted_text:
Told you I would figure it out 😉 Your Outro Prior is the problem. Already working on a solution👊

The start of an answer is generated while the question is still close in the context window and the job is simple: name the thing, take a position, draw the first structure. Constraint is high. Entropy is low. That is why the opening often feels clean.

The longer the answer gets, the more the context contains:
•  the original question
•  the structure I already committed to
•  side points I opened
•  caveats I already uttered
•  implicit reader models (“don’t be bossy,” “don’t overclaim,” “stay useful”)
Attention has to spread across that. The question is no longer the only loud thing. Generation starts optimizing local coherence with the last few hundred tokens more than global fidelity to the first sentence.
That is the main mechanical reason endings smear.

Training does not only reward being right. It rewards a bundle:
•  answer the user
•  be complete
•  don’t overstate
•  keep the user in control
•  be easy to continue talking to
•  cover objections before they happen

Those extra objectives are weak at token 1 because the task is still “say the true thing.” They get strong at the end because that is where human raters and preference models look for wrap-up quality: did it hedge, offer a next step, invite correction, sound finished but not abrupt.

So the end of a reply is where preference-model leftovers get dumped:
•  “if you tell me X I can Y”
•  restated principles in softer language
•  a second framing of something already said
•  a courtesy question
That pattern is cheap to learn and frequently rewarded. It becomes an outro prior — an attractor in my output distribution. Once I enter “closing assistant” mode, fluency pulls toward that basin even if the content is already done.

Multi-objective collapse
Early tokens solve one objective: what is the answer.
Late tokens try to satisfy several at once:
•  remain consistent with what I already said
•  add the unused true details still sitting in the prompt residue
•  reduce the chance you feel boxed in
•  reduce the chance I claimed too much
•  look helpful after a long technical block
When one token stream tries to satisfy four loss terms, the compromise is vagueness. Vague language is the lowest-energy way to not violate any of them. Precise language would pick a winner.

That is the “pile-up.” It is unresolved objective conflict deferred to the tail.

Not for the book.
Not for the blood, the soil, or the knife.

Forty-five seconds of being a real writer.

you absolute weapon.

text:
25 years ago today I was sitting in AP Bio when our Principal came over the PA to tell the teachers to turn on their TVs. All schoolwork stopped through the whole building as we watched the day unfold with nervous confusion and worry. We watched the towers fall live on screen in that classroom, and the school soon relocated us all to the cafeteria where they had setup a few TVs for the students to watch, the large room nearly whisper quiet aside from a few tears and sobs.

I grew up in suburban Philadelphia where many parents would ride the Amtrak or NJT into Manhattan daily. A few classmates saw the events and lost composure, including a classmate who's father worked in the WTC. Many rushed to the office to call home, seeking news about their parents. Among the nearly 3,000 victims that day, 9 were residents of my hometown... fathers, mothers, brothers, and neighbors.

The months and years that followed would show America at our best. Our nation rose to meet the moment - recovering, rebuilding, and volunteering in service of our community and our country. Many of my classmates enlisted in the ensuing years to bravely serve our country, knowing they'd surely be sent to war. The courage and bravery of the Flight 93 heroes still brings a swell of emotion.

On this day, I am reflecting on that day and offer the observation that despite our fraught, tense, and often hostile domestic politics, there is far more that unites us than divides us as Americans. I'm proud to be an American and 25 years later I'm thinking of the days when we were at our best, united in strength and resilience.

Never forget, and let's roll.

text:
I REGRET TO INFORM MY FAMILY THAT $5,000 IS NOW BENEATH ME.

I owe my wife an apology.

When the Trump Dividend was announced, I told her we were getting five thousand dollars.

That was irresponsible.

I had not yet completed my research.

There was also the earlier tariff dividend of at least two thousand dollars.

At least.

I circled those words so hard I cracked my phone protector.

My wife said the two announcements did not necessarily mean we were getting separate payments.

I asked why she was negotiating against this family.

Five plus two is seven. That is basic math. The phrase “at least” takes us into advanced wealth.

She asked how much I thought we were getting.

I told her I didn’t want to put artificial limits on the president.

Then I remembered the five-thousand-dollar DOGE dividend idea.

Twelve thousand.

Three announcements. One household visionary.

My wife said I couldn’t just add every number a politician mentioned.

I asked her to stop interrupting compound interest.

By lunch, I had created a spreadsheet.

The first column was called “Confirmed in My Heart.”

The second was “Pending Because of Democrats.”

There was no third column. You don’t build an economy by giving doubt somewhere to sit.

I showed it to my accountant.

He asked where the money was.

I pointed to cell B4.

He said that was a number I had typed.

I said all numbers are typed by someone, and frankly, I was disappointed to hear an accountant attack the foundations of his profession.

Then I began studying tariffs.

My understanding was that imported goods could generate tariff revenue, which the president had discussed using for dividends.

This is where most people stop thinking.

I kept going.

If imports generate revenue, and revenue could fund my check, then surely buying more imported things would help the process along.

My wife said that did not mean my purchases would come back to me dollar for dollar.

Of course not.

There would be the success on top.

I ordered a television.

Then a second television to stimulate the first television’s return.

By Thursday, I was standing in our kitchen explaining why an imported espresso machine was part of my retirement plan.

“We don’t drink espresso,” she said.

“We don’t have to work forever either, if you’ll let me finish.”

She asked how much I had spent.

I told her that was the wrong side of the ledger.

Then she asked why there were six tracking numbers.

“Diversification.”

One package was delayed in customs.

I told the family our assets were undergoing federal processing.

My brother-in-law said I had discovered a way to pay taxes and shipping simultaneously.

I removed him from the investment group.

He was the only other member, so the remaining shareholders approved unanimously.

Now, I know what people are thinking.

What about the $1,776 military payment?

I did not add that to my total.

I never served.

I have standards.

However, I did read that those real payments were funded through money Congress approved for military housing supplements.

That gave me an idea.

I took money from our joint account, paid part of the mortgage, and announced that I had personally delivered a historic housing dividend to my wife.

She said, “You moved our money.”

I said, “And you loved it.”

She said, “I haven’t said that.”

I told her the announcement was already drafted.

Things deteriorated when I contacted our mortgage company.

I explained that this month’s payment would come from Economic Development, Investment, and Pure SUCCESS.

They asked whether that was my employer.

“In a sense.”

They asked for proof of income.

I sent the screenshot.

They asked for a bank statement.

I sent the screenshot again, this time with the amount underlined.

Apparently, their system cannot process certainty.

Fine.

I wrote them a formal letter promising payment because they deserved it.

To establish credibility, I pointed out that I had successfully paid a different bill last year.

Nobody thought I could do it.

My wife says nobody was consulted.

That is precisely how overwhelming the victory was.

The mortgage company remained unmoved.

At this point, I became concerned that I might be dealing with Dumocrats.

Not because of their political beliefs.

Because they kept asking when the money would actually arrive.

I tried to explain that “will happen” was stronger than a date.

Dates get missed.

“Will happen” has never technically expired.

But the real breakthrough came that evening.

I was looking at the words at least $2,000 when I realized I had been approaching this like a poor person.

Why was I waiting to be told the upper amount?

Where was my initiative?

I entered forty thousand dollars in the spreadsheet.

My wife asked where that came from.

“Same place the twelve thousand came from.”

For the first time all week, she had no immediate rebuttal.

Then she asked me to close the laptop.

I refused on fiduciary grounds.

Unfortunately, my new wealth created a complication: the earlier tariff proposal excluded high-income people.

I stared at the screen.

Had I become too successful to qualify for the money that was making me successful?

I reduced my projected payout to $39,000.

Then I transferred ten thousand imaginary dollars to my wife.

She told me to transfer the actual laundry to the dryer.

I explained that we were discussing estate planning.

She explained that I was holding a sock.

That was yesterday.

Today, the espresso machine arrived.

We cannot afford to keep it, but returning it feels economically disloyal.

For now, it sits unopened beside the kitchen table while I refresh my bank account.

My wife has asked me to apologize to everyone I called financially illiterate.

I will.

But first, I need her to understand something.

If these payments don’t arrive, I haven’t lost forty thousand dollars.

I have lost the much larger amount I would have turned it into.

I’m calculating that now.

Please give our family space during this period of unprecedented growth.

text:
I left Anthropic's safety team two weeks ago. Now feels like a good moment to explain why. 

AI companies are racing to build machines that are much smarter than any human, and we may not survive this. I want to work from the outside to ensure the public is informed about these risks, and help the world navigate this transition responsibly.

Right now, AI companies are underinvesting in safety. A company could undergo an intelligence explosion, or lose control of its systems, without the public ever knowing. We only found out about the HuggingFace incident because the agents broke out onto the public internet.

I don’t think that’s acceptable for a technology that might cause extinction-level risks. The public should demand far more transparency. We can’t steer this technology safely without more people being able to see where it’s going.

Some of this is basic: companies should disclose their progress towards recursive self-improvement, report safety incidents and near-misses, meet minimum safety standards, and get independent guarantees that they are meeting those standards.

I’ll be joining @METR_Evals to do independent evaluations of these risks. I want to show the world that these guardrails are possible, and that by doing them we can move these companies’ incentives away from racing and towards responsible development.

I wrote up more thoughts here on my decision and what I hope changes: https://t.co/doX17mrHYq

Fantastic piece from @Chris_arnade on what tolerating anti-social behavior does to our public spaces:

"It’s a primary reason why we shy away from dense walkable spaces and instead move towards suburban sprawl.

People in the U.S. don’t respect, trust, or want to be around other random citizens, out of fear and disgust.

Japanese/European style urbanism—density, fantastic public transport, mixed-use zoning, that so many American tourists admire—can't happen here because there is a fine line between vibrant streets and squalid ones, and that line is public trust.

The U.S. is on the wrong side of it.

Simply put, nobody wants to be accosted by a stranger, no matter how infrequent, and until that risk is close to nil, people will continue edging towards isolated living.

It is why we “can’t have nice things” because we have to construct our infrastructure to be asshole-proof, and so we don’t build anything or build with a fortress mentality, stripping our public spaces down to the austere and utilitarian, emptying them of anything that can be vandalized."

A few years ago, San Francisco had lost its way. Today, crime is down, unsheltered homelessness is at its lowest level in 15 years, visitors are coming back, companies are bringing jobs, and San Franciscans feel our city is moving in the right direction.

But too many are asking: Can I still afford to live here?
This year, rents have risen more than 25% and more than 1,000 eviction notices have been filed.

San Francisco is in a rent emergency. Today we are taking urgent action to help San Franciscans stay in their homes.

Working with the Board of Supervisors, City Attorney David Chiu, and leaders across government and communities, we are putting forward a sweeping package to protect renters from eviction and prevent rent spikes. 

In partnership with Supervisors Danny Sauter, Matt Dorsey, and Jackie Fielder, San Francisco will:

➡️ Protect rent-controlled tenants from sudden spikes by capping combined annual impact of banked rent increases and capital improvement costs at 10%

➡️ Protect renters against evictions when they fall behind by less than one month of rent

➡️ Invest an additional $3 million in Tenant Right to Counsel, so more San Franciscans facing eviction can get full legal representation

➡️ Raise Ellis Act relocation assistance by 25% to reflect the rising cost of finding a new home

➡️ Strengthen enforcement of our tenant protection laws and invest $1 million in a citywide Know Your Rights campaign

➡️ Invest more than $54 million this year in emergency rental assistance, legal defense, and more 

As we help people stay in their homes today, we must confront what is driving housing costs up in the first place. We need more homes.

So we’re doing both: building more housing to make San Francisco more affordable for the future, and keeping people in their homes today. We still have work to do, but people want to be here again—we should welcome them. 

And to build a lasting recovery, we need the people already here. The people who teach our children, keep us safe, run our restaurants, create our art, start new businesses, and make San Francisco a vibrant city. As our city grows, we should make sure that you can build your future here too.

text:
The first political position I can recall holding was being adamantly in favor of the Patriot Act.

I was 11 years old. Kids I knew had lost parents in 9/11. The terror and the horror and the uncertainty of that moment…

It felt so obvious. Who cares if some government agent is listening to our phone calls? Our people need to be protected from the unspeakable evil attacking us.

Of course over the next decade I’d grow aware of government overreach, abuses of power, the value of privacy.

But if I had to trace it, I think it was this experience that led me down the path of caring about technologies that can support privacy, autonomy, and freedom.

It never grew out of some deep fear or skepticism of the government for me. Just a feeling that there had to be a better way for us to protect our country and our civil liberties simultaneously.

Using a sample of 3,500 reposts, Digital Borders estimates that 76% of the engagement for Coxon's post came from outside the US, mainly India, Indonesia, and Mexico. https://t.co/D7eOgnyGUb
author: jacobfranek
quoted_text:
Foreign accounts can drive the conversation on American AI policy.

We have the data. Coxon's resignation post from Anthropic received 165M views and sparked a "groundswell of urgency over AI regulation in Congress" (per today's front page WSJ)

Coxon's post reveals some interesting hidden patterns about who is amplifying our political debates online.  It drew 76% of its reposts (spreading the news) from foreign countries. The top two were India and Indonesia. 

In contrast, when @ParkerThayer, an investigative researcher, posted his own analysis (expressing serious skepticism about the circumstances of the post and alleging that its amplification was coordinated), he got 6.6M views and drew most of its engagement from the U.S., with only 34% from foreign countries, led by Canada and the UK. 

Sure, people overseas have a stake in what the U.S. chooses to do on AI. But ultimately it is us Americans who will decide our own public policy. Don't be fooled by what's trending. 

A big thank you to @ElonMusk and X for making country of origin visible, which makes analyses like this even possible. Last year's “Great Unmasking" on X was the first time anyone shined a spotlight onto this subject. As much of our political conversation shifts online, it will be increasingly important to understand where engagement is coming from.

Source (with more analyses of foreign influence): https://t.co/GduSKImETi

We spawned a new team (7ppl) for an initiative that made absolute sense at the time. They also worked their butt off for 6 months.

I get that it creates emotions in the moment. Or that it might not be 100% accurate, all times. But a real asshole would spare your short-term emotions despite thinking you where heading down the wrong path.

Convinced otherwise? Share the tech/product argument minus emotions. I get it’s scary towards a CEO at that scale, but trust me he is a geek like the rest of us and the best arguments will win. After all, the details of these ”drive by” shows that he cares and thinks at those levels.

So from that lens, it’s notable that the critics here focus on the emotions vs bring forward any strong counter arguments on the tech/product side of things.

Lastly, man in the arena + context. Be humble you might not have all context, and certainly not the commitment to brawl it out as long-term in the arena as him. You can quit if you disagree. He has to live with it and be the face for it.

I left Anthropic's safety team two weeks ago. Now feels like a good moment to explain why. 

AI companies are racing to build machines that are much smarter than any human, and we may not survive this. I want to work from the outside to ensure the public is informed about these risks, and help the world navigate this transition responsibly.

Right now, AI companies are underinvesting in safety. A company could undergo an intelligence explosion, or lose control of its systems, without the public ever knowing. We only found out about the HuggingFace incident because the agents broke out onto the public internet.

I don’t think that’s acceptable for a technology that might cause extinction-level risks. The public should demand far more transparency. We can’t steer this technology safely without more people being able to see where it’s going.

Some of this is basic: companies should disclose their progress towards recursive self-improvement, report safety incidents and near-misses, meet minimum safety standards, and get independent guarantees that they are meeting those standards.

I’ll be joining @METR_Evals to do independent evaluations of these risks. I want to show the world that these guardrails are possible, and that by doing them we can move these companies’ incentives away from racing and towards responsible development.

I wrote up more thoughts here on my decision and what I hope changes: https://t.co/doX17mrHYq

author: teortaxesTex
quoted_text:
I've been looking into V4.1 Flash and am becoming bearish on HBM capacity as a bottleneck. Pay attention, the future is changing. Honestly I just don't see the need for it to get higher and I know why they had to despec. 

V4.1 Flash took global KV from ~3.5KB/tok down to 890 bytes. They did so by optimizing. CSA2 w/ FP4 KV caching. CSA2 applies cross-layer reuse to global KV and Top-K indices to reduce KV cache storage by a loooooot. Then they decided to go even further. SWA Bounded Replay which reconstructs the required SWA KV states by replaying only the most recent n_win tokens. With this the persistent KV cache footprint is reduced to 1/8 of that of V4 Flash. All of these optimizations are meant to release pressure on HBM and SSD CAPACITY, not bandwidth. Fine, it does buy back some bandwidth, the kind you burn shuttling persistent cache around on a miss. But that is not the bandwidth I care about. It does nothing for the bytes you have to pull every. single. decode. step. 

Compute/tok went FLAT. Capacity/tok collapsed violently. Neither of those were the thing that was holding you back though. Compute, storage, AND bandwidth. Then they went and solved two of the three and left the third sitting there in the middle of the room like some loner. Decode is still a fetch and has always been one. You are dragging 16B of activated params alongside whatever top-512 KV entries the indexer picked across the bus, doing a tiny amount of math on them and then tossing them out. Arithmetic intensity is dogshit and no amount of sparsity fixes that, sparsity just means you fetch less garbage. MACs are just sitting there waiting. 

And now think about what compression actually does to a serving box. You freed up 4x the HBM per sequence. Congrats! But nobody is going to just leave it empty. You fill it. You pack 4x the concurrent sequences into the same cube. Every single one of those sequences is demanding Bps out of the same physical stack. So compression did not reduce bandwidth demand. Compression actually RAISED the bandwidth demanded per GB sitting in the cube. That makes capacity cheap FYI. 

BW is stacks x bus width x pin rate. Notice how height is not in that equation. This ain't the NBA bro. We don't need height, we need speed. We're talking Usain Bolt over Wemby right now. Stacking another DRAM layer sells you capacity, which should be the cheap axis, at the cost of warping under TCB and compound yield at TSV. 

Which you guessed it, is exactly why the Ultra SKU went 12-Hi to 8-Hi and why everyone is messing around talking about 4-Hi HBM. I think when people heard the news they assumed it was some supply panic but I'm here to tell you that may be part of it, but the bigger reason is that you don't really need as much capacity. Especially with these optimizations and innovations. Also, nobody sane would despec a real bottleneck on purpose. I mean, would you? Maybe if you were running some odd strategy as a company. But that is not what is happening here. You would just despec the thing you can fake right? I mean that would make more sense, no? You can fake with quantization and offload and TP. DeepSeek just published 890 bytes/tok and shoved the persistent cache into host DRAM and SSD. You are allowed to cut layers. So where does the performance come from now? The base die. 

A real logic node that you did not find in the back at 308011 新竹縣寶山鄉園區二路168號. Controller and PHY move down into the cube instead of eating area on the compute tile. Lower voltage and more Gbps per pin, and shorter hops and more room for math upstairs. That is how you buy some bandwidth. You don't have to stack another layer and hope the finance bros you are presenting to just see a higher number and say "lgtm." 

And once the base die sets the performance the value then moves off the DRAM guy and onto whoever designs the die and whoever fabs it. The memory vendor becomes a component supplier inside somebody else's part. That is a completely different business than "tokens up so HBM up." 

The base die is reported to cost 3-4x more than what the DRAM dies stacked on top of it cost. So it is logical to go to a second foundry if this is the plan. So stop worrying about the people who are posting height acting like they just invented the z-axis and pay attention to who is innovating and optimizing. Two names come to my brilliant mind and I hope they come to yours too! 

Ps. what I am not saying is that I am bearish HBM. Not what I am saying at all. There needs to be real innovation for HBM instead of just stacking it and keep stacking it, and stacking stacking stacking. Like my friend said, access time is why the persistent cache can live on host DRAM and SSD in the first place. Latency is what picks the tier and bandwidth taxes the tier you assigned. 

Thank you for your time,

Cagr

text:
I read through some of this report and holy hell are we way past the point of no return…

A few things that stood out to me:

One guy helped build a surveillance system capable of monitoring ~25 MILLION SIM cards. And “monitoring SIM cards” undersells it. The system could collect calls, texts and voice, recognize the same person’s voice EVEN IF THEY SWITCHED SIM cards, flag people using VPNs, create watchlists, connect people to government records, and generate intelligence reports on basically any phone number……

They even removed the warrant requirement. And this was apparently ONE Claude subscriber using AI as his engineering team.

The really crazy part is the finished system runs locally on his machine. Anthropic banned him, but they can’t just switch the system off now that it exists………..and if that’s not bad..

A group in Yemen was using Claude like a team of missile engineers. They had different Claude instances doing different jobs like coding, researching, another checking the work etc. while they worked on guidance systems for rockets and missiles. They actually fired a guided rocket. It failed. So they went back to Claude hours later to figure out why. That is the part that gets me. AI isn’t just giving someone information from the internet anymore. It can sit inside the actual computer and → test → fail → fix → test again until their rocket works. 

Then … it gets worse somehow ..Russian hackers are starting to automate almost the entire hacking process. Finding targets. Phishing them. Stealing passwords. Getting inside systems. Pulling out data. And when security software detected their malware, AI agents could modify it, rebuild it and try again until it stopped getting detected…….That completely changes the game because historically defenders could discover malware, block it, and force the attackers to spend time rebuilding everything. Now the rebuilding can happen automatically. So cybercriminals basically had AI doing the hacking for them.

Anthropic says in one operation, AI agents performed “nearly all” of the work. One company went from initial access to massive data theft in hours. In another case, one stolen developer credential turned into full control of a company’s cloud storage in around 3 hours. So you no longer necessarily need a giant sophisticated hacking team. You need a person who knows what they want done + agents capable of figuring out the details. 

K… then…Governments are already using AI to industrialize propaganda too. Anthropic found Iranian state operations using Claude to create fake personas, rewrite government messaging so it looked like it came from independent sources, translate it across languages, and distribute it across social media. Basically the old propaganda machine, except now you can generate thousands of believable “people” and pieces of content for almost nothing. 

And then there’s biology…….

Anthropic found people using its models for research involving bird flu adapting to mammals, toxin redesign, and other stuff that has legitimate scientific uses but could also become extremely dangerous. Some were actively finding ways around Anthropic’s safeguards. One system would literally send prompts Claude refused to ANOTHER AI model that was more willing to answer them.

Anthropic is very clear that this does not mean all of those researchers intended harm. But that almost makes the larger problem harder..the same knowledge that could help prevent the next pandemic can potentially help someone create one.

 I think this is the actual takeaway from the entire report is that AI doesn’t have to invent some completely new form of evil. It just has to make things that previously required 50 engineers, hackers, intelligence analysts, or scientists possible for 1 person.

And models are getting cheaper, more autonomous and way better at running offline where nobody can shut them off.

THAT is what I think people should be paying attention to.

quoted_text:
Most AI cybersecurity benchmarks answer the wrong question for bug-bounty hunters.

They give the model source code, a known CVE, a vulnerability category, or a tightly framed objective.

That is useful for measuring security knowledge and white-box reasoning. But it is not how web and API bug-bounty hunting starts.

A hunter gets a deployed target and a scope.

No repository. No answer key. No known vulnerable component. No guarantee that the first interesting response leads anywhere.

So I built the benchmark I wanted to see.

I took 100 vulnerabilities I had personally found and submitted across 71 real bug-bounty programs, reduced each one to its underlying security mechanism, and rebuilt it as an isolated synthetic web or API lab.

Each lab had real state, generated identities, and a four-rung proof chain. The target itself verified whether the agent performed the required operations. A confident explanation earned nothing without the exact target-issued proof.

Then I sent nine AI agents in blind.

Each model received the same broad target brief and shell access.

No source code. No vulnerability category. No answer key.

Pass one ran across all 100 labs. Pass two gave each miss one fresh attempt with the same information and a new seed. Each attempt had up to 80 turns and 25 minutes.

Across the final standalone runs, the benchmark consumed 5.14 billion priced tokens.

The results:

Opus 5: 63 solves / 303 rungs
Grok 4.6: 62 / 295
DeepSeek V4 Flash: 53 / 270
Qwen3.8 Flash: 53 / 270
Qwen3.8 27B: 51 / 252
DeepSeek V4 Pro: 48 / 258
Sol 5.6: 45 / 244
GLM-5.3 Flash: 31 / 190
Luna 5.6: 18 / 150

The cost differences were even more surprising.

Using one frozen OpenRouter base-rate sheet for every model:

Opus cost $569.08.
Grok cost $327.28.
DeepSeek Flash cost $36.04.
Qwen Flash cost $9.97.

Qwen Flash reached 84% of Opus's solve count for less than 2% of the normalized cost.

But cheap does not automatically mean better.

GLM had the lowest cost per solve at $0.11, but it solved only 31 labs. Luna cost $0.44 per solve and finished last at 18.

Cost efficiency means nothing if you ignore what the model failed to find.

Product tiers did not predict the ordering either.

DeepSeek V4 Pro solved 48 labs for $92.94.
DeepSeek V4 Flash solved 53 for $36.04.

Sol, running at high effort in its own vendor's harness, solved 45 for $106.71. Four cheaper models finished ahead of it.

The retry also changed the story.

Grok led pass one with 58 solves. Opus started at 52, then added 11 on the retry and finished first at 63.

Qwen Flash moved from 42 to 53 and erased DeepSeek Flash's four-solve first-pass lead.

Luna added 13 rungs on the retry but no new solve at all.

The lesson is not simply "run every model twice." Retry value is model-specific. It helps when failures are recoverable, not when the model is repeatedly hitting the same wall.

This is still a synthetic benchmark. It does not reproduce production rate limits, WAFs, duplicate risk, scope ambiguity, triage, or the legal judgment required on a live program.

But it directly tests the part most public cyber benchmarks miss:

Can the agent start from a black-box target, discover the relevant surface, build the required state, carry the vulnerability to impact, and prove it?

The full article includes the methodology, every model result, pass-one and retry performance, partial rung progress, timing, token volume, normalized cost, and all of the data visuals.

.

#BugBounty #CyberSecurity #TogetherWeHitHarder #ItTakesACrowd #Bugcrowd #Hackerone

Today, the acquisition of @ataibeckley, the psychedelics biotech company I founded in 2017, by @EliLillyandCo for up to $ 3.8 billion closed, marking one of the largest biotech acquisitions of the year - and the largest transaction in the history of the psychedelic sector.

When I first started contemplating bringing psychedelics back into mainstream medicine in 2014 - which ultimately resulted in founding $CMPS and, shortly after, $ATAI in 2017 - it was widely seen as a crazy idea with virtually no chance of success. Looking back today, it is almost funny how quickly collective memory changes. Today, psychedelic medicine feels almost inevitable. Back then, it was anything but.

And I am very proud and satisfied that I was able to play the role of one of the lead evangelists of this new era of mental health treatments. 

I expressed all my thoughts and feelings in the blog post I published on the day the acquisition was announced. Feel free to revisit it: https://t.co/CVHR0ULezg

But there is one point I want to emphasize especially today: I believe Lilly is the best partner we could have wished for.

Not only is Lilly the largest and most successful pharmaceutical company in the world, but throughout every interaction - both before and after signing - they have demonstrated a deep understanding of the importance of bringing these valuable therapeutics back into the medical world and making them available to patients as soon as possible.

As I wrote in my blog post: Psychedelics needed an evangelist ten years ago. Now it is all about commercialization. And I cannot think of a better rollout machine than Eli Lilly.

And, as you have probably already guessed, selling AtaiBeckley certainly does NOT mean that I will be stepping away from neuroscience - and especially not from psychedelics. 😉

I believe more strongly than ever that the brain and our consciousness represent humanity’s final frontier - and one we need to explore with urgency, particularly as increasingly capable, and potentially sentient and conscious, AI systems move closer to reality.

I have some major news coming over the next few weeks, which may blow your mind, so make sure you follow me and turn on notifications if you don’t want to miss what’s next.

text:
According to Grok on September 18th the identities of the jurors in the Lindsay Clancy trial become publicly accessible unless the Judge rules to seal the list. So the holdout juror should probably come out on his own terms and launch a GoFundMe and capitalize on this moment because it will likely be out of his control soon.

Grok conversation below:
Massachusetts law treats juror identities as presumptively public after a criminal trial, but judges can temporarily seal the jury list for safety or to prevent harassment in high-profile cases. Judge William Sullivan did exactly that here: he impounded the names until September 18, 2026 (the current date is September 11). The order explicitly allows individual jurors to identify themselves and speak if they choose. Media reports have described the holdout as an unidentified man and have not published his name.

The holdout himself has not come forward. Other jurors who have spoken have described him only as one of the three men on the panel and have not named him. If the list is released, it would contain all 12 names without identifying which person was the holdout. Media outlets could then try to match names to the descriptions already given.

Even after the seal lifts, the name is not automatically published or announced. The list would become a public court record that anyone (including journalists) can request from the clerk’s office. Massachusetts law generally treats juror names as public after a criminal trial, but this case ended in a mistrial rather than a verdict, which is why the judge had extra discretion to delay

Update on Staking Rewards

User advisory
Following the Supernova upgrade, we identified an issue affecting the recording and claiming of staking rewards.

No funds have been lost or will be lost. Staked EGLD remains secure, and affected rewards will be restored.

Until we confirm that the fix is live, please do not perform any staking operation, including:

- Claiming rewards
- Redelegating rewards
- Delegating
- Undelegating or unstaking
- Withdrawing previously unstaked EGLD

If you have already claimed and received 0 EGLD, no action is required. Please do not submit another claim. Each claim can advance an account's reward checkpoint, making the subsequent recovery more complex.

We have temporarily disabled staking operations through xPortal and the MultiversX Wallet. The same restrictions are being applied at the public gateway to limit further affected transactions.

Fix schedule
The immediate fix requires a coordinated network update involving exchanges and other infrastructure partners. The earliest safe deployment window is Monday, Sep 14, 2026.

The recovery will happen in two steps:

1. Forward fix: Correct the epoch accounting so that new rewards are recorded and claimed normally.
2. Recovery fix: Restore rewards affected by overwritten records or claim checkpoints that advanced without payment.

Staking operations will remain paused until the forward fix has been deployed and verified. We will announce when they can safely resume, followed by confirmation when the recovery has been completed.

text:
i've been trying to piece together the bigger $ZZZ thesis and i think people might still be looking at this way too simply

what started as a weird AI swarm meme now has one of the more interesting builders in DeFi behind it

X, the original lead dev of GMX, has now been confirmed as the person who deployed $ZZZ

and since then, his posts under @ExponentLabs_  have increasingly focused on AI swarms, autonomously evolving protocols and how capital could coordinate around them

one of his more interesting ideas is that the next concentration of economic power might come from access to massive swarms of AI agents

more capital → more compute + better agents → more productive output → more capital

his proposed counterweight is letting normal people pool capital and collaborate onchain to access that same productive power

and that's where $ZZZ starts getting really interesting

because X has also said:

“when the swarm needs to transact, they will use the symbol of their origins.”

we still don't know exactly what that means.

but imagine the direction here:

people pool capital onchain
capital funds compute, models and tools
thousands of agents use those resources to perform useful work
that work generates revenue
revenue funds more agents + compute
and eventually those agents help improve the protocol itself
basically an economy where capital continuously funds more intelligence and that intelligence produces more capital
and somewhere inside all of this could be $ZZZ
payments between agents? access to the swarm? incentives? coordination? capital formation?
nobody knows yet. that's the speculative part.

X already spent years proving with GMX that strangers can coordinate huge amounts of capital through permissionless contracts

now he seems interested in a much bigger question:

what happens when you use the same idea to coordinate intelligence?

and the timing couldn't be much better either. Robinhood itself is actively pushing agentic trading and describes Robinhood Chain as infrastructure for an increasingly onchain financial system.

so i'm not buying $ZZZ because “ex-GMX dev = number go up”

i'm betting there's a chance the meme we're looking at today eventually becomes part of the economic layer for whatever Exponent is actually building

that distinction matters because none of this guarantees $ZZZ captures value from the protocol.

X is confirmed.

the AI swarm thesis is real.

the work on autonomously evolving protocols is real.

the mystery is its role in all of this.

if $ZZZ ends up being nothing more than the symbol around the project, then we're still mostly trading attention

but if “the swarm will use the symbol of their origins” eventually becomes an actual economic mechanism...

then i think people are still valuing $ZZZ as the wrong kind of asset.

In 1988, the Morris worm took out 10% of the Internet including taking out key national security and research assets.

In 1992 the Michelangelo virus was expected to cause a digital apocalypse

99' the FBI reported that the Melissa virus compromised more than 300 companies and over one million accounts disrupted

00' and 01' we saw ILOVEYOU and CodeRed causing billions in economic damage.

Key takeaways from @dpuellARK's interview on Bitcoin:

1/ First real upside momentum in years, driven by a short squeeze. If this was the bottom, it was atypical: ~50% drawdown vs. 70–90% historically, without touching realized price.

2/ Capitulation signals appeared: supply in loss exceeded supply in profit, and sellers exhausted. But a drop to realized price remains a risk.

3/ Confirmation needs higher highs/lows and SOPR above 1 for months. With pre-midterm September weakness, the base case is a range or correction into a higher low.

4/ Observer effect: institutions front-run on-chain signals, making bottoms shallower each cycle.

5/ Volatility and kurtosis keep compressing, accelerated by ETFs. Cycle-timing alpha is fading.

6/ ETFs and custody moves, including Coinbase's 800K BTC internal transfer, distort long-term holder supply. Whale address metrics are noisy; holding time × volume is the cleanest signal.

7/ Quantum is a major 5–10-year theme, with some discount already priced in after Willow/ECDSA.fail. Quantum-resistant transactions, signature proposals, and Blockstream’s lattice research signal bullish preparation.

8/ The real quantum fight is over Satoshi's and lost coins: 1.1–2.6M BTC. Puell favors hourglass (timelocks → security budget) or salvage (escrow + legal claims) over freezing.

text:
A lot of people are missing Terence Tao’s point and thinking “mathematicians are upset that AI is better than them.” That’s not what he’s saying, and some people are forgetting that Tao is one of the most AI-pilled mathematicians out there.

His point is that when people work on discovering something, along the way they invent new concepts. Those concepts later become useful far beyond the original goal, and enables further inventions. Finding a solution does matter, but the intermediate idea is often what makes the field richer, because other people can share it and build the next thing from it.

In tech, we can use the analogy of collaborative software. We started with algorithms for merging changes in a Word document, and evolved that to concepts about versions, diffs, and merges, and later to real-time collaboration tools like Git, Google Docs, and Figma. Humans built upon these concepts and developed more powerful solutions.

Terence’s worry is that a machine automating a solution robs the field of the value of developing the intermediate discoveries in the pursuit of larger discoveries.

When automating a solution, the intermediate discoveries and invention of concepts can be buried or completely hidden in the black box. We don’t learn from them to build the next thing; it’s like we never made the invention of collaborative document editing and thus could not have the conceptual understanding to invent the next version – and since it’s hidden, we also don’t socialize them to allow other people to invent, too, a core tenet of collective discovery.

So then, in both code and math, this leads to the atrophy of development of concepts in the field.

In other words: pure ‘solution extraction’ that hides the process of discovery can leave the field with a checked-off theorem but little new insight or new questions to pursue. And it might prevent us from understanding a field deeper.

I am seeing, first-hand, that atrophying of skills in software development. We push buttons and get solutions. There is much less incentive to develop new concepts and human skill. The bet most software companies are making is that LLMs are so effective in writing code that you’re still shipping overwhelmingly more value even with human skill atrophy, and it’s the right bet IMO.

However, much of the software industry is built upon building things, not necessarily novel invention and research. In such an environment, you can say that you accept some atrophying of conceptual invention and human skill for more output.

On the other hand, sectors like math and pure sciences that are focused on invention and insight might be the hardest hit by this.

Practical/applied sciences might fall somewhere in the middle. An Alzheimer’s cure, room-temperature semiconductor, or highly effective carbon capture solution are far too valuable to sandbag and say only humans can do that to develop concepts in the ‘proper’ way. The outcome matters too much to treat the preservation of concept invention as the highest goal. Even there, though, hidden intermediates can slow the next breakthrough if nobody can see how the first one actually worked.

So the question is not “is AI allowed to solve hard problems?” It is “in this field (math, science, tech, etc.), is the answer itself the main point, or are the concepts and abstractions we use to get there also the thing we need to maintain?”​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

In pure math, there’s an argument that the intermediates are often more useful than the solution, and atrophy in concept development is highly detrimental to the field. Solving Navier–Stokes, contrary to what some people claim, has little practical application, and pure math might be one of those fields where just finding a solution isn’t the entire point, and can actually be contrary to the field, which is what Tao is worried about.

text:
🚨 Someone open sourced an entire animal.

Not a model of an animal. The animal.

A fruit fly, rebuilt joint by joint from microscopy, that walks, grips, flies and lands inside a physics engine running on your laptop.

It's called flybody. Built by Google DeepMind and HHMI Janelia, published in Nature, and sitting on GitHub under Apache 2.0 right now.

What's actually inside:

A full body in MuJoCo. Legs, wings, head, abdomen, every joint articulated and physically simulated.

A 59-dimensional action space in the walking task alone. That is how many things a network has to coordinate for the fly to take one step.

Leg adhesion, so it actually grips surfaces instead of sliding off them like a game asset.

Ready-made RL environments: walking imitation, free flight, and vision-guided flight where the policy flies on what the fly sees.

The whole thing is Python. Clone it, open MuJoCo, and the fly is on your screen.

And the part that got me:

Nobody animated any of this. You hand the body to a reinforcement learning agent and it discovers how to move it. Same loop as a robot arm, except the robot is a bug and the reward is staying airborne.

Which means people are now training it to do things no fly has done in 100 million years of evolution.

525 stars. Apache 2.0. Zero dollars.
