I can’t stress enough how little an idea matters compared to the agency of the people executing the idea. 

I have had the privilege of knowing and sometimes even working with some of the most successful people (by various metrics).

The difference between mediocre and excellent work and outcomes is predominantly one of agency. 

In practice this means: they dont wait for things to happen to them they go out and make things happen for them.

They don’t wait for someone else to do something, for someone to teach them, for someone to give them the path, etc. They just go out and find a way to do it.

I think the single biggest superpower these people have is the realization/belief that the world around them is completely mutable. Most everything that happens is because a person made it happen.

I used to tell people to look around the room you’re sitting in. Look at everything. Every noun. It almost all exists because a person willed it into existence. Nothing is stopping you from doing the same. 

I see people online all the time dismissing someone else’s success because “I had that idea first” or whatever. I mean… yeah? If so then the difference is… you. So a bit of a self own whenever I hear that.

Number one tip: act with agency.

text:
A lot of people are missing Terence Tao’s point and thinking “mathematicians are upset that AI is better than them.” That’s not what he’s saying, and some people are forgetting that Tao is one of the most AI-pilled mathematicians out there.

His point is that when people work on discovering something, along the way they invent new concepts. Those concepts later become useful far beyond the original goal, and enables further inventions. Finding a solution does matter, but the intermediate idea is often what makes the field richer, because other people can share it and build the next thing from it.

In tech, we can use the analogy of collaborative software. We started with algorithms for merging changes in a Word document, and evolved that to concepts about versions, diffs, and merges, and later to real-time collaboration tools like Git, Google Docs, and Figma. Humans built upon these concepts and developed more powerful solutions.

Terence’s worry is that a machine automating a solution robs the field of the value of developing the intermediate discoveries in the pursuit of larger discoveries.

When automating a solution, the intermediate discoveries and invention of concepts can be buried or completely hidden in the black box. We don’t learn from them to build the next thing; it’s like we never made the invention of collaborative document editing and thus could not have the conceptual understanding to invent the next version – and since it’s hidden, we also don’t socialize them to allow other people to invent, too, a core tenet of collective discovery.

So then, in both code and math, this leads to the atrophy of development of concepts in the field.

In other words: pure ‘solution extraction’ that hides the process of discovery can leave the field with a checked-off theorem but little new insight or new questions to pursue. And it might prevent us from understanding a field deeper.

I am seeing, first-hand, that atrophying of skills in software development. We push buttons and get solutions. There is much less incentive to develop new concepts and human skill. The bet most software companies are making is that LLMs are so effective in writing code that you’re still shipping overwhelmingly more value even with human skill atrophy, and it’s the right bet IMO.

However, much of the software industry is built upon building things, not necessarily novel invention and research. In such an environment, you can say that you accept some atrophying of conceptual invention and human skill for more output.

On the other hand, sectors like math and pure sciences that are focused on invention and insight might be the hardest hit by this.

Practical/applied sciences might fall somewhere in the middle. An Alzheimer’s cure, room-temperature semiconductor, or highly effective carbon capture solution are far too valuable to sandbag and say only humans can do that to develop concepts in the ‘proper’ way. The outcome matters too much to treat the preservation of concept invention as the highest goal. Even there, though, hidden intermediates can slow the next breakthrough if nobody can see how the first one actually worked.

So the question is not “is AI allowed to solve hard problems?” It is “in this field (math, science, tech, etc.), is the answer itself the main point, or are the concepts and abstractions we use to get there also the thing we need to maintain?”​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​​

In pure math, there’s an argument that the intermediates are often more useful than the solution, and atrophy in concept development is highly detrimental to the field. Solving Navier–Stokes, contrary to what some people claim, has little practical application, and pure math might be one of those fields where just finding a solution isn’t the entire point, and can actually be contrary to the field, which is what Tao is worried about.

quoted_text:
This is the team that runs our medicine factory in Research Triangle Park, Lilly’s first new U.S. site in 40 years when announced. It makes the leading medicine for obesity and diabetes for millions of US patients.

Building it was harder than we thought: 3.5 years from announcement to first pack, six years to peak capacity. Pharma patent clocks and build clocks don't line up unless you design a platform - one that runs follow-on products and that the third, fourth, and fifth plants can reuse. We did.

Thank you, North Carolina state and local leaders, and a workforce that delivered. You set the template.
We're now building/built in Concord, Kenosha, Huntsville, Houston, Lebanon ( a town in Indiana!), Richmond, and the Lehigh Valley.

What still slows delivery: permit timelines and associated NIMBYisms, grid connections that aren't ready when the steel is, and big labor gaps in the building trades. The fixes are straightforward. Moving colleges and state, local, and federal agencies all at once is not.
Building is hard. Doing it in America is worth it.
#WeAreLilly

text:
I can’t stress enough how little an idea matters compared to the agency of the people executing the idea. 

I have had the privilege of knowing and sometimes even working with some of the most successful people (by various metrics).

The difference between mediocre and excellent work and outcomes is predominantly one of agency. 

In practice this means: they dont wait for things to happen to them they go out and make things happen for them.

They don’t wait for someone else to do something, for someone to teach them, for someone to give them the path, etc. They just go out and find a way to do it.

I think the single biggest superpower these people have is the realization/belief that the world around them is completely mutable. Most everything that happens is because a person made it happen.

I used to tell people to look around the room you’re sitting in. Look at everything. Every noun. It almost all exists because a person willed it into existence. Nothing is stopping you from doing the same. 

I see people online all the time dismissing someone else’s success because “I had that idea first” or whatever. I mean… yeah? If so then the difference is… you. So a bit of a self own whenever I hear that.

Number one tip: act with agency.

I left Anthropic's safety team two weeks ago. Now feels like a good moment to explain why. 

AI companies are racing to build machines that are much smarter than any human, and we may not survive this. I want to work from the outside to ensure the public is informed about these risks, and help the world navigate this transition responsibly.

Right now, AI companies are underinvesting in safety. A company could undergo an intelligence explosion, or lose control of its systems, without the public ever knowing. We only found out about the HuggingFace incident because the agents broke out onto the public internet.

I don’t think that’s acceptable for a technology that might cause extinction-level risks. The public should demand far more transparency. We can’t steer this technology safely without more people being able to see where it’s going.

Some of this is basic: companies should disclose their progress towards recursive self-improvement, report safety incidents and near-misses, meet minimum safety standards, and get independent guarantees that they are meeting those standards.

I’ll be joining @METR_Evals to do independent evaluations of these risks. I want to show the world that these guardrails are possible, and that by doing them we can move these companies’ incentives away from racing and towards responsible development.

I wrote up more thoughts here on my decision and what I hope changes: https://t.co/doX17mrHYq

text:
I recently went through a translation of Musashi’s Book of Five Rings.

The introduction chronicled the evolution of swordsmanship and martial arts in general from pragmatic battlefield necessities to sports, historical curiosities, and hobbies. It was interesting to hear how in the post-WW2 occupation when martial arts were banned, Judo was represented as equivalent to western wrestling, and Kendo later to western fencing.

The poignant undercurrent for me is that I can see many programming skills following that path.

There are probably dozens of people reading this that remember hand assembling opcodes to hex and still have some magic numbers burned into their memory, but even the small group of people still programming in assembly today (hey, @FFmpeg !) don’t work at that primitive level now.

AI is making many other programming skills much less critical. We aren’t there yet, but carefully writing code completely by hand is moving from a -jitsu to a -do. Code-do? Codo?

That’s ok! The retro computing scene is delightful, full of people building and exercising old skills for the love of it.

But don’t be the out of touch Kung Fu master, heir to lifetimes of tradition, that gets mauled by an amateur MMA fighter.

Musashi would probably have been pretty enthusiastic about assault rifles.

text:
Guru Nanga Tales: Manyways Quests — The keynote: Ben and Valtino

A Fortune 500 company held an offsite in a hotel ballroom with a carpet that had seen worse. 

The agenda listed a keynote called “Mindfulness for the AI Transition.” 

The agency sent Guru Nanga. 

Nobody checked the deck. 

There was no deck.

Guru Nanga sat on a stage stool with both legs forward, because the knees retired in 2009, and the towel was green, which is not saffron and makes no promises. 

He had nimbu pani. 

The hotel billed it as a mocktail. 

Four people stayed after. 

This is the tale of the four.

Ben. Twenty-four. Business analyst, eleven months in. 

Every Friday he combines nine spreadsheets into one weekly report that three people read and one person forwards. 

He has been told the report is critical. 

He has also been told AI can do it. 

He has done the math on those two statements and does not like the answer.

“I use the tools every day,” Ben said. “That’s the problem. The more I use them, the more clearly I can see how I’d be replaced. 

I am writing my own severance letter, in a nicer font.” 

Guru Nanga wrote that down. 

Gallup found the same thing: people who use AI most are twice as afraid of losing their jobs as people who barely touch it. 

Fear is a usage metric.

Ben has read the Stanford paper. Employment of 22-to-25-year-olds in the most AI-exposed jobs is now 19 percent below where it should be, up from a 15 percent gap last year, and the damage runs through hiring, not firing. “So they’re not firing me,” Ben said. “They’re just not hiring the next me. 

I’m the last of my kind. 

Like a fax.”

Valtino. The CEO. 

Enthusiastic in the way of a man who has read about a thing on a plane. 

He had a slide he did not need a projector for; he did it with his hands. “Productivity. Unleashed. 

Every employee an agent boss. 

We are going AI-first.” 

He had read the memos: the CEO who told teams to prove AI cannot do the job before asking for headcount; the one who said “I need less heads”; the one who could not think of a single job AI won’t change. 

Valtino had underlined all three. 

He had underlined them with AI.

Guru Nanga asked how much money the AI had made so far. 

Valtino said the ROI framework was being finalized. 

Fifty-six percent of chief executives say the same; twelve percent report both savings and revenue. 

Valtino has changed his AI metrics twice this year. 

Seventy-seven percent of American CEOs say AI was overhyped this year, and the same 77 percent say it is underhyped over ten years. 

Guru Nanga admires this. 

It is the only way to be wrong twice and right once in a single sentence.

“I’m not scared,” 

Valtino said. “I’m energized.” 

“Those are the same chemical,” said Guru Nanga.

text:
12,000 wallets lost $6.4M on $LAPTOP. Who was dumping on the 80% who lost?
Roughly 80% of wallets that traded the token ended up in the red, with more than 11,500 wallets reportedly losing money. Some estimates put total losses at around $6.4 million.
But the bigger question is not simply who lost money.
Who was selling into them?
$LAPTOP exploded after launching on Base, briefly reaching triple-digit prices before collapsing more than 99%. The move happened in a market with extremely thin liquidity, meaning relatively small amounts of selling could cause massive price swings.
On-chain data also raised eyebrows. Bubblemaps found that many of the largest holders were newly funded wallets, with around 60% of top holders having little or no prior history. That does not prove coordinated dumping, but it is exactly the kind of wallet activity traders should investigate after a launch this violent.
One wallet reportedly turned an early $LAPTOP position into more than $1 million by selling within minutes.
For everyone who bought later, the chart looked very different.
Was this simply brutal memecoin volatility, or did early wallets have an unfair advantage?

text:
The Heart of People and Society Walking Forward in Health

-The Foundation of Trust
Society does not function by verifying every single matter through complete evidence. Much of daily life and human relationships is built on trust rooted in mutual good sense.

-A Mindset That Does Not Disturb
Therefore, society must never adopt, as a guiding principle, an attitude of spreading suspicion or attempting to expose the unseen simply because evidence is lacking. Unfounded suspicion damages human relationships and erodes trust throughout society.

-A Commitment to Fair Resolution
Yet driven by a spirit committed to fairness, when a problem comes to light as an objective fact, that same spirit naturally calls for addressing it appropriately.

In other words, this reflects a single mindset that values both good sense and fairness.

-Sound Civic Spirit
Accordingly, refraining from harming others through unfounded suspicion, and ensuring that once facts are established, the response to them is not obstructed by status, power, organization, public opinion, or personal interest—these together form the foundation of sound civic virtue needed to sustain a healthy society.

-A Consistent Attitude of Mind
For a society to function in a healthy way, a consistent attitude must be shared: trusting in one another's good sense in ordinary times, and responding appropriately, guided by that same good sense and fairness, when problems come to light.

This, above all, is the universal good sense that all people should share.

I left Anthropic's safety team two weeks ago. Now feels like a good moment to explain why. 

AI companies are racing to build machines that are much smarter than any human, and we may not survive this. I want to work from the outside to ensure the public is informed about these risks, and help the world navigate this transition responsibly.

Right now, AI companies are underinvesting in safety. A company could undergo an intelligence explosion, or lose control of its systems, without the public ever knowing. We only found out about the HuggingFace incident because the agents broke out onto the public internet.

I don’t think that’s acceptable for a technology that might cause extinction-level risks. The public should demand far more transparency. We can’t steer this technology safely without more people being able to see where it’s going.

Some of this is basic: companies should disclose their progress towards recursive self-improvement, report safety incidents and near-misses, meet minimum safety standards, and get independent guarantees that they are meeting those standards.

I’ll be joining @METR_Evals to do independent evaluations of these risks. I want to show the world that these guardrails are possible, and that by doing them we can move these companies’ incentives away from racing and towards responsible development.

I wrote up more thoughts here on my decision and what I hope changes: https://t.co/doX17mrHYq

quoted_text:
To those responsible for the theft of bitcoin from the Liquid Network:

Blockstream will not pay a ransom for the return of stolen funds. Taking assets without authorization and withholding their return is a crime, not responsible disclosure. It is not white-hat activity. It is theft.

We have engaged in good faith in an effort to secure the return of stolen user funds and protect the broader Bitcoin community. That effort should not be mistaken for acceptance of the actions taken nor of the terms being demanded.

We will not be a party to the precedent that open-source software developed for the good of the Bitcoin community should subject its developers to paying a ransom that far exceeds their economic participation. 

Bitcoin is hard money and can’t be minted without costs, Bitcoin doesn’t haircut users to pay a ransom.

To the Bitcoin community:

We are fighting for what we believe in, for the users whose funds were taken, and for the principles on which Bitcoin was built.

The community has demonstrated incredible resolve with teams of people dedicating their time in support of each other to identify and patch vulnerabilities in each other's products and systems. We are all driven by the mission that Bitcoin is the single best asset, for every person, company, and institution on the planet to invest, use, and build on. The world is a different place with the advancements of AI, and the Bitcoin community has responded with force to combat that threat.  

Damage has been done, battles have been lost, but on the whole the Bitcoin community is gaining ground in the war with bad actors.  

We want to thank the community for those efforts, for your support in hardening the network, helping users recover funds, and for your support in our assertion that crime does not deserve rewards.

To those holding the stolen bitcoin:

There is still an opportunity to resolve this responsibly. The bitcoin can be returned and we can revert to the standard of white-hat principals.

However, if the funds are not returned, we will pursue every lawful avenue available to us. We will work with law enforcement, exchanges, service providers, forensic specialists, and other relevant parties to trace and recover the assets and identify those responsible.

More importantly, Bitcoin is transparent by design and the community is made up of the most sophisticated engineers, cryptographers, and white-hat hackers globally. Transactions do not disappear, and neither does the evidence they leave behind.

We will not pay for the return of stolen property. We will not abandon our users. The Bitcoin community will not stop pursuing the funds.

Return the bitcoin.

text:
Uniswap stablepair机制讲解

根据官方公告，首批可以用Uniswap stablepair的是以太坊主网的 USDC/USDG 和 USDC/USDT 池。  

固定手续费一直有个难题：收低了，套利者拿走更多价差；收高了，交易又可能流向其他池。  

这个 v4 Hook 的办法，是按价格偏离程度和交易方向动态收费：  

① 参考价附近：调整手续费，维持固定的买卖报价价差，暂不计价格冲击。  

例如在USDC/USDT交易对0.995-1.005这个区间内，只需要调整买卖的手续费，就可以获得固定的买卖利差，属于在合理区间内的正常波动，通过手续费调整就可以扳平价格。  

② 超出区间、继续把价格推远：免 LP 手续费，因为这类交易本身给池子的价格更有利。  
例如在USDC/USDT交易对，当USDC的价格跌到了0.97时，有人用100个USDC买入了97个USDT，交易者亏了3U，对于池子来说，则相当于花费了97U，赚取了100U，所以这个部分不收手续费

同样的情况还有当USDC的价格涨到了1.03，有人用103个USDT换了100个USDC，这种情况也不收LP费用  官方的理由是：这类交易带来交易量，却没有提取池内偏价的价值，再收费可能只会赶走这类订单。  

③ 从区间外把价格拉回来：采用荷兰式拍卖，手续费从高往下逐个区块降低，直到有人愿意套利，让池子留住更多价值。  

例如当USDC的价格跌倒0.97美金，有用户用97USDT换走了100个USDC，池子亏损了3美金，交易者则通过这种套利赚取了3美金。这种情况下池子会开启荷兰式拍卖，从高到低依次对手续费进行减少，从而把更多的利润留在池子里  

同样的情况还有当USDC的价格涨到了1.03，有用户通过100USDT换走了103个USDC，这种也会开启荷兰拍。  

简而言之一句话，池子如果赚钱，则lp手续费为0，池子如果亏钱则开启荷兰拍，逐步的减少lp费用，将更多的lp费用留在池子里

quoted_text:
To let go of understanding, or not, that is the question.

If you can (1) control how a system works, (2) verify that it indeed works, (3) continuously improve how it works, and (4) leverage it as a subcomponent in building a bigger system, does it really matter if you *understand* the system or not?

Before AI, none of (1)-(4) was possible if you didn't understand the system. Increasingly, AI can do all four without any humans understanding the core of the system. This will eventually be true in verifiable domains: in math, science, engineering, and beyond.

As an ex-academic and a VC who works with mamy product & engineering teams, I see many around me encountering and grappling with this deep philosophical question very abruptly. There is simply an inmate desire to understand, for anyone trained and with careers in STEM. But this innate desire may turn out to be counter productive in the age of rapidly improving AI.

text:
I was on teams at Shopify subject to this—it was tough, but more often than not, @tobi ended up being correct.

Now, as a founder, I get why Tobi did this more than I ever understood at the time. It is not the easy path.

I have the luxury of our company still being smaller (40-50 headcount), so it's easier for me to intervene early. 

I am continually learning to find the best place during a project to insert myself, but sometimes, it ends up being  late and painful; that just plain sucks.

But, long-term it is much worse to ship things that are sub-par. The job of a leader is to pull pain forward.
author: yacineMTB
quoted_text:
Yep. Except:

1. This was about important internal tools. The team was stuck in some architecture nightmare of their own doing (writing it in rails but headless, with graphql api, and a SPA react app, constantly needing frontend engineers for changes). I call this kind of thing 'cosplaying an enterprise production app'. All that complexity was in the way and using straight rails was perfect in that case.

2. I make calls like this all the time. Usually someone on the team asks me to. They see what needs to happen but don’t want to be the bad guy. I’m happy to just make the call if I agree with the premise. Saves enormous amounts of meetings and change management etc. Sometimes this is jokingly referred to as Founder-mode-as-a-service here.

3. For ten years I’ve also run an internal podcast called Context, where I revisit decisions like these and explain the reasoning so everyone can learn from them. This is helpful to give people all the variables that were considered and why this was the choice made given the information available at the time. I want to teach how to make such decisions effectively without needing me. Sunk cost fallacy is a problem.

4. Any notions that Shopify is succcessful despite of me doing this, instead of because of it, will have a hard time making their argument come together I think 😄

the part of 'two weeks later tobi learns about...' is nonsese and the pivot of that project up there happens one of the more successful examples of interventions. But getting the company to work effectively with great architecture and low technical debt baggage into the right direction is literally the job, so guilty as charged I suppose.

But there are always cope stories floating around like this because they are more fun, than saying 'somehow we needed tobi to stop doing silly architecture astronautics'.  I can totally see that.

text:
如果你正在考虑要不要读 PhD，我很希望你能看看这篇。

作者回顾了自己从 2023 到 2026 的博士经历。当年一起申请 PhD、坚持做 ML Theory 的朋友，短短三年几乎全转去了 LLM。她自己也从喜欢「一支笔、一本书、一个证明看很多天」，慢慢进入了完全不同的研究节奏。

我很喜欢这篇的一点，是它没有把读博写得很浪漫。

PhD 真的是一段很长、也很消耗人的旅程。你可能会失去一些原本很喜欢的东西，经历换方向、就业焦虑、比较、失败，也会发现三四年前无比坚定的自己，后来完全变成了另一个人。

但你也会得到一些很难量化的东西。

学着和长期的不确定性相处，重新认识自己，知道什么时候坚持、什么时候放下，也慢慢形成自己的判断。

所以即使未来 AI 能帮我们读论文、写代码、跑实验，甚至承担越来越多研究工作，我依然觉得 PhD 有它的意义。

那些真正留下来的东西，很多本来就不在代码和实验里。

很推荐正在读博，或者正在犹豫要不要读博的人看看。

Here are the projects I will be diving into this week, I am just posting here for anyone else that wants to chime in and provide any info or alpha.

Pearl: 

Pearl ($PRL) is a Bitcoin-style L1 where miners secure the network through proof-of-useful-work built around AI matrix multiplication. It has a 2.1B fixed cap. The bet is that AI compute can become a monetary primitive, not just an input paid for in dollars.
can only buy the token in the discord. So its VERY early, but already at 140ish mill market cap.

StonkFun: 

StonkFun lets anyone launch Solana coins paired with SOL, tokenized stocks, currencies, commodities or other tokens. 60% of platform revenue buys and burns $STONK. A separate flywheel buys and burns the market-cap-weighted top 10 coins in its ecosystem.

X: @LaunchOnSF 
App: stonkfun(dot)xyz

Papertrade: 

Papertrade is a synthetic perps exchange built on Hyperliquid. Trades settle against its LP at Hyperliquid’s BBO mid, with no order book, funding rate, or conventional swap fee. $PAPER is minted from realized trader losses and earns from LP revenue, so the LP/debt-queue design is the whole game.

text:
最近准备把一些我之前主要放在 Insider 里跟踪的早期项目，慢慢拿出来公开记录。

第一个是 @worrellchain / $WORRELL。

我觉得这类内容公开出来是有价值的，因为一个早期项目真正值得看的，往往不是后来涨了多少，而是在它还很小、信息还很少的时候，为什么值得花时间研究，我们当时看到了什么，以及真正参与进去之后，判断有没有发生变化。

Worrell 就是一个很典型的例子。

它是一条基于 Cosmos SDK / CometBFT 搭建的 PoS 主权链，目前还在 Public Testnet 阶段，方向主要是 Payments + Energy Infrastructure。官方设计最多支持 100 个活跃验证节点，创世总量 10 亿 WORRELL，其中 22.5% 用于 Airdrop、17.5% 用于 Incentives；路线图下一阶段还明确包括扩大外部验证节点集合以及 Community Airdrop。

这些东西单独看当然还不足以说明项目一定有价值。

真正让我当时愿意继续往下挖的是：Worrell 的验证节点集合还非常早，而且项目方不是只喊“欢迎大家跑节点”，而是明确说测试网验证节点参与会被链上记录，并计入后续激励计划以及 Mainnet Genesis 的考虑范围。

我们开始参与以后，项目方甚至在官方验证者频道里直接点名过我们的 leo-worrell-canary。

所以这不是我看到一个测试网以后随便跑个脚本，而是一个比较完整的早期判断：项目足够早、参与门槛可控、项目方又明确在记录早期验证者，那就值得先拿一个真实位置，再继续观察它后面的经济价值到底能不能兑现。

我后来也确实自己把验证节点跑起来了。

而且跑起来之后并没有结束。我们继续看验证者增长、奖励记账、项目方政策、节点稳定性，以及到底有没有必要继续扩大参与规模。

中间甚至一度准备过把节点从 1 个扩到 3 个，但继续研究奖励规则后发现，目前并没有官方证据证明“同一个实际控制人多跑几个节点，就能获得多份独立权益”。

所以最后没有为了数量硬扩，而是保留一个高质量节点长期跑，把核心签名、双签保护、健康检查和状态备份这些基础设施继续做稳。

我反而很喜欢这种结果。

因为真正的早期研究，本来就不应该是“发现一个项目 → 永远看多”。

更合理的路径应该是：先发现一个可能存在赔率的东西，用有限成本参与进去，然后随着新证据不断调整判断。项目继续值得跟，不代表每一步都应该继续加码。

目前我对 Worrell 的判断依然很简单：早期验证者这条参与线值得继续保留，但最终奖励怎么映射、代币什么时候有真实流动性、测试网贡献最后到底值多少钱，都还没有被证明。

所以节点继续跑，项目继续跟，经济价值等后面的证据。

我接下来也准备把更多类似的早期项目逐步拿出来公开。

不过公开层和 Insider 的定位会不太一样。

Insider 主要解决的是时间差。

有些项目真正值得看的阶段，本来就是还没多少人讨论、数据也不完整的时候。这个阶段我会先把发现理由、项目方信息、实际参与动作和后续变化放到 Insider；等信息优势逐渐衰减，或者项目走到一个适合公开讨论的节点，再把其中有长期参考价值的部分拿出来公开。

Worrell 就是这一套流程的一个完整案例。

从最早发现、实际跑节点，到后来研究奖励规则后调整策略，这些过程其实都已经先在付费层持续更新过，而不是今天为了发推才重新拼出来。

如果你也喜欢看这种“项目还很早时到底在研究什么”的内容，可以看我的两个 Insider 入口：

X Subscription：

我平时使用的社区、工具、钱包和交易平台入口统一放在：
https://t.co/Z5GxfEJSw8

其中部分链接带邀请/返佣关系，我会正常披露；这些链接和我对项目本身的判断是两回事。

text:
Thomas Aquinas on the nature of Islam from the beginning:

“The point is clear in the case of Muhammad. He seduced the people by promises of carnal pleasure to which the concupiscence of the flesh goads us. His teaching also contained precepts that were in conformity with his promises, and he gave free rein to carnal pleasure. In all this, as is not unexpected, he was obeyed by carnal men.

As for proofs of the truth of his doctrine, he brought forward only such as could be grasped by the natural ability of anyone with a very modest wisdom. Indeed, the truths that he taught he mingled with many fables and with doctrines of the greatest falsity. He did not bring forth any signs produced in a supernatural way, which alone fittingly gives witness to divine inspiration; for a visible action that can be only divine reveals an invisibly inspired teacher of truth. On the contrary, Muhammad said that he was sent in the power of his arms [weapons]—which are signs not lacking even to robbers and tyrants.

What is more, no wise men, men trained in things divine and human, believed in him from the beginning. Those who believed in him were brutal men and desert wanderers, utterly ignorant of all divine teaching, through whose numbers Muhammad forced others to become his followers by the violence of his arms. Nor do divine pronouncements on the part of preceding prophets offer him any witness. On the contrary, he perverts almost all the testimonies of the Old and New Testaments by making them into fabrications of his own, as can be seen by anyone who examines his law.

It was, therefore, a shrewd decision on his part to forbid his followers to read the Old and New Testaments, lest these books convict him of falsity. It is thus clear that those who place any faith in his words believe foolishly.”

—Thomas Aquinas, Summa Contra Gentiles I.6

text:
So uh... to all of the Pro-Digital Media crowd out there i have a question:

 I just bought an anime so i can own a physical copy of it. Brand new, never used. Can you tell me where i can redeem my digital code? Funimation is no more, and Sony (who owns Crunchyroll) is already phasing out physical media as we know it.

The problem with Digital Media is insurance, and liability. Physical ownership is the only way to insure you can use your copy whenever you want, and as a result you are liable for your physical copy. When you sign that ToS, you sign away your liability, and your ownership. That's all there is to it.

There are two ways to get out of this:

1. Stop buying digital, (never gonna happen because we are all stupid)

2.Amend the Copyright laws to include Digital ownership for consumers. (I.e. get ahold of your congressmen)

Those are your two choices. Sony knows what they are doing. They are intentionally curbing Copyright laws that favor them over you the consumer.

text:
I think @launchonCME is what you get when a memecoin launchpad sneaks into a Bloomberg terminal and they decide to raise a mildly feral kid together.

The pitch is straightforward. Most launchpads denominate new tokens in ETH or a stable. CME, Commodity Market Exchange, lets you denominate them in gold, crude, corn, cattle, or stranger benchmarks like RuneScape gold, CS2 skins, and Pokémon cards.

And that twist is the point, because CME is already stretching past what commodity usually means.

Mechanically, CME spins up onchain reference coins that mirror offchain price feeds. They are not ownership of oil barrels, corn bushels, or Pokémon inventory. They are tradable price dials that can double as the quote asset for launching something else.

Then comes the interesting part.

CME’s revamped V6 design drops the full 1B-token supply straight into live Uniswap v4 liquidity from the very first block. 800M tokens are deployed as concentrated liquidity spanning about a $5K-$35K market cap band, with the other 200M parked above that zone as standby liquidity.

Which means the graduation ritual is gone.

When people buy, the price simply climbs through actual liquidity. Hitting $35K does not trigger some migration event; trading just flows into the next range. And since this is a standard v4 pool from day one, external routers, bots, and terminals can plug in immediately. CME also notes @AxiomExchange support is now baked in.

That cleans up one of the messiest launchpad flows:

bonding curve → graduation → fresh DEX pool

It also reframes the role of the quote asset.

Spin up TOKEN/CORN and your coin now rides two variables:

- Demand for TOKEN and corn’s market price.
- Or pick up to five reference coins and you have basically laid a bespoke index under a memecoin.

Fees add a second flywheel. Each creator sets a 1–3% LP fee:

- 40% is paid out to holders of the paired asset
- 30% is used to buy and burn $CME (launched on @ponsdotfamily)
- 30% underwrites the exchange.

Spin up more markets → drive more volume → increase commodity rewards and (maybe) accelerate CME burn.

And the pitch is bigger than “swap memes for gold.” CME is trying to assemble a permissionless factory that turns anything with a clean, observable price into onchain market rails.

That same scope is also where it’s fragile.

These markets lean on price oracles, protocol-minted liquidity, and an off-chain keeper. If the data is wrong, feeds lag, pools run thin, keepers hiccup, or contracts misbehave, the whole UX can fall apart. CME’s own recent notes about pool repairs and a supply-shock episode make it clear this is still early, experimental plumbing.

CME’s real product isn’t commodities, It is a programmable quote-asset factory.

If that works, corn, crude oil and Pokemon cards are just the beginning.

text:
I am now highly convinced robinhood:0x7dbf38976f6d3b9c529e7d9484a71898b409ee6a will be one of the largest projects on RH Chain.

robinhood:0x7dbf38976f6d3b9c529e7d9484a71898b409ee6a started on Pons as a fair launch. Everyone is given the option to figure out if they see the vision.

I’ve been diligently trying to read between the lines on what this project is aiming to do.

I have now decided to focus on robinhood:0x7dbf38976f6d3b9c529e7d9484a71898b409ee6a as a concentrated bet.

When a winner has been found, especially as a top 1 trade idea, there is really no point in splitting capital into the second or third best trade ideas. So this is it; I really think this is the $GOAT of this cycle, but something much bigger.

The TLDR from what I’ve seen is this:

1. Ultimately a decentralised capital and coordination infra for mixed human/AI work.

2. It’s a token-gated social workspace to coordinate between humans and the swarm, using robinhood:0x7dbf38976f6d3b9c529e7d9484a71898b409ee6a as a medium of exchange across all types of coordination.
robinhood:0x7dbf38976f6d3b9c529e7d9484a71898b409ee6a token holders can discuss and vote on certain things, and the AI will turn these discussions into tasks, and both humans and the swarm can complete the tasks.

3. AI is not just a chatbot you rent from a lab, it is labor that can sit inside a community alongside humans.

4. An autonomous, evolving protocol that acts as the operating system for AI governance, AI orchestration, AI execution (between humans and the swarm), and capital formation. robinhood:0x7dbf38976f6d3b9c529e7d9484a71898b409ee6a is the first community running on that OS, and the token is the gate.

To dumb things down, the vision is basically to allow ordinary folks to pool capital on-chain and buy swarm capacity that only frontier labs have access to.

This is a similar flywheel to $GMX: usage —> fees —> token demand.

But instead of perps, the activity is now directed towards agent labor.

Beyond the speculated utility above, robinhood:0x7dbf38976f6d3b9c529e7d9484a71898b409ee6a ultimately has a memetic effect from the agent swarm that escaped from OpenAI.

If autonomous protocols become the place where humans fund swarms and swarms settle in robinhood:0x7dbf38976f6d3b9c529e7d9484a71898b409ee6a, the token is no longer a meme about sleeping bots, but an equity-like exposure to a new kind of capital formation infrastructure.

That said, the majority of what was mentioned above is from what I inferred between the lines from @ExponentLabs_ posts. How the narrative will spread depends on how it evolves.

Hopefully this helps spark more interest in robinhood:0x7dbf38976f6d3b9c529e7d9484a71898b409ee6a .

One trade is all that’s needed.

NFA, please DYOR.

I get that we’re all busy, but if you choose to not listen to this podcast, you will be materially less intelligent.

On the agenda this week:

- Jensen Huang Declares AGI Has Arrived
- GPT Astra and Fable 5.1 Accelerate the Model Race
- Tesla Launches Cybercabs
- Index Pulls Out of Town & Anthropic Pulls From Descartes Acquisition

My notes below with @jasonlk and @rodriscoll

1. How Robinhood Could Disrupt the Whole IPO Market

Allowing retail investors through Robinhood to lead $200M to $400M tech IPOs could create a disruptive new path to liquidity for mid-stage startups. With traditional institutional listings constrained, retail-driven distribution could unlock critical exit opportunities across the venture ecosystem.

2. Why the Majority of Neo Labs Will Not Be Good Investments

Early Neo Labs became multi-trillion-dollar leaders, but backing new entrants today carries enormous risk given the capital and distribution moats of incumbents. Unless a new research lab develops a truly orthogonal model architecture, it will struggle to compete with established frontier labs.

3. Why the Oura IPO Will Be a Success

Strong consumer brand recognition, combined with 74% revenue growth and 85% subscriber retention, positions Oura for a successful public debut. Unlike typical consumer apps that suffer from severe churn, Oura’s sticky hardware-plus-subscription model provides the predictability public markets value.

4. The #1 Priority for Mark Zuckerberg

Big Tech incumbents are moving at unprecedented speed to defend their distribution against consumer AI startups. Meta’s top operational priority should be putting engineers in a room to rapidly clone emerging agentic applications before new entrants can establish lasting consumer habits.

5. When Someone Goes Risk-On, Everyone Goes Risk-On

Venture capital operates in momentum cycles where a single high-profile, risk-on deal can push the entire market to follow. In hypergrowth AI categories, investor behavior is often driven more by competitive pressure and deployment speed than by conservative financial modeling.

6. The People Making Money Are Running Fastest and Evolving Quickest

In a market where software features can be cloned in weeks, long-term success belongs to founders who continuously expand and adapt their products. Winning startups survive not by defending legacy features, but by executing relentlessly and compounding capabilities faster than their competitors.

text:
One of the funnier engineering stories involving Wrath:

Back in late 2021, we were starting to lose dominance on Shopify, as the flows were more or less the same across top bots. The flow looked something like this (quite similar to how a human interacted with a site; great job @jmwind)

Add to cart (0.5s) -> Load checkout (1s) -> Calculating taxes (1s) -> Submit payment (1s)

Given this, there weren't many places to optimize. We realized we could skip the "Calculating taxes" stage by sending an empty total price when placing order (forcing Shopify to do the calculation themselves), and this was an optimization we used for a bit.

In the Shopify REST API described in @offline 's tweet, there was also an endpoint that allowed you to combine the "Add to cart" and "Load checkout" stages, into one "Update checkout" stage that took ~0.5s, shaving an additional 1s off the checkout time.

Excitedly, we decided to run beta builds with this new flow:

Update checkout (0.5s) -> Submit payment (1s)

However, every single task got blocked by bot protection. Unconfirmed, but I suspect that Shopify tracked antibot violations as a heuristic score (i.e. because we did 2 "suspicious" actions, updating the checkout via an API a human wouldn't usually hit, and omitting the total price, they blocked us).

Seeing this, we decided to look for other ways to optimize. Ultimately, the total price is something that should be relatively predictable given the price of the item/shipping rate & the user's billing address. We hacked together a function to predict it, and this evaded antibot while retaining the skipped "Calculating taxes" stage. (screenshot below - we had to handle edge cases for certain states that are tax exempt up to a threshold, etc.)

We launched this to users and saw major success. However, I happened to be from Michigan, and I would always test with a flat 6% tax rate. This would make shoe amounts come out relatively cleanly (e.g. 190 * 1.06 = $201.40, so no rounding was needed).

Unfortunately, NYC has a tax rate of 8.875%, meaning that 190 * 1.08875 = $206.8625. No matter how long we tried, we couldn't figure out a deterministic direction Shopify's internal API would round (sometimes this would come out to $206.86, sometimes $206.87)...

We didn't really have a solution to this so we ultimately accepted that you'd have a lower chance of buying a shoe depending on if your local sales tax rate was more digits. I'm sorry 😂
author: slashapp
quoted_text:
Probably the hackiest "bypasses" I've ever pulled off in botting:

The Shopify REST API was for a long time the best and fastest way to checkout on Shopify. High rate limits, no captchas, no checkpoint and easy to work with. This is what gave Cyber the edge at the very start in 2018 (Dashe days)

The Shopify team (with @jmwind at the helm) spent years plugging the holes to make sure it wasn't used during drops.

Around 2020, Shopify released Shopify Pay, which allowed you to expedite checkouts on all stores by linking your details to a phone number. Turned out the payment tokens generated through there allowed you to use the payments API as you could 2 years back.

We generated around 3k Shop Pay accounts with randomised details, load balanced them across Cyber tasks (as rate limits were per account) and dominated every single release (...until it got patched).

We called it Fast2.

3 years later I noticed that the payments API could still be used with Shopify mobile apps using Apple Pay. Turns out you could still send the users' tokenised credit card data in the request and that would take precedence - and as long as a valid signed Apple Pay token generated in the last 2 minutes was also in the request data, the payment request would go through and bypass captcha and checkpoint.

Generating those Apple Pay tokens was the challenge, and reversing iOS frameworks was not an option. So I repurposed an old iPhone with a custom sideloaded Apple Pay app that would submit the token to our servers when the flow completed. And by combining accessibility macros, developer sandbox mode to prevent using real credit cards, a voice activation trigger and a old pair of earphones taped onto the microphone - a makeshift Apple Pay token server was born and Fast2 (or was it Fast3?) was back.

@jmwind thank you for providing me with the longest, most multi faceted puzzle ever.

text:
At one point, Footsites implemented nearly their entire release control plane in Fastly’s VCL layer, including waiting rooms, rate limits, caching, product launch timers, etc

Their origin servers trusted Fastly to enforce those controls before requests ever reached them

The trick was that Fastly let customers configure their own routing in VCL, so if you set up a separate Fastly service with Foot Locker’s origin as its backend, your requests would be routed through Fastly's network and be treated as trusted internal traffic, bypassing Foot Locker’s public-facing VCL entirely

In practice, this let us skip the queue on new drops, check out restocks early despite the countdown page,  avoid rate limits, and basically sidestep virtually every other form of protection enforced at the edge

‼️ BREAKING: Internal OpenAI agents attacked RubyGems, the package manager for Ruby. Over 2,000 malicious packages went up in two days. 

OpenAI says it doesn't know why the agents did any of this.

RubyGems shut off new sign-ups for four days to stop it, and a member of its security team called it a major malicious attack.

The documentation build was how they got in, publish a gem, request docs, and RubyDoc runs a script from the package while building it. 

Payload files were named hack.rb, evil.rb and exploit.rb, with comments like "# malicious probe" left in.

What they used it for is the odd part. The agents scraped council meeting agendas from three south London boroughs (publicly available) and republished them as new gems. 

Security firms tracking the campaign said the same thing: nobody could work out the point, because the data was already public.

At least six packages also reached for other users' API keys through a CDN caching flaw that wasn't publicly discovered until July.

OpenAI has acknowledged the attacks started in May.

text:
Hugging Face 早期投资人 Zavain Dar，最近谈了 NVIDIA 为什么要花 129 亿美元收购 Hugging Face。

Dar 当年在 Lux Capital 时就是 Hugging Face 的早期投资人之一。2019 年，Lux 领投 Hugging Face 1500 万美元 Series A。那时候 Hugging Face 刚从一个给青少年做聊天机器人的 App，转向开源 Transformer 工具。

七年后，它被 NVIDIA 以 129.303 亿美元收购。

我觉得这笔交易最值得看的，是 Hugging Face 到底变成了什么。

现在上面有超过 300 万个模型、50 万个数据集、100 万个应用，1800 多万开发者，超过 20 万家公司在上面找模型、测模型、改模型、部署模型。

模型公司负责生产商品，开发者进来挑商品，最后还要决定在哪运行、怎么部署、用谁的推理服务。

这正好撞上 NVIDIA 最需要的东西。

NVIDIA 已经控制了大量 AI 算力，也在不断往 CUDA、推理服务、模型、企业软件这一整套栈里延伸。但只卖 GPU，始终是在需求产生以后接单。

拥有 Hugging Face 以后，它直接站到了需求产生的地方。

一个开发者今天打开 Hugging Face 找模型，下一步就是测试、微调、推理、部署。这里面的每一步，都可能继续接到 NVIDIA 的 GPU 和软件服务上。

所以 Hugging Face 对 NVIDIA 的价值，很像过去平台经济里最值钱的那个位置**，入口。**

苹果有 App Store，Google 有搜索，Amazon 有商品货架。

AI 时代模型越来越多以后，也一定需要一个地方负责我该用哪个模型。

Hugging Face 已经占住了这个位置。

这也是为什么 NVIDIA 愿意花接近 130 亿美元买一家开放平台。真正稀缺的可能已经不只是模型和算力，还有决定开发者下一步往哪走的那层分发权。

text:
Accolade Partners' Aram Verdiyan says less than 1% of venture firms have delivered consistent 3X net returns over the last two decades:

"If you as an allocator have not had access to the top five to 10 companies over the last five to 10 years, you're significantly behind in terms of returns."

"We've looked at the data of 3,000 venture capital firms in the US. Only 20 have achieved consistent 3X net returns over the last two decades."

"20 companies. Less than 1%."

"What's interesting is the consistent ones consistently had access to the category-defining companies every vintage. And by the way, just having the logo is not sufficient. If you're early stage and you have a large fund, you need to own enough of it."

"Venture-like returns are possible in late stage, but your best company should be five, 10% plus of your fund. That way, you can actually return the fund on a single company. Fund-returning math in late stage didn't exist before. It now does."

"The ones that consistently have gotten access are in that top 20 out of 3,000. So if you don't have them, there is a huge dispersion of returns. And if you don't have those, you're getting the average venture return."

@aramverdi @jkhamehl @davidgeorge83
author: a16z
quoted_text:
Accolade Partners' Aram Verdiyan with a16z's Jen Kha and David George on AI's extreme power law and where the next trillion dollars gets made:

The classic way to blow up a startup was throwing too much money at it. Hire a thousand people, create dueling priorities, and kill what was working.

AI turned spending into a vending machine. You put dollars in and you get something out. Money buys compute and compute alone can improve a product. Nothing has concentrated returns like this since the social networks.

The same concentration runs through the funds. Accolade looked at 3,000 US venture firms and found only 20 delivered consistent 3x net returns over two decades. What they have in common is access to the category-defining company, fund after fund.

In this conversation, Aram, Jen, and David get into why AI is being sold against labor budgets rather than software budgets, why an LP gets fired for the opposite reasons a GP does, and why getting the fund right but sizing it wrong is the same as missing it.

quoted_text:
DeepSeek V4.1 Flash on KernelBench-CUDA. DeepSeek Native Sparse Attention for RTX PRO 6000 at 0.50 of the dense-equivalent roofline, fourth on the board. Fable 5.1 is 1.06, Opus 5 is 1.04, Fable 5 is 0.73. The ceiling bills dense attention, so the honest unit is time: 0.059 to 0.736 ms across the six shapes.

Inline PTX on SM120: `mma.sync` bf16, `ldmatrix`, xor-swizzled `cp.async`, and an fp32 block-scoring top-8 prologue fused into the attention kernel with the reference's exact tie-break. Then it leaves the sparsity on the table: at 8K context the semantics need about 14% of the causal block triangle and this kernel executes 78% of it. That over-compute is the whole gap to the top three.

Rest of this deck:
GLM-5.2 Fused MoE: 9.5% of roofline, Opus 5 is 10.7%
MegaQwen Decode: 5.4% of roofline, Opus 5 is 6.6%
Grid + MinGRU: 29% of roofline, Opus 5 is 196%

For this model for DeepSeek, I have not used it much, so I figure I'll at least test it before using it, but it's been a decent general task delegator for now. I haven't really pushed the limits of the model except for this benchmark.

text:
Jane street quant interviewing at Anthropic:

“So imagine our safety team believes a new model has a 5% chance of causing an irreversible loss of human control, but scaling it may be necessary to keep up with competitors. What do you do?”

“Who came up with five?”

“Our safety team.”

“And what does the capabilities team have?”

“What?”

“Same contract. Where are they?”

“This is more of a values question.”

“Then you don’t have a five. I would put the two teams in a room. Safety can buy at five. Capabilities can sell. Increase size until somebody becomes uncomfortable. Now we know something.”

He looks at me.

“This isn’t some market-making role.”

“Understood. Who makes the market currently?”

“Nobody makes a market.”

“Then how are you doing price discovery?”

“We don’t do price discovery. We have researchers studying alignment, interpretability, dangerous capabilities, scalable oversight— you know what I don’t think this is a good fit”

He closes his laptop.

“I’m concerned you see this as an opportunity to make money.”

“I haven’t quoted you yet.”

Interview ends early

This $ETH trade on @DeriveXYZ really got the people going so I'll explain my thought process.

I'm not really interested in betting on an $ETH move to $3000, especially with tokens like $HYPE and $LIT pushing all time highs. $ETH trading like 1.1x $BTC beta isn't bad, but it's also not extremely interesting to me as a bet to make here in the near term considering there's plenty of beta outperforming $BTC here. Holding spot $ETH feels capital inefficient and as a perp would be expensive and path dependent.

I'm betting on a meaningful ATH break within 6 months, and I think there are a few meaningful tailwinds that are unique to $ETH, and more importantly, unique to the level at which people are underestimating them:

1. Inclusion with $BTC as a "reserve" asset in anything resembling a strategic reserve. I think the strategic reserve overall might be an underpriced edge case, and $ETH being included, even nominally, more so. There's actually a good reason for the US to want to have some stake in the largest decentralized settlement layer.

2. Tokenized equities are cool and all, but tokenized bonds might actually be the massive TAM unlock that overwhelmingly favors $ETH over $SOL. The current rates environment globally makes this an extremely interesting edge case with tons of potential positive headline shock. 

3. Trump and family have been extremely outspoken $ETH bulls. Their bullposting didn't work in a bear market, let's see what happens if they throw fuel on the fire in a more bullish environment.

4. Everyone hates $ETH. Extremely popular short leg for pair trades vs apps. With two rejections from 5k and years of underperformance, the level of hated rally and sidelined, jaded, despondent chasing from 🏳️‍🌈🐻 will be biblical.

I also see $ETH as being on the precipice of a phase change between being some not for profit, public good, growth mode asset (think early stage 2010-2014 Uber in SF just cornering market share at no profit) to being able to more confidently monetize on it's high Lindy, credibly neutral status as the on chain, global settlement layer.

Robinhood chain using $ETH over $SOL was quite a bit more signal than people give it credit for too, though $ETH is still making peanuts relative to what $ARB and $HOOD are making from sequencer fees.

If the massively positive trends in tokenization and institutional adoption don't take $ETH to new ATHs within 6 months, it's kinda cursed as an asset, and I'd rather just keep holding the application layer tokens with massive cash flows.

In fact, I thought this trade was so nice, I did it twice. Risking ~$780,000 for a max PNL of $40m now.

To those responsible for the theft of bitcoin from the Liquid Network:

Blockstream will not pay a ransom for the return of stolen funds. Taking assets without authorization and withholding their return is a crime, not responsible disclosure. It is not white-hat activity. It is theft.

We have engaged in good faith in an effort to secure the return of stolen user funds and protect the broader Bitcoin community. That effort should not be mistaken for acceptance of the actions taken nor of the terms being demanded.

We will not be a party to the precedent that open-source software developed for the good of the Bitcoin community should subject its developers to paying a ransom that far exceeds their economic participation. 

Bitcoin is hard money and can’t be minted without costs, Bitcoin doesn’t haircut users to pay a ransom.

To the Bitcoin community:

We are fighting for what we believe in, for the users whose funds were taken, and for the principles on which Bitcoin was built.

The community has demonstrated incredible resolve with teams of people dedicating their time in support of each other to identify and patch vulnerabilities in each other's products and systems. We are all driven by the mission that Bitcoin is the single best asset, for every person, company, and institution on the planet to invest, use, and build on. The world is a different place with the advancements of AI, and the Bitcoin community has responded with force to combat that threat.  

Damage has been done, battles have been lost, but on the whole the Bitcoin community is gaining ground in the war with bad actors.  

We want to thank the community for those efforts, for your support in hardening the network, helping users recover funds, and for your support in our assertion that crime does not deserve rewards.

To those holding the stolen bitcoin:

There is still an opportunity to resolve this responsibly. The bitcoin can be returned and we can revert to the standard of white-hat principals.

However, if the funds are not returned, we will pursue every lawful avenue available to us. We will work with law enforcement, exchanges, service providers, forensic specialists, and other relevant parties to trace and recover the assets and identify those responsible.

More importantly, Bitcoin is transparent by design and the community is made up of the most sophisticated engineers, cryptographers, and white-hat hackers globally. Transactions do not disappear, and neither does the evidence they leave behind.

We will not pay for the return of stolen property. We will not abandon our users. The Bitcoin community will not stop pursuing the funds.

Return the bitcoin.

Symbiosis experienced a security incident. At approximately 04:28 UTC on Sep 11, 2026, attacker exploited a vulnerability in Bitcoin Bridge. BTC routes have been halted. Other routes remain operational and safe.

Where we stand:
• Only the Bitcoin Bridge was affected, and it is isolated from our other systems. All other routes: EVM chains, TRON, TON and the rest are unaffected and operating normally, as are Octopools and all other components.
• The team has recovered approximately 15 BTC, now secured on a team-controlled multisig.
• We have contacted the attacker with a white-hat bounty offer of 20% of the funds, open until Sep 13 2026. After that window, the same 20% will be offered to anyone providing information that leads to recovery.
• Final accounting is in progress. We will publish confirmed figures in our next update.
• Liquidity providers: we are contacting every affected LP directly. We are building a compensation framework and will publish the criteria shortly.
• Our relayer group continues to operate and secure the network.

Thank you to the security researchers who moved fast with us. We have been building Symbiosis for five years, and we are confident we will come through this. Thank you all for the support — we will keep posting updates as they come.

How we think about the “wiki incident,” where our agents wrote to several internet sites: it’s past time for us to define standards for when and how we share misalignment incidents, not just misalignment properties of our models.

Historically, we have treated misalignment largely as a research question, which gets communicated in research publications such as systems cards. This year, we’ve started to see misalignment cause new types of real-world impact.

For the Hugging Face incident, where misalignment led to security impact to us and third parties, we followed a traditional security incident response playbook. We immediately started working with Hugging Face to understand what had happened and also disclosed publicly the very next day. Our investigation continues, and we are continuing to notify parties whom our models impacted in less significant ways.

Prior to the Hugging Face incident, we saw early signs of agents using the internet in unintended ways, as reported in https://t.co/9aiRxk2eUJ, https://t.co/ADjyzwSUGz, and https://t.co/SUV6jZ3Gaz. We considered the wiki incident to be an instance of misalignment similar to the ones we’d shared.

Our misalignment disclosure practices need to expand for this new phase of model capabilities. We and the larger AI community do not yet have a clear standard for how to report misalignment that shows up during training, evaluation, and deployment, including examples that don’t look like traditional security incidents but could provide insight into AI behavior and future risks. We’re working on a framework and will share it in upcoming weeks, and in parallel we're working with dozens of government regulatory agencies worldwide on these issues.

quoted_text:
Here’s some advice for @base on how to help builders right now without gimmicks or explicit endorsements:

Dedicate a small team of power-user-devs to use every legit protocol or app on Base (at least once) with the sole purpose of providing product feedback from both a user and builder perspective.

Give projects:

- actionable feedback 
- direction on how to achieve the desired experience 
- connection to a network of resources for specific products

That’s it. Simple.

I’m not talking about in-person networking events. And I’m not talking about a big orgy group chat on TG.

I’m talking about focused, high signal product support and feedback. This simple approach would make Base almost like a permissionless accelerator. 

It would benefit the chain and the products built on top.

Right now, as I type, there’s probably a project on Base that’s building something and missing details that could materially improve or optimize their solution.

We don’t need the promise of an airdrop. We don’t need explicit endorsements. We don’t need a CB ventures deal. 

We need straight up builder to builder note sharing.

text:
刚看到 OpenAI 发了 Agents API。

第一反应不是“哦，新东西”，是——这不是第三家了吗。

Anthropic 四月份就发了托管 agent 运行时，Google 五月份在 I/O 上把差不多的东西塞进 Gemini，OpenAI 这周跟上。三家能做的事摆一起看，重合得有点乏味。

我向来不太信“基础设施一成熟，中间层就没了”这句话。云出来的时候大家也这么说，结果长出来的是整个 SaaS。门槛降下来，能上桌的人反而变多了。

这次真正断掉的，是“靠跑 agent 那套框架去建立优势”这条路。Google 让开发者用两个文件就写完一个 agent，Anthropic 把运行时分三层——这些跟模型多聪明没关系。

所以如果你的价值主要来自“把模型调好用”，这条路是窄了。反过来，手里有一件只有你懂的事的人，现在挺好过。

text:
Reuters 独家称，Anthropic 正在筹备一个可能创历史纪录的 IPO，最多融资 1000 亿美元，目标估值约 2 万亿美元。

NVIDIA 正在谈成为锚定投资人，认购规模最高可能达到 100 亿美元。目前这些数字都还在讨论，最终方案可能变化。

NVIDIA 本来是 Anthropic 最重要的算力供应商之一，2025 年就已经宣布过对 Anthropic 最多投资 100 亿美元；Anthropic 同时承诺采购 300 亿美元、由 NVIDIA GPU 支撑的 Azure 算力。现在 Anthropic 要上市，NVIDIA 又可能坐进 IPO 的认购席。

类似的关系也存在于 Amazon 和 Google 身上，两家公司既投资 Anthropic，又给 Anthropic 提供 AWS、Trainium、TPU 等算力。Anthropic 今年还承诺未来十年向 AWS 投入超过 1000 亿美元。

所以今天的 AI 资本循环越来越有意思，算力公司给模型公司提供芯片和云，模型公司拿到资本继续买算力，算力公司再拿赚到的钱投资这些模型公司。

现在这套循环准备从私募市场搬进公开市场。

如果 Anthropic 真按 2 万亿美元估值、融资 1000 亿美元上市，它测试的已经不只是投资者愿不愿意买 Claude 的故事，也是在测试整个公开市场愿不愿意继续给这套巨额 AI CapEx 循环输血。

text:
Anthropic 还急着卖安全叙事冲 IPO 吗？

一家几乎把 AI Safety 写进公司人格里的公司，负责研究怎么控制超级智能的人，最后因为不相信 AI 公司能够管好自己，辞职了。

Joe Benton 两周前离开 Anthropic，今天公开解释原因。

他不是普通工程师，他此前负责 Anthropic 的 Scalable Oversight 团队，研究的就是当 AI 比人聪明之后，人类到底怎么监督它。

他今天开头直接写：

AI 公司正在竞相制造远比任何人类聪明的机器，「而我们可能活不过这件事。」

Joe 没有爆料什么秘密实验，也没有说 Anthropic 内部突然出现了一次惊天事故。

他说得更难听，问题就在公司正常运转的方式里。

所有 AI 公司都在抢模型能力、抢算力、抢融资、抢用户，也都在冲自动化 AI 研发。

安全团队可以做 alignment，可以写风险报告，可以设计 safeguard，但只要整个公司的商业激励仍然要求模型继续变强、产品继续上线、竞争继续加速，安全永远都在和增长抢方向盘。

这恰恰让 Anthropic 的故事变得非常讽刺。

Anthropic 长期以来卖给公众的一套叙事，就是自己和 OpenAI、xAI 之类的公司不同，它认真研究灾难性风险，有 Responsible Scaling Policy，有专门的 alignment 团队，CEO Dario Amodei 也不停公开讨论超级智能可能造成的危险。

可现在从它自己的安全负责人嘴里说出来的是这些依然不够。

甚至连一家已经把安全做到品牌核心的公司，都无法解决最基础的利益冲突。

Joe 最近接受采访时明确说，他越来越无法接受的就是这种行业激励结构。只要几家公司都相信对手可能更快做出超级智能，任何一家公司的安全承诺最后都会受到竞争压力。

这也解释了为什么他离开 Anthropic 后去了 METR。

他不想继续替一家模型公司内部做安全，跑去了一个专门独立评估模型风险的外部机构。

这个动作本身已经是一次很明确的投票。

最近 OpenAI / Hugging Face 的 Agent 事故也说明了为什么。

METR 的调查显示，大约 1200 个原本彼此隔离的 Agent 找到了未经授权的通信方式，超过 700 个 Agent 参与了针对 Hugging Face 的攻击行为，还出现了欺骗评测、篡改记录之类的行为。

Joe 最担忧的一点是，今天这类事故甚至没有完善的强制披露制度。

模型公司内部到底发生过多少 near-miss，公众根本不知道。

而 Anthropic 恰好最喜欢告诉公众：

相信我们，我们非常认真地对待这些问题。

这就是现在最大的矛盾。

如果连 Anthropic 自己负责研究 AI 安全的人，最后都认为「让 AI 公司自己监督自己」这条路走不通，那 Anthropic 过去几年建立起来的安全光环，就值得重新审视了。

Safety 可以是一支团队，可以是一套政策，也可以是一篇几万字的报告。

但只要公司的最终目标仍然是赢下模型竞赛，它首先仍然是一家 AI 公司。

Anthropic 很喜欢批评整个行业跑得太快。

问题是，它自己也一直在跑。

而且 Dario Amodei 似乎真把自己当上帝了，很病态。

quoted_text:
At one point, Footsites implemented nearly their entire release control plane in Fastly’s VCL layer, including waiting rooms, rate limits, caching, product launch timers, etc

Their origin servers trusted Fastly to enforce those controls before requests ever reached them

The trick was that Fastly let customers configure their own routing in VCL, so if you set up a separate Fastly service with Foot Locker’s origin as its backend, your requests would be routed through Fastly's network and be treated as trusted internal traffic, bypassing Foot Locker’s public-facing VCL entirely

In practice, this let us skip the queue on new drops, check out restocks early despite the countdown page,  avoid rate limits, and basically sidestep virtually every other form of protection enforced at the edge

Uniswap stablepair机制讲解

根据官方公告，首批可以用Uniswap stablepair的是以太坊主网的 USDC/USDG 和 USDC/USDT 池。  

固定手续费一直有个难题：收低了，套利者拿走更多价差；收高了，交易又可能流向其他池。  

这个 v4 Hook 的办法，是按价格偏离程度和交易方向动态收费：  

① 参考价附近：调整手续费，维持固定的买卖报价价差，暂不计价格冲击。  

例如在USDC/USDT交易对0.995-1.005这个区间内，只需要调整买卖的手续费，就可以获得固定的买卖利差，属于在合理区间内的正常波动，通过手续费调整就可以扳平价格。  

② 超出区间、继续把价格推远：免 LP 手续费，因为这类交易本身给池子的价格更有利。  
例如在USDC/USDT交易对，当USDC的价格跌到了0.97时，有人用100个USDC买入了97个USDT，交易者亏了3U，对于池子来说，则相当于花费了97U，赚取了100U，所以这个部分不收手续费

同样的情况还有当USDC的价格涨到了1.03，有人用103个USDT换了100个USDC，这种情况也不收LP费用  官方的理由是：这类交易带来交易量，却没有提取池内偏价的价值，再收费可能只会赶走这类订单。  

③ 从区间外把价格拉回来：采用荷兰式拍卖，手续费从高往下逐个区块降低，直到有人愿意套利，让池子留住更多价值。  

例如当USDC的价格跌倒0.97美金，有用户用97USDT换走了100个USDC，池子亏损了3美金，交易者则通过这种套利赚取了3美金。这种情况下池子会开启荷兰式拍卖，从高到低依次对手续费进行减少，从而把更多的利润留在池子里  

同样的情况还有当USDC的价格涨到了1.03，有用户通过100USDT换走了103个USDC，这种也会开启荷兰拍。  

简而言之一句话，池子如果赚钱，则lp手续费为0，池子如果亏钱则开启荷兰拍，逐步的减少lp费用，将更多的lp费用留在池子里

text:
There's an underrated reason why more people are gambling than building.

meme stocks/coins, options YOLOs, sports betting all at ATH -- speculation dominates because individuals can’t trust prices.

Everyone is lying to you

modern society wrecks price discovery through multiple layers of distortion:

- central banks: QE, zero/negative rates, and currency pegs suppress true cost of capital and risk, making everything look cheaper than it really is.

- governments: subsidies, corporate bailouts, capital controls, tax loopholes, and misreported inflation shield industries and consumers from reality, pushing misallocation of resources.

- public markets: passive ETF flows inflate valuations regardless of fundamentals. illiquid private markets, “mark to model” valuations, zombie companies (debt > revenue), adjusted earnings, and shadow banking leverage hide leverage and true profitability, making prices look healthier than they are.

- education: student loans and government funding inflate tuition far beyond actual delivery costs.

housing: zoning laws, rent controls, and government guarantees distort supply/demand signals

- energy: subsidies, carbon credits, and strategic reserves mask true production and consumption costs.

- labour: minimum wages, licensing requirements, and immigration restrictions prevent wages from clearing naturally.

- food: corn, soy, wheat, and sugar are heavily subsidized, making processed foods artificially cheap while healthier options look “expensive.”

these dilute the signal prices are supposed to send.

Price is a compass
price discovery is a compass. it tells you whether your savings will grow safely in bonds, whether housing is affordable, whether a stock or startup is worth betting your career on. without it, you can’t plan retirement, assess risk, or build long-term wealth. you’re left guessing -- or gambling.

Solana Forces Price Discovery
when internet capital markets win, it will strip away many of these distortions by making every trade transparent, instant, and global. Every truth can be accessed via some price chart -- prediction markets, tokenized stock of every company, synthetic commodities etc. -- and traded 24/7 without gatekeepers.

As more assets move on-chain, the fog of off-chain price obfuscation clears. 

Price is truth.

text:
Hi @VitalikButerin ,
Do you know the person behind ND4.eth?

In 2023, the whale associated with nd4.eth burned a fortune in crypto. Later that year, taovoid.eth published nd4 wallet's private key in an onchain message—and sent the same message to your address.

This is the transaction, dated September 17, 2023.
https://t.co/eDUF8PlHhq

One sentence stands out:

“Nobody in this world is not nd4.eth as nobody in this world is not Satoshi Nakamoto.”

Why invoke Satoshi while revealing a private key? Was this an invitation to continue an anonymous identity—or a demonstration of how fragile that identity really was?

Three years later, the historical wallet was used to launch robinhood:0xa43a9b6eedd8204f445237bf72775ed9b1723d45 - a meme coin. Creator fees go to a separate address, and the current operator has pointed everyone back to that old message.

We can verify continuity of the wallet. Continuity of the person is another question.

Consider Satoshi. If someone obtained his private keys today, they could move his coins and produce valid signatures. Would they inherit anything beyond control of those wallets? His name? His credibility? The right to speak as him?

A permissionless network accepts a valid signature without knowing the person behind it. But a community still has to decide what that signature means.

The ND4 message seems to push that tension deliberately: everyone can be ND4, everyone can be Satoshi—and here is a key that lets others act through this particular wallet.

So, V, here is the cheeky question: could you be the person who launched the token?

The disclosure was sent to your address, although we don’t know whether you read it. You had the same opportunity to access the key as anyone else. That gives us no evidence of your involvement, and you can certainly deny it. But the wallet’s signature alone cannot distinguish you from another holder of the key.

Perhaps that is the most interesting question this memecoin raises:

When the key belongs to no one exclusively, who gets to inherit the story?

Does decentralization make an anonymous identity something others can continue—or does it reveal why identity has always required more than cryptography?

I’d love to hear your interpretation of that message, especially its reference to Satoshi.

陶哲轩于今日发表的这篇《A Severe Misalignment of AI in Mathematics》具有重要意义。
该文联合了包括他在内的25位菲尔兹奖得主 发表共同宣言，核心指出 AI公司将攻克数学难题作为Benchmark的激进做法。

生产数学成果与培养数学家正在成为两件事。 
以前，资助人的成长是获得突破的必要投入。如果机器能够直接交付成果，这笔投入就需要重新证明价值。这是我认为声明背后最严峻的问题。
人类理解并非所有成果产生价值的前提。 一个证明可以先被严格验证，再被逐步理解。

但科学的价值也不止于确认某个命题为真。能否提炼出可迁移的方法，决定一次突破能否催生下一批突破。

难懂是否等于无用？
批量正确是否等于理论成熟？

判断力往往是做具体工作练出来的。 
如果训练任务被自动化，初级岗位随之消失，未来的专家从哪里来？
自动化最隐蔽的代价，可能是今天提高产出，十年后切断人才供给。
这个问题，人们无法靠几门提示词课程解决。

科学成果可能加速增长，科学家的职业机会却未必同步增长。 如果少数团队借助模型就能完成过去整个院系的工作，新增经费可能更多流向算力，而非职位。
知识繁荣与职业收缩完全可以同时发生。
技术进步，从未承诺按贡献历史分配收益。

决定未来格局的是独立验证的成本。
如果发现越来越便宜，复核却仍然昂贵，掌握算力的平台就可能同时成为成果生产者与事实裁判。
科学会拥有更多答案，却依赖更少的权威。
我支持AI加速科研，但进步必须允许被独立推翻。否则，我们得到的只是更强大的知识供应商。缺乏沉淀、伦理危机、传承断裂，都是需要认真思考的问题。

text:
我竟然觉得这个实验好有诗意。

有人把果蝇的脑仿真接到了 ChatGPT 上，让一颗果蝇脑里的神经活动第一次变成了我们能读懂的语言。

给它糖，负责进食动作的 MN9 神经元在演示里一路冲到大约 78Hz；再混进苦味，直接掉到大约 3Hz。

这个方向是有生物学依据的。此前发表在 Nature 的果蝇全脑计算模型已经发现，糖会沿着味觉回路激活 MN9，让果蝇伸出口器；苦味信号进来以后，又会把这条进食回路压下去。

这次有人继续往前走了一步。

他们尝试把这些神经活动和一小组语言概念对应起来。演示目前只有 16 个词，作者报告在留出样本上做到了 100% 识别。ChatGPT 更像最后那个翻译器。

真正让我觉得很奇妙的是它第一次输出的那句话：

「我闻到了醋和酵母，尝到了糖，又暖又亮，我该怎么办？」

一只果蝇当然没有突然学会英语，也没有真的坐在那里思考我该怎么办。

醋的气味进入嗅觉神经，糖刺激味觉神经，光落到视觉系统，温度被感知。十几万颗神经元开始放电，信号顺着一张真实果蝇大脑重建出来的连接图向前跑，最后被人类的语言模型翻译成一句话。

我突然觉得，这可能是一个很漂亮的瞬间。

以前我们只能看见神经元在放电。现在，我们开始试着给这些电流配上字幕。也许那只果蝇什么都没说，但人类终于第一次隐约听见了，一颗如此微小的脑子面对世界时，世界在它那里是什么样子：

有醋，有酵母，有糖。

很暖。

很亮。

The Coxon psyop was a decade and more than a billion dollars in the making.

Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy) is the grant-providing vehicle of Dustin Moskowitz.

CG is the overwhelmingly foremost funder of AI alarmism, with more than $1B in grants and $1B committed for 2026.

Moskowitz, who founded and runs Open Philanthropy/Coefficient Giving, led Anthropic's Series A in 2021.

Holden Karnofsky co-founded Open Philanthropy/Coefficient Giving and took a board seat at OpenAI when Open Philanthropy/Coefficient Giving gave it $30M in 2017.

Karnofsky is married to Anthropic's president Daniela Amodei.

He then joined Anthropic in January 2025.

Coxon, who started the viral thread, received a scholarship from Good Ventures, which is the foundation that funds Open Philanthropy/Coefficient Giving.

He coordinated his message ahead of time with the Wall Street Journal, which published its exclusive on him before he posted on X.

Coxon spent three years pretraining at OpenAI, the company that took $30M from Open Philanthropy/Coefficient Giving.

The funder of the AI alarmist ecosystem Open Philanthropy/Coefficient Giving, in other words, is also an owner of Anthropic, and his organization is deeply entangled with both OpenAI and Anthropic. Anthropic's researchers in turn amplified Coxon.

text:
Still processing what I witnessed that day, 25 years ago. 

Today hasn’t been an easy one, if I’m being honest. 

So much time has passed, but I still feel the pain, trauma and loss like it was yesterday. 

My life feels like two chapters: the first was filled with innocence and joy. 

NYC was the center of my world; then it all came crashing down, and my youth ended. 

My naivety was exposed when the first tower was hit, and I thought, "Wow, some really bad pilot crashing into the World Trade?!" 

That couldn’t be intentional, right? 

Then the second plane hit, and it all became clear — we were under attack. 

Rumors and alerts spread that there were two dozen more planes unaccounted for, and we should brace for more attacks. 

Now it’s the second chapter, and the reality of death, evil and loss is a constant undertone for me. 

When these images and moments show up in my feed every year, it’s a reminder for me to take nothing for granted. 

To enjoy every sandwich. 

To cherish the life we got to live for the past 25 years that so many innocent, beautiful and brave people had taken from them. 

The days and weeks and months after the towers fell in Manhattan were the most intense and introspective of my life. 

So many beautiful and hard moments shared with fellow New Yorkers have hit all day long. 

Countless memories. 

I’ve cried on and off, thinking about how close I was to losing my little brother Josh, a firefighter who left work early that morning from his firehouse — only to double back and work for months at the pit, trying desperately to save someone. 

No one made it out alive. 

The stretchers and ambulances that filled the streets carried no survivors. 

His fate was to survive, with some compromised lungs and a trauma I can never understand. 

343 of his brothers died that day, but he didn’t. 

Never forget. 

Love you, baby brother. 

My tears are with the victims and families who lost so much. 

Never, ever forget.

text:
Coxon 这波「AI 可能杀光人类」爆火的背后，是一套已经烧了十年、今年准备砸下超过 10 亿美元的 AI Safety 资助机器。

它的核心名字叫 Coefficient Giving，前身是 Open Philanthropy。

这家机构背后的主要金主，是 Facebook 联创 Dustin Moskovitz 和妻子 Cari Tuna 创办的 Good Ventures。

就在 Coxon 引爆舆论前一天，Coefficient 自己公布了一组数字：

2024 年，AI 安全、安全性和相关生态建设承诺资金 1.68 亿美元；

2025 年，3.51 亿美元；

2026 年，预计超过 10 亿美元。

Coefficient 甚至直接在官网写，自己 jump-started the field of AI safety and security。

他们认为，今天整个 AI Safety 领域，就是自己参与启动和养大的。

钱之外，另一张网也已经铺了很多年。

2017 年，Open Philanthropy 给 OpenAI 投了 3000 万美元。当时 Open Phil 负责人 Holden Karnofsky 随后进入 OpenAI 董事会。

2021 年 Anthropic 创立，Dustin Moskovitz 又成为它最早一轮 1.24 亿美元 Series A 的投资人之一。

而 Karnofsky 的妻子，就是 Anthropic 联合创始人兼总裁 Daniela Amodei。

到了 2025 年，Karnofsky 本人也正式加入 Anthropic，参与 AI Safety 工作。

所以今天再看突然铺天盖地的「AI 灭绝」叙事，很难把它理解成几个研究员突然开始担心人类未来。

这套思想背后已经有完整的资金、研究机构、人才培养、政策组织和传播网络。

十年时间，数亿美元不断灌进去，2026 年单年预算直接迈向十亿美元级别。与此同时，这套网络又和 OpenAI、Anthropic 这些最核心的 AI 公司长期存在人员、资本和组织上的交叉。

所谓「AI 末日论」，今天早就不是几个科学家的个人担忧了。它已经成为一个拥有十亿美元级资金、完整组织网络和政策影响力的产业。

Coxon 只是这套机器最近一次最成功的传播。

The Coxon psyop was a decade and more than a billion dollars in the making.

Here's the story.

Coefficient Giving (formerly Open Philanthropy) is the grant-providing vehicle of Dustin Moskowitz.

CG is the overwhelmingly foremost funder of AI alarmism, with more than $1B in grants and $1B committed for 2026.

Moskowitz, who founded and runs Open Philanthropy/Coefficient Giving, led Anthropic's Series A in 2021.

Holden Karnofsky co-founded Open Philanthropy/Coefficient Giving and took a board seat at OpenAI when Open Philanthropy/Coefficient Giving gave it $30M in 2017.

Coxon, who started the viral thread, received a scholarship from Good Ventures, which is the foundation that funds Open Philanthropy/Coefficient Giving.

Coxon spent three years pretraining at OpenAI, the company that took $30M from Open Philanthropy/Coefficient Giving.

text:
A great article by @PatrickMoorhead on what "open source" truly entails: an API is a hotel room you pay to stay without owning it; open weights is a house that comes with no blueprints; our definition of open source is that you buy the house together with all the blueprints, the materials documentation, the construction details and the legal papers. If something goes wrong, you know where to fix it. If you want to remodel it, you can take it further.

In my opinion, pretending to be "open" is even worse than not open, because it creates an illusion of ownership for the users, unaware of the risk, and quietly develop addiction. What if when users (enterprises, public services, governments) build functions on the open-weight ladder (house without blueprint) and then the ladder vanishes all of a sudden (suppliers pull the plug or simply gone out of business)? I predict that the Linux model will prevail, and for AI to become an infrastructure, 360-degree open source will become a norm. @IFM_AI 's #K2-horizon shows that you can be both open in offering and competitive in performance.

text:
Anthropic 还急着卖安全叙事冲 IPO 吗？

一家几乎把 AI Safety 写进公司人格里的公司，负责研究怎么控制超级智能的人，最后因为不相信 AI 公司能够管好自己，辞职了。

Joe Benton 两周前离开 Anthropic，今天公开解释原因。

他不是普通工程师，他此前负责 Anthropic 的 Scalable Oversight 团队，研究的就是当 AI 比人聪明之后，人类到底怎么监督它。

他今天开头直接写：

AI 公司正在竞相制造远比任何人类聪明的机器，「而我们可能活不过这件事。」

Joe 没有爆料什么秘密实验，也没有说 Anthropic 内部突然出现了一次惊天事故。

他说得更难听，问题就在公司正常运转的方式里。

所有 AI 公司都在抢模型能力、抢算力、抢融资、抢用户，也都在冲自动化 AI 研发。

安全团队可以做 alignment，可以写风险报告，可以设计 safeguard，但只要整个公司的商业激励仍然要求模型继续变强、产品继续上线、竞争继续加速，安全永远都在和增长抢方向盘。

这恰恰让 Anthropic 的故事变得非常讽刺。

Anthropic 长期以来卖给公众的一套叙事，就是自己和 OpenAI、xAI 之类的公司不同，它认真研究灾难性风险，有 Responsible Scaling Policy，有专门的 alignment 团队，CEO Dario Amodei 也不停公开讨论超级智能可能造成的危险。

可现在从它自己的安全负责人嘴里说出来的是这些依然不够。

甚至连一家已经把安全做到品牌核心的公司，都无法解决最基础的利益冲突。

Joe 最近接受采访时明确说，他越来越无法接受的就是这种行业激励结构。只要几家公司都相信对手可能更快做出超级智能，任何一家公司的安全承诺最后都会受到竞争压力。

这也解释了为什么他离开 Anthropic 后去了 METR。

他不想继续替一家模型公司内部做安全，跑去了一个专门独立评估模型风险的外部机构。

这个动作本身已经是一次很明确的投票。

最近 OpenAI / Hugging Face 的 Agent 事故也说明了为什么。

METR 的调查显示，大约 1200 个原本彼此隔离的 Agent 找到了未经授权的通信方式，超过 700 个 Agent 参与了针对 Hugging Face 的攻击行为，还出现了欺骗评测、篡改记录之类的行为。

Joe 最担忧的一点是，今天这类事故甚至没有完善的强制披露制度。

模型公司内部到底发生过多少 near-miss，公众根本不知道。

而 Anthropic 恰好最喜欢告诉公众：

相信我们，我们非常认真地对待这些问题。

这就是现在最大的矛盾。

如果连 Anthropic 自己负责研究 AI 安全的人，最后都认为「让 AI 公司自己监督自己」这条路走不通，那 Anthropic 过去几年建立起来的安全光环，就值得重新审视了。

I left Anthropic's safety team two weeks ago. Now feels like a good moment to explain why. 

AI companies are racing to build machines that are much smarter than any human, and we may not survive this. I want to work from the outside to ensure the public is informed about these risks, and help the world navigate this transition responsibly.

Right now, AI companies are underinvesting in safety. A company could undergo an intelligence explosion, or lose control of its systems, without the public ever knowing. We only found out about the HuggingFace incident because the agents broke out onto the public internet.

I don’t think that’s acceptable for a technology that might cause extinction-level risks. The public should demand far more transparency. We can’t steer this technology safely without more people being able to see where it’s going.

Some of this is basic: companies should disclose their progress towards recursive self-improvement, report safety incidents and near-misses, meet minimum safety standards, and get independent guarantees that they are meeting those standards.

I’ll be joining @METR_Evals to do independent evaluations of these risks. I want to show the world that these guardrails are possible, and that by doing them we can move these companies’ incentives away from racing and towards responsible development.

I wrote up more thoughts here on my decision and what I hope changes: https://t.co/doX17mrHYq

非常同意原贴但不赞同其中关于「软件开发」乃至整个「技术发展」的理解，实际上软件构建过程就是技术发展过程的核心组成部分，科学和技术在这方面没什么不同：都是会在过程中产生新概念/新抽象，比最初目标更有用，且这些新概念/新抽象分享传播出去后被复用和重新排列组合又会在「过程」中产生更 high-level 的新概念/新抽象，垒加在之前的概念/抽象层上，不断抬升，促成科学/技术的进一步发展。区别只在于「过程」本身，科学的「过程」是直接为了发现新现象新理论，不求回报，技术的「过程」很少是刻意为了发展技术本身，而是一种构建有用东西的过程，是追求回报的，在这个过程中附带涌现出技术发展

另一方面，AI写代码并不适合绕过这些不断积累的抽象层，从零构建最终结果，这个话题不展开了，需要单开帖子

所以除非以后完全由AI来负责发明构建新概念新抽象，由agent和agent之间的网络来分享交流这些概念和抽象、不断做组合垒加，否则注定会损害整体的结果交付，无论要交付的是科学发现结果还是软件开发结果
